pools.title: Asking the Computational Question
pools.covers: reading §3.0 (the unnumbered opening), §3.1.1 · lecture 3.1 slides one_cell_three_questions, not_a_ladder

items.stem: What is the computational question about neurons, as this chapter asks it?

options.text: What problem was being solved when neurons evolved, and for whom that difference mattered enough to be selected.
options.why: Correct. A computational question asks what problem a thing addresses and why solving it matters, which for a biological structure means asking what favored it.

options.text: What procedure a neuron follows when it takes signals in, combines them, and passes one signal along to other cells.
options.why: That is the algorithmic question, asked in §3.2. It is about how the job is done rather than about which job is worth doing.

options.text: What physical material a neuron is built from, and by what means that material carries a signal from one end to the other.
options.why: That is the implementational question, asked in §3.3. It is about the stuff and the mechanism rather than about the problem.

options.text: Which regions of a nervous system contain the most neurons, and how that distribution differs between one species and another.
options.why: That is a descriptive anatomical question. Counting where neurons are does not say what having them solves for the animal.

items.stem: Which pair of disciplines does this chapter name as the ones that answer questions about what a biological structure was selected for?

options.text: evolutionary biology and ecology
options.why: Correct. Each of the chapter's three sections names its level and its discipline as it opens, and §3.1 opens with these two.

options.text: cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence
options.why: Those are the disciplines the chapter attaches to the algorithmic level, where the question is what procedure the cell follows.

options.text: neuroscience and molecular biology
options.why: Neuroscience is the discipline the chapter attaches to the implementational level, where the question is what physical stuff does the work.

options.text: comparative anatomy and paleontology
options.why: Both study the history of biological form, but neither is the pairing this chapter names for computational-level questions.

items.stem: The chapter asks three questions about the neuron, one per level of Marr's framework. Which arrangement matches each level to the question it asks?

options.text: The computational level asks why neurons evolved, the algorithmic what a neuron computes, and the implementational how a living cell manages it and at what cost.
options.why: Correct. The three sections map one to one onto Marr's three levels, and the chapter announces the correspondence in its opening.

options.text: The computational level asks what a neuron computes, the algorithmic how a cell physically manages it, and the implementational why neurons evolved in the first place.
options.why: The three questions are right and the order is wrong. The chapter runs computational, then algorithmic, then implementational.

options.text: The computational level asks how a cell physically manages signaling, the algorithmic why neurons evolved, and the implementational what a single neuron computes.
options.why: This reverses the chapter's order entirely. The implementational account comes last, once the functional description exists to be explained.

options.text: The computational level asks what a neuron is made of, the algorithmic which animals have neurons, and the implementational how many neurons a human brain holds.
options.why: None of these three is one of Marr's levels. Counting neurons and listing which animals have them are descriptive questions rather than explanatory ones.

items.stem: A student writes that a neuron exists "in order to let animals think faster." What is wrong with that answer, on the chapter's account?

options.text: It states a purpose without saying who benefited, and a structure in a living thing is explained by the descendants its bearers left rather than by an aim.
options.why: Correct. Living things have no designer, so the only non-magical answer to "what is it for?" is a historical one about differential reproduction.

options.text: It names a benefit that is too small, since the real advantage of having neurons is the ability to store memories over a lifetime.
options.why: The size of the benefit is not the problem, and memory is not what §3.1 identifies as the pressure. The form of the explanation is what fails.

options.text: It applies to the whole animal rather than to a single cell, and the computational level only ever describes structures smaller than an organ.
options.why: Marr's computational level applies at any scale. §3.1 aims the question at a cell type on purpose, and that is not the error here.

options.text: It describes a procedure rather than a physical mechanism, and a computational answer has to say which molecules carry out the work.
options.why: Naming molecules is the implementational level's business. A computational answer is not improved by adding chemistry to it.

items.stem: How does this module extend the logic of natural selection beyond the way Module 2 used it?

options.text: Module 2 pointed that logic at species and at the traits species have; this module points the same three-part logic at a kind of cell.
options.why: Correct. The move is to treat a cell type as an adaptation in exactly the sense Module 2 gave the word, with nothing new added to the logic.

options.text: Module 2 pointed that logic at individual organisms; this module points it at whole populations changing over many generations.
options.why: Selection has always operated on populations rather than individuals, and Module 2 said so. Nothing about the unit of selection changes here.

options.text: Module 2 described selection as a force pushing populations toward better designs; this module replaces that with an account based on energy.
options.why: Module 2 rejected the force picture rather than teaching it, and §3.1 inherits the rejection rather than correcting anything.

options.text: Module 2 studied traits that can be observed directly; this module restricts the logic to traits that leave a fossil record behind them.
options.why: The fossil record plays no part in the argument, and §3.1 reasons about cells that fossilize hardly at all.

items.stem: A reader finishes the evolutionary account and concludes that animals are further along than plants because animals evolved neurons and plants did not. Which correction does the chapter make?

options.text: Neurons are an expensive solution to a problem only some ways of living face, so lacking them is a different strategy rather than a lower rung.
options.why: Correct. The section walks forward through time, which reads easily as walking upward, and it blocks that reading explicitly.

options.text: Plants do have neurons, but they are so slow and so sparsely distributed that they were not recognized as neurons until recently.
options.why: Plants have no neurons at all. The chapter's point is that they solve the coordination problem another way, not that they solve it the same way badly.

options.text: Animals evolved earlier than plants did, so the comparison is really between an older lineage and a younger one rather than between two rungs of any ladder.
options.why: The relative timing is not the chapter's argument, and reordering the two lineages would leave the ladder reading intact anyway.

options.text: Neurons appeared in plants and were later lost, because the energy they consumed could not be met by a diet built on sunlight alone.
options.why: No such loss is described anywhere in the chapter. Plants are the standing counterexample to the ladder rather than a lineage that fell off it.

items.stem: In the chapter's opening sentence, what is a neuron said to be?

options.text: The cell that turns an event into a fast, precisely aimed signal.
options.why: Correct. Speed and aim are the two properties the opening picks out, and both are cashed as the trade §3.1.7 describes.

options.text: The cell that stores an animal's memories and retrieves them later.
options.why: Storage is not what the opening claims for the cell, and how a connection changes with experience is held over to Module 5.

options.text: The cell that converts food into the energy an animal's body runs on.
options.why: That describes metabolic machinery. Neurons are unusually large spenders of that energy rather than producers of it.

options.text: The cell that divides most rapidly during an animal's early development.
options.why: Rate of division is not what defines the cell, and the chapter never makes a claim about how fast neurons divide.

items.stem: The chapter names two facts about the neuron that organize everything that follows. Which two are they?

options.text: Neurons are the animal's answer to chemical signaling being too slow, and neurons are the body's first great metabolic outlier.
options.why: Correct. The first fact drives §3.1 and §3.2, and the second is the thread that runs from §3.1's opening through §3.3's close.

options.text: Neurons are the only cells capable of processing information, and neurons are the most numerous cell type in an animal's body.
options.why: Both are false in the chapter's terms: §3.1.3 says single cells processed information long before neurons, and neuron counts are not claimed as a maximum.

options.text: Neurons are the fastest-dividing cells in the body, and neurons are the cells most likely to be replaced across an animal's lifetime.
options.why: Neither claim appears in the chapter, and replacement over a lifetime is not a topic the module takes up at all.

options.text: Neurons are unique to vertebrates, and neurons are what allowed multicellular bodies to arise in the first place.
options.why: Both are contradicted: the chapter's worked example is an invertebrate worm, and multicellularity precedes neurons in its narrative.

items.stem: The chapter says the story it opens with and the story it closes with are the same story. What makes them one story rather than two?

options.text: Both are about the same energy budget: the opening asks how life got rich enough to afford neurons, and the close asks what running them still costs.
options.why: Correct. The energy thread is the chapter's spine, and stating it as a single arc is what keeps §3.3's accounting from reading as a separate topic.

options.text: Both are about the same cell type: the opening introduces the neuron and the close returns to it after a long detour through other kinds of cell.
options.why: Every section of the chapter is about the neuron, so sharing a subject would not make the opening and the close one continuous story.

options.text: Both are about the same time period, since the origin of neurons and the modern brain's metabolism are studied by the same methods.
options.why: They concern very different time scales, and no shared method is claimed. The connection the chapter draws is about cost, not about dating.

options.text: Both are about the same misconception, since each of the two passages opens by correcting the idea that evolution climbs steadily toward greater complexity.
options.why: The anti-ladder warning appears in both halves, but it is a discipline the chapter keeps rather than the arc it says the two stories share.

items.stem: The chapter says the comparison between biological and artificial neurons will be pressed hardest at one particular point. Where does it say the two differ most?

options.text: In what they are made of, rather than in what they compute.
options.why: Correct. The opening states the divergence in advance, and §3.3.9 is where the substrate difference is finally worked out in detail.

options.text: In how many of them a working system needs, rather than in how each one behaves.
options.why: Numbers come up in the energy comparison, but scale is not named as the place the resemblance breaks down.

options.text: In how quickly each one can be built, rather than in how either one operates.
options.why: Ease of construction is not a comparison the chapter draws anywhere, at either level.

options.text: In which one came first historically, rather than in how closely the two resemble each other.
options.why: The chapter does say the artificial unit was copied from the biological one, but priority is not where it locates the strain.

items.stem: Stated one level at a time, what is the neuron's problem at the computational level, and what is it at the implementational level?

options.text: Computationally, fast and reliable long-distance signaling for an animal that must act before something else does; implementationally, ion gradients across a membrane, a pump, and the action potential.
options.why: Correct. The first names a problem the animal way of life poses, and the second names the physical means by which a cell answers it.

options.text: Computationally, ion gradients across a membrane and the sodium-potassium pump; implementationally, signaling fast enough for an animal to act in time.
options.why: The two answers have been swapped. Gradients and pumps are physical means, which places them at the implementational level.

options.text: Computationally, receiving and integrating inputs against a threshold; implementationally, producing an all-or-nothing spike at a set rate.
options.why: Both of these belong to the algorithmic level, which is the middle row of the chapter's table rather than either of the outer two.

options.text: Computationally, deciding which behavior an animal should produce; implementationally, storing the outcome of that decision for later use.
options.why: Neither describes what the chapter puts in those rows, and storage over time is Module 5's subject rather than this module's.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the chapter says that asking what a neuron is for is the same as asking what selective pressure favored building one.
items.answer: Living things have no designer, so a purpose cannot have been assigned to any structure in advance. The only account of what a biological structure is for that does not appeal to magic is a historical one: the structure is here because the organisms that had it left more descendants than the organisms that did not. So a claim about what a neuron is for is really a claim about what made having one pay, which is a claim about selective pressure.
rubric: States that living things have no designer, so purpose cannot be assigned in advance.
Gives the historical form of the answer: the structure persists because its bearers left more descendants.
Draws the equivalence explicitly, so that a "what for" question becomes a "what favored it" question.
Avoids treating the neuron as an improvement or an achievement rather than a solution to a particular problem.

items.stem: The chapter walks forward through time, from chemistry to cells to animals, and then warns that the walk is not a climb. In a short paragraph, explain what the warning rules out and why plants are the example it uses.
items.answer: The warning rules out reading the sequence as a ranking, with the lineages that ended up with neurons counted as further along and the ones without them counted as having failed at something. What the sequence actually records is that an expensive solution became available and that some lineages took it, because the way they made a living made it worth the price. Plants are the example because they are complex, multicellular and successful without neurons at all: by every measure that matters to a plant, having no nervous system costs it nothing.
rubric: Names what the warning rules out: reading the forward walk as a ranking or an achievement.
States that neurons are an expensive solution to a particular problem rather than a general improvement.
Uses plants as a lineage that is doing fine without neurons rather than one that failed to evolve them.
Connects the availability of the solution to the way a lineage makes its living, rather than to how advanced it is.

items.stem: The lecture contrasts asking a computational question about a machine with asking one about a living thing. What is the difference?

options.text: For a machine somebody built it and had something in mind; for a living thing there is no designer, so the question has to be answered historically.
options.why: Correct. That is why the only non-magical answer names the descendants a structure's bearers left rather than anyone's intention.

options.text: For a machine the answer is settled by measurement, while for a living thing it can only ever be a matter of informed speculation about the distant past.
options.why: The lecture does not treat the biological answer as speculative; it treats it as a different kind of answer with its own evidence.

options.text: For a machine the computational question is the only one worth asking, while a living thing needs all three of Marr's levels to be understood.
options.why: Marr's three levels apply to machines as readily as to organisms, and the course uses them that way throughout.

options.text: For a machine the question is about what it was sold to do, while for a living thing it is about what the organism itself is trying to achieve.
options.why: Attributing an aim to the organism is the teleology the lecture spends its next minutes ruling out.

items.stem: The lecture opens by saying the shape of the module is the shape of every module from here to the end of the course. What is that shape?

options.text: One capacity, three sections in the reading, three meetings, one per level.
options.why: Correct. Module 3 is where Module 1's promise starts being kept, and the levels table gets its first reprint with a new example.

options.text: One capacity examined in three different species, one per meeting.
options.why: That is Module 2's comparative structure rather than the Marr structure this module introduces.

options.text: Three capacities examined at one level each, to cover more ground.
options.why: The arrangement is the reverse: one capacity gets all three levels, which is what makes the rhythm repeatable.

options.text: Three readings and one meeting, with the lectures filling the gaps.
options.why: The correspondence is one section to one lecture to one level, not a division of labor between reading and class.

items.stem: The lecture rejects the ladder as a picture of evolutionary history and offers branching in its place. What does branching assert that a ladder denies?

options.text: That plants, fungi and animals sit at the same height from one eukaryotic beginning, and only one branch built neurons.
options.why: Correct. The lecture asks the room to hold that picture for the whole hour, because the walk forward through time reads so easily as a walk upward.

options.text: That the three lineages arrived at neurons independently, which makes their shared possession of them a case of convergent evolution.
options.why: Only one of the three ever built neurons; convergence would require at least two arrivals at the same solution.

options.text: That animals branched off most recently, so the apparent ranking is really a statement about when each lineage appeared.
options.why: Recency is not what the figure shows, and reordering the branches by date would leave the ladder reading untouched.

options.text: That the three lineages are still competing, and which one ends up at the top has not been settled by the evidence yet.
options.why: A contest with an outcome still pending is the ladder picture in another form rather than an alternative to it.

items.stem: The lecture names two facts that organize the whole module, and tells the room to hold on to one of them in particular. Which one, and why?

options.text: That neurons are extraordinarily expensive to run, because it is the thread tying the far ends of the module together.
options.why: Correct. The story opening this lecture and the story closing the third are the same story, told at two ends of one arc.

options.text: That neurons are the animal's answer to a speed problem, because everything in the remaining two lectures follows from that problem.
options.why: That is the first of the two facts. The lecture singles out the expense as the one to carry forward.

options.text: That neurons are the only cells that process information, because the rest of the module depends on that being true of them alone.
options.why: The lecture is emphatic that neurons invented neither information processing nor behavior.

options.text: That neurons are named after the unit in artificial intelligence, because the comparison runs to the end of the course.
options.why: The naming runs the other way, and it is introduced as a second thread rather than as one of the two organizing facts.

items.stem: The lecture says a computational question about a machine has an easy answer and one about a living thing does not. In a few sentences, explain the difference and what the biological answer looks like instead.
items.answer: For a machine, somebody built it and had something in mind, so what it is for is settled by the intention behind it. A living thing has no designer, and nobody had anything in mind, so no intention is available to appeal to. The only answer that does not appeal to magic is a historical one: the structure is here because the organisms that had it left more descendants than the organisms that did not. So asking what a neuron is for turns into asking what selective pressure favored building one, which is a question about the past rather than about a purpose.
rubric: States that a machine has a designer whose intention settles what it is for.
States that living things have no designer, so no intention is available.
Gives the historical form of the biological answer, in terms of descendants left.
Restates the question as one about selective pressure rather than about purpose.

pools.title: From Chemistry to Cells
pools.covers: reading §3.1.2, §3.1.3 · lecture 3.1 slides before_there_were_cells, a_boundary, behavior_is_older

items.stem: What is a cell, on the definition the chapter gives before the origin-of-life story begins?

options.text: A bounded, organized system of chemistry that maintains and repairs itself, takes energy and materials from its surroundings, and belongs to a lineage that can make more cells.
options.why: Correct. Each clause does work: the boundary, the self-maintenance, the traffic with the environment, and the lineage.

options.text: Any collection of organic molecules held together by a membrane, whether or not that collection is able to repair itself or reproduce.
options.why: A membrane is one of the four requirements rather than the whole of it, and §3.1.3 is explicit that early vesicles were not yet cells.

options.text: The smallest unit of living matter that contains a nucleus, which is what separates living material from the chemistry around it.
options.why: Nuclei are a later development. §3.1.5 introduces them as what distinguishes eukaryotes from the cells that came before them.

options.text: A system of chemistry capable of copying its own genetic material, which is the single property that marks the boundary of life.
options.why: Copying alone is what the replicating molecules of §3.1.2 already did, and the chapter says plainly that they were not yet cells.

items.stem: Which hypothesis does the chapter name as one leading account of the transition from lifeless chemistry to life?

options.text: the RNA-world hypothesis
options.why: Correct. It is offered as one leading hypothesis about that transition, and the chapter is careful to say it is not a settled finding.

options.text: the endosymbiotic hypothesis
options.why: That is §3.1.5's account of how eukaryotes arose, long after life already existed, rather than an account of life's beginning.

options.text: the Great Oxygenation Event
options.why: That is an episode in Earth's history described in §3.1.4, and it is a mass extinction rather than a hypothesis about origins.

options.text: the last universal common ancestor
options.why: LUCA is a population the chapter reconstructs, and it explicitly marks a point well after life began rather than the beginning.

items.stem: A student's summary reads: "Life on Earth began with RNA." What does the chapter actually commit to?

options.text: That the RNA-world hypothesis is one leading account, that simpler chemical systems may have come first, and that how RNA arose is unresolved.
options.why: Correct. The section teaches something genuinely unsettled and hedges it three ways, and those hedges are part of the claim.

options.text: That RNA was certainly the first replicating molecule, but that the conditions under which it formed have not been established yet.
options.why: The chapter does not settle which molecule was first. Saying only the conditions are open overstates what it commits to by a long way.

options.text: That life began with DNA and that RNA appeared some time afterward, once the copying of longer sequences had become reliable enough to be genuinely useful.
options.why: §3.1.3 puts DNA after RNA in the standard account, so this reverses the order the chapter gives.

options.text: That the question is not answerable in principle, because no evidence from that period could survive to the present in any form.
options.why: The chapter says no surviving evidence tells us exactly when or where, which is narrower than saying the question cannot be answered.

items.stem: What makes RNA remarkable, in the role the RNA-world hypothesis assigns it?

options.text: It can both carry information in its sequence and, folded into certain shapes, speed up chemical reactions.
options.why: Correct. Doing both jobs is what lets one kind of molecule stand in for what later became two separate systems.

options.text: It is far more stable than DNA, so a sequence written in it survives for much longer without being repaired by anything.
options.why: §3.1.3 says the opposite: DNA was less vulnerable to spontaneous breakdown, which is why information later moved into it.

options.text: It can pass through a membrane freely, so an early cell could exchange genetic material with its neighbors at very little cost.
options.why: Membrane passage is not a property the chapter attributes to RNA, and §3.1.3 says the longer strands were what membranes retained.

options.text: It assembles itself without any external source of energy, which is what allowed it to form on a planet that had no life on it.
options.why: The chapter names sunlight, discharges, impacts, geothermal heat and chemical gradients as the energy that drove those reactions.

items.stem: The chapter concludes that evolution may have begun before cells did. What supports that conclusion?

options.text: Copies resembling their templates give inheritance, imperfect copying gives variation, and differential survival gives selection — all available to molecules.
options.why: Correct. The three ingredients of Darwinian evolution are the whole of the requirement, and none of them needs a cell.

options.text: Fossil evidence of pre-cellular replicating systems has been recovered from rocks that formed before the earliest known cells.
options.why: No such evidence is claimed. The chapter says explicitly that nothing surviving tells us exactly when or where any of this happened.

options.text: Cells are too complicated to have arisen without a period of selection acting on their component parts one at a time.
options.why: This is an argument the chapter does not make, and it assumes the conclusion it would need to establish.

options.text: Modern viruses reproduce without cells of their own, which shows that cellular machinery was never required for evolution.
options.why: Viruses are not discussed anywhere in the chapter, and they depend on host cells rather than doing without them.

items.stem: Replicating molecules were missing one thing that a cell has. What was it, and what did acquiring it buy?

options.text: A boundary. A membrane retained the longer strands, kept cooperating molecules together, and let selection act on the whole package.
options.why: Correct. Once a vesicle could grow and split, the unit selection worked on became the package rather than the naked molecules.

options.text: A source of energy. A membrane let the enclosed molecules capture sunlight, so a replicating system could power its own copying.
options.why: Photosynthesis arrives much later, in §3.1.4, and is not what enclosure is said to have provided.

options.text: A genetic code. A membrane concentrated the molecules enough for a stable mapping between sequence and protein to become established.
options.why: The code is credited to LUCA's era rather than to enclosure, and the chapter does not tie its origin to the membrane.

options.text: A means of movement. A membrane gave the enclosed system a surface that a protein motor could push against to relocate it.
options.why: Motility appears in the chemotaxis example, in cells that already exist, rather than as what enclosure first bought.

items.stem: In the division of labor that settled in early cells, which job does each of the three molecule types hold?

options.text: DNA stores the instructions, RNA copies them and uses them to build proteins, and proteins became the principal catalysts.
options.why: Correct. RNA keeps some of its earlier catalytic roles, which is why the chapter says it retained rather than surrendered them.

options.text: DNA catalyzes the cell's chemistry, RNA stores the instructions long-term, and proteins carry copies between compartments.
options.why: This assigns each molecule the wrong job. Catalysis is what proteins took over, and long-term storage is what moved to DNA.

options.text: RNA stores the instructions, DNA copies them under changing conditions, and proteins hold the whole arrangement together physically.
options.why: The storage and copying roles are reversed here, and structural support is not the role the chapter gives proteins.

options.text: Proteins store the instructions, DNA reads them out, and RNA builds the membrane that keeps the whole system enclosed.
options.why: None of the three is assigned correctly, and membranes are built from fatty molecules rather than from RNA.

items.stem: What is LUCA, as the chapter describes it?

options.text: The ancestral population from which all cellular life alive today descends, already possessing the genetic code, ribosomes, protein enzymes and a complex metabolism.
options.why: Correct. LUCA marks the deepest common ancestor that surviving organisms let us reconstruct, not the beginning of life.

options.text: The first living organism on Earth, and the point at which lifeless chemistry crossed the threshold into biology for the first time.
options.why: The chapter says explicitly that LUCA was not the first life and that considerable evolution had occurred before it.

options.text: The single cell whose descendants split into the three domains, and from which every gene now in existence was directly copied.
options.why: LUCA was not necessarily a single organism, and the chapter treats it as an ancestral population rather than an individual.

options.text: The earliest eukaryote, formed when one cell engulfed another and kept it as an internal compartment for aerobic respiration.
options.why: That describes endosymbiosis in §3.1.5, which happens long after LUCA and produces a very different kind of cell.

items.stem: A swimming E. coli moves toward a nutrient without a nervous system of any kind. What is it actually doing?

options.text: Comparing the concentration it meets now against the concentration a few seconds ago, and continuing if things are improving or tumbling if they are worsening.
options.why: Correct. The comparison is over time rather than across the cell's body, which is what makes a single cell enough to do it.

options.text: Detecting which side of its body the concentration is higher on, and steering toward that side by bending its whole length toward it.
options.why: The chapter describes a comparison across time rather than across the cell. A bacterium is far too small for a spatial gradient of that kind.

options.text: Releasing a chemical signal that other bacteria respond to, so that the population as a whole drifts toward the richer patch of water.
options.why: Signaling between bacteria is not part of this example, and the behavior described is an individual cell's own movement.

options.text: Growing preferentially on the side where the nutrient is denser, in the way a plant grows toward a source of light over hours.
options.why: Growth toward a stimulus is the plant strategy §3.1.6 contrasts with the animal one, and it is not how the bacterium moves.

items.stem: Given that single cells were already sensing and acting billions of years before neurons, what did neurons actually add?

options.text: A specialized way of moving information rapidly between distant parts of a multicellular body, so many cells could act as one.
options.why: Correct. The loop itself is old, and what was new is getting its results across a body quickly enough to matter.

options.text: The ability to respond to the environment at all, which no cell could do before a nervous system existed to detect changes.
options.why: This is exactly what the section denies. A single cell closes the sensing-and-acting loop using receptors, signaling pathways and a motor.

options.text: The capacity to store information over time, which single cells had no mechanism for and which behavior of any complexity requires.
options.why: Cells already stored and used information genetically, and storage is not the addition §3.1.3 credits to neurons.

options.text: A way of processing information, which is a different operation from the chemistry that had been going on inside cells until then.
options.why: The chapter names two senses in which cells already processed information, and says neurons invented neither of them.

items.stem: The chapter says early cells were processing information in two different senses. What distinguishes the two senses?

options.text: One is sensory: reading the surroundings and changing behavior. The other is genetic: transcribing DNA into RNA and translating RNA into proteins.
options.why: Correct. Both were present in cellular life, and the chapter is careful to say they are different operations rather than one.

options.text: One happens inside the cell and one happens outside it, since a cell is able to process only the information that its own membrane has already admitted.
options.why: Location is not the distinction drawn, and both operations described are internal to the cell.

options.text: One is fast and one is slow, and the difference in speed is what later made a specialized signaling cell worth the cost of building.
options.why: Speed is §3.1.7's argument about diffusion, not the difference between these two senses of processing.

options.text: One is inherited and one is learned, so that a cell could acquire new sensory responses within its own lifetime.
options.why: Learning within a lifetime is not claimed for these cells, and it is a Module 5 topic rather than a §3.1.3 one.

items.stem: Which term names a bacterium's gradual movement toward nutrients and away from harmful substances, produced by comparing concentrations over time?

options.text: chemotaxis
options.why: Correct. The chapter uses it as the concrete case of a single cell closing the loop from sensing to acting on its own.

options.text: endosymbiosis
options.why: That is one cell engulfing another and keeping it, which §3.1.5 gives as the origin of eukaryotes rather than a form of movement.

options.text: saltatory conduction
options.why: That is the jumping of a spike from gap to gap along a myelinated axon, introduced much later in §3.3.5.

options.text: photosynthesis
options.why: That is using light to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, which is a way of capturing energy rather than of moving.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what LUCA is, how it differs from the first life on Earth, and why that difference matters for how the chapter tells its story.
items.answer: LUCA is the ancestral population from which all cellular life alive today descends, and it already had the genetic code, ribosomes, protein enzymes and a complex metabolism. It is not the first life, and not necessarily a single organism. The distinction matters because it means considerable evolution had already happened before LUCA: LUCA marks the deepest common ancestor that surviving organisms let us reconstruct, which is a limit on our evidence rather than a beginning in the history.
rubric: Identifies LUCA as an ancestral population rather than an individual organism.
States that it was not the first life, and that much evolution preceded it.
Names at least one of the features it already possessed.
Explains that LUCA marks the limit of what can be reconstructed rather than the start of the story.

items.stem: The chapter is careful to establish what neurons did not invent. In a short paragraph, say what was already in place before neurons and what remained for them to contribute.
items.answer: The loop of taking in information from the world, transforming it internally, and changing behavior in response was already billions of years old, and a single cell could close it using receptor proteins, signaling pathways and a protein motor — chemotaxis is the worked case. Cells were also processing information genetically. So neither behavior nor information processing was new. What neurons added was a specialized means of moving information rapidly between distant parts of a multicellular organism, so that many specialized cells could sense and act as one coordinated whole.
rubric: States that the sensing-and-acting loop long predates neurons, ideally naming chemotaxis or a single-celled case.
Notes that information processing of some kind was already present in cells.
Names the addition as rapid transmission between distant parts of a multicellular body.
Connects that addition to coordination across specialized cells rather than to behavior as such.

items.stem: The lecture draws out something about chemotaxis that the chapter leaves implicit. Comparing the concentration now against the concentration a few seconds ago requires what?

options.text: Something in the cell is holding a trace of the recent past, since the comparison is across time rather than across the cell's body.
options.why: Correct. The lecture stops on the point deliberately: a comparison between now and a few seconds ago can only be made by something that has kept the earlier value.

options.text: Something in the cell is comparing its front end against its back end, which is how the direction of the surrounding gradient is recovered.
options.why: The lecture describes a comparison between two moments rather than between two places, which is what makes a stored trace necessary.

options.text: Something in the cell is signaling to neighboring bacteria, so that the population can average its measurements together.
options.why: No communication between cells is part of this example; a single cell closes the whole loop by itself.

options.text: Something in the cell is counting the number of nutrient molecules it has encountered since it last divided.
options.why: A running total over that span would not distinguish improving conditions from worsening ones on the timescale involved.

items.stem: The lecture says a membrane buys three things at once. Which three?

options.text: It lets small building blocks pass while retaining longer strands, it keeps cooperating molecules together, and it shields them from being diluted away.
options.why: Correct. Once a vesicle could also grow and split, selection could act on the whole package rather than on naked molecules.

options.text: It supplies energy, it stores genetic information, and it catalyzes the reactions the enclosed molecules depend on to reproduce.
options.why: Those are jobs later taken by ATP, DNA and proteins respectively, none of which the boundary itself performs.

options.text: It protects against oxygen, it maintains a voltage, and it allows the enclosed system to move toward nutrients under its own power.
options.why: Oxygen and voltage both arrive much later in the story, and motility is not credited to enclosure.

options.text: It concentrates RNA, it excludes water entirely, and it prevents the enclosed molecules from being copied imperfectly.
options.why: Imperfect copying is the source of variation the account needs, so preventing it would remove the ingredient rather than supply one.

items.stem: Having traced the steps from replicating molecules to LUCA, the lecture tells the room to notice the overall shape of that account. What is the shape, and what does it answer?

options.text: Each stage keeps everything the stage before it had, so complexity accumulated rather than being assembled in one step — which answers the module's question about where a cell's complexity came from.
options.why: Correct. The lecture places that answer here rather than saving it for the close, so the accumulation reading is available for the rest of the hour.

options.text: Each stage replaces the one before it, so complexity arrived through a series of clean transitions from one kind of system to the next.
options.why: Replacement is precisely what the figure denies; every stage retains what preceded it.

options.text: Each stage is more energy-hungry than the last, so the sequence answers the question of why oxygen was needed before cells could exist.
options.why: Oxygen answers the module's second question, and it arrives well after cells rather than before them.

options.text: Each stage is better adapted than the last, so the sequence shows selection improving cellular systems toward a definite endpoint.
options.why: An endpoint of that kind is the ladder reading the previous slide spent its whole length rejecting.

items.stem: The lecture says it will be careful about what neurons contributed, and lists what they did not invent. What is on that list, and what is left over?

options.text: Neurons invented neither information processing nor behavior; what they added is moving information fast between distant parts of one body.
options.why: Correct. Both were in place billions of years earlier, closed inside a single cell by receptors, signaling pathways and a protein motor.

options.text: Neurons invented neither the membrane nor the energy currency; what they added is a way of spending that currency on a signal.
options.why: Membranes and ATP are indeed older, but they are not what this slide says neurons did not invent.

options.text: Neurons invented neither speed nor aim; what they added is the ability to send a message that can afterward be switched off.
options.why: Speed and aim are exactly what the trade buys, so listing them as pre-existing reverses the lecture's argument.

options.text: Neurons invented neither multicellularity nor specialization; what they added is a means of building bodies larger than a colony.
options.why: Both precede neurons, but the lecture's list names information processing and behavior, and body size is not the addition claimed.

items.stem: Walk through what a swimming bacterium has to do in order to perform chemotaxis, and say what the lecture concludes from the fact that one cell can manage it.
items.answer: It has to receive information from the world, through receptor proteins. It has to transform that information internally, by comparing the concentration now against the concentration a few seconds ago — a comparison across time, which means something in the cell is holding a trace of the recent past. And it has to change its behavior in response, using a protein motor: carrying on if conditions are improving, tumbling and setting off in a new direction if they are worsening. What the lecture concludes is that the whole sensing-and-acting loop is billions of years older than neurons and can be closed inside one cell, so neurons invented neither information processing nor behavior.
rubric: Names receiving through receptors, transforming internally, and acting through a motor.
Identifies the comparison as one across time rather than across the cell's body.
Gives the behavioral rule: continue if improving, tumble if worsening.
Concludes that the loop long predates neurons, so neurons invented neither behavior nor information processing.

pools.title: Energy, and What the Surplus Allowed
pools.covers: reading §3.1.4, §3.1.5, §3.1.6 · lecture 3.1 slides one_currency, poison_into_windfall, nothing_was_waiting, the_coordination_problem, three_ways_to_be_complex, sense_decide_act

items.stem: What is ATP?

options.text: A small molecule that stores energy in a chemical bond and releases it where the cell needs it.
options.why: Correct. Every cell runs its whole economy on making ATP and spending it, which is why the chapter calls it the currency.

options.text: A protein that drives sodium out of a cell and potassium in, against the direction those ions would otherwise drift.
options.why: That is the sodium-potassium pump of §3.3.2, which is one of the largest consumers of ATP rather than the molecule itself.

options.text: A sugar built out of carbon dioxide and water using the energy in sunlight, and stored for later breakdown by the cell.
options.why: That describes the product of photosynthesis. Sugar is broken down in order to make ATP rather than being ATP.

options.text: A gas released as waste by photosynthesis, which later became the best available acceptor of electrons stripped from food.
options.why: That is oxygen, whose story §3.1.4 tells alongside ATP but which plays a completely different part in the cell's economy.

items.stem: Which term names the small molecule that every cell uses as its single energy currency, storing energy in a chemical bond and releasing it where it is needed?

options.text: ATP
options.why: Correct. A cell's whole economy runs on making it and spending it, and once it was the currency it became very hard to replace.

options.text: RNA
options.why: RNA carries information and can catalyze reactions, and one of its building blocks happens to be the energy currency, but it is not that currency.

options.text: glutamate
options.why: That is the dominant excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, introduced in §3.3.5, and it carries signals rather than energy.

options.text: myelin
options.why: That is the fatty sheath wrapped around many axons in segments, which makes conduction faster and cheaper without storing any energy.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say ATP did not have to be invented to serve as the cell's energy currency?

options.text: It is one of the four building blocks RNA is assembled from, so it was already abundant and already carrying energy in its phosphate bonds.
options.why: Correct. The phosphates were what activated those building blocks so they could join into chains, which is the same energy the cell later spent.

options.text: It forms spontaneously in water whenever phosphate is present, so a cell never has to manufacture any of the ATP that it goes on to spend.
options.why: Cells make ATP continuously, and §3.1.4's whole account of chemiosmosis is a description of how that manufacture works.

options.text: It was carried into early cells by the engulfed bacteria that became mitochondria, so the currency arrived along with the machinery for making it.
options.why: Endosymbiosis comes much later, in §3.1.5, and the chapter puts ATP in place long before eukaryotes existed at all.

options.text: It is the simplest molecule that can hold energy at all, so any chemistry complex enough to store energy would have arrived at it eventually.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: why this particular nucleotide became the currency rather than one of the other three is still argued over.

items.stem: What makes phosphate bonds well suited to the job of storing a cell's energy?

options.text: They release a great deal of energy when broken, and they do not break on their own in water.
options.why: Correct. Both halves matter: without the second, stored energy would leak away instead of being spent when the cell chooses.

options.text: They break easily under almost any conditions, so a cell can always get at the energy in them without needing any machinery.
options.why: Bonds that broke on their own would make storage impossible. The point is that a cell decides when to break them.

options.text: They can be formed without any input of energy at all, which is what allows a cell to build up a reserve when food is scarce.
options.why: Making ATP means pushing phosphate groups together against their electrical repulsion, which is exactly what takes energy.

options.text: They bind tightly to the membrane, so the stored energy stays where it will be needed rather than diffusing away through the cell.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter attaches phosphate bonds to the membrane, and ATP is described as carrying energy to wherever it is needed.

items.stem: In the way early cells made ATP, what does the proton gradient across the membrane actually accomplish?

options.text: Protons pumped to one side flow back through a protein that spins, and the spinning pushes phosphate groups together against their repulsion.
options.why: Correct. Storing energy as a difference held across a barrier, then collecting it on the way back down, is the trick the dam comparison captures.

options.text: Protons crossing the membrane bind directly to sugar molecules and convert them into a form that the cell is then able to break down for the energy it needs.
options.why: Building sugar from carbon dioxide and water is photosynthesis, and it is a separate process from the gradient described here.

options.text: The gradient keeps the cell's interior negatively charged, which is what allows an electrical signal to travel along its surface.
options.why: That is the resting membrane potential of §3.3.2, a much later use of a gradient and one about readiness rather than manufacture.

options.text: The gradient repels oxygen from the interior of the cell, which protected early life from the poison that photosynthesis released.
options.why: Nothing of the kind is described. Oxygen's aggressiveness is answered by using it, not by keeping it out with a gradient.

items.stem: The chapter calls the earliest way of making ATP "ingenious and meager at once." What is the meager part?

options.text: It did not produce very much, so early life could make energy but remained energy poor.
options.why: Correct. That poverty is what makes the later oxygen windfall the turning point the rest of the chapter depends on.

options.text: It worked in only a few lineages, so most early cells had no way at all of storing the energy they took in from their surroundings.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: the scheme works in essentially every cell alive today, which is the ingenious half of the verdict.

options.text: It required sunlight, so cells living below the surface could not use it and were confined to the top few meters of water.
options.why: Light-driven energy capture is photosynthesis, which arrives afterward as a revolution rather than as the original meager scheme.

options.text: It destroyed the membrane a little more with each cycle, so a cell could only run it for a limited number of generations.
options.why: No such damage is described, and the chapter treats the arrangement as sustainable rather than self-limiting.

items.stem: Oxygen is described first as a catastrophe and then as a windfall. What single property of oxygen accounts for both?

options.text: Its chemical aggressiveness, which wrecks molecules not built to handle it and also makes it an unusually good acceptor of electrons.
options.why: Correct. The same property does both jobs, which is why the turn from poison to windfall is one fact rather than two.

options.text: Its abundance, which first suffocated the organisms that could not use it and later fed the ones that could.
options.why: The chapter's account turns on how oxygen reacts rather than on how much of it there was.

options.text: Its lightness, which let it escape into the atmosphere and so removed it from the water where early life was living.
options.why: Escape into the atmosphere is not the mechanism given, and it would not explain either the extinction or the energy gain.

options.text: Its stability, which meant that once oxygen had accumulated in the atmosphere it did not break down again, so its effects persisted across geological time.
options.why: Stability is close to the opposite of what the chapter attributes to oxygen, and it explains neither half of the story.

items.stem: Which process uses oxygen as the final acceptor of electrons stripped from food, and yields something like fifteen times as much ATP from a molecule of sugar as the older methods?

options.text: aerobic respiration
options.why: Correct. That multiple is the windfall out of which everything expensive life built afterward was paid for.

options.text: photosynthesis
options.why: That is building sugar out of carbon dioxide and water using light, which supplies the food rather than extracting energy from it.

options.text: endosymbiosis
options.why: That is one cell engulfing another and keeping it, which is how the compartments that perform respiration came to be inside cells.

options.text: the Great Oxygenation Event
options.why: That is an episode in Earth's history rather than a process in a cell: the accumulation of oxygen that made this process possible.

items.stem: The chapter warns against a misreading of the word affordable. Which statement is the one it rules out?

options.text: That complexity-increasing mutations were waiting to appear until enough energy existed to support them.
options.why: Correct. Such mutations arose all along and died out because they cost more than they returned; what changed was the arithmetic, not the variation.

options.text: That the same mutation could be worth keeping under one energy budget and not worth keeping under another one.
options.why: This is precisely what the chapter says happened, and it is the reason the arrival of oxygen mattered so much.

options.text: That natural selection compares only the variants that already exist rather than the ones that would be useful later.
options.why: That is the chapter's own statement of how selection works, offered as the reason the waiting picture is wrong.

options.text: That a large and reliable energy surplus can make arrangements affordable that were not affordable before it arrived.
options.why: That is the principle the section opens with, and the warning is about how to read it rather than a retraction of it.

items.stem: What is a eukaryote?

options.text: A cell with its DNA enclosed in a nucleus and its chemistry divided among internal compartments.
options.why: Correct. Plants, fungi and animals are all built from cells of this kind, which is what makes §3.1.6's three-way comparison fair.

options.text: A cell that has acquired the ability to use oxygen as the final acceptor of the electrons it strips from food.
options.why: Aerobic respiration precedes eukaryotes and is not confined to them, so using oxygen is not what the word picks out.

options.text: An organism made of many cells that stay together and function as one rather than living independently of each other.
options.why: That is multicellularity, which is a separate development and has arisen many times in lineages of this kind of cell.

options.text: A cell that carries no nucleus, and that keeps its genetic material loose in the same compartment as the rest of its chemistry.
options.why: That describes the kind of cell eukaryotes are contrasted with rather than eukaryotes themselves.

items.stem: On the account the chapter gives, where did mitochondria come from?

options.text: One cell engulfed another and, instead of digesting it, kept it; the engulfed oxygen-users became compartments for aerobic respiration.
options.why: Correct. That is endosymbiosis, and it is what lets a cell pay for a great deal more machinery than one without internal power plants.

options.text: A region of the cell's own membrane folded inward and closed off, forming a compartment specialized for extracting energy from food.
options.why: Infolding is not the origin the chapter gives, though it is a real proposal about other compartments in other accounts.

options.text: Free-living bacteria attached to the outside of larger cells and passed energy inward across the two membranes between them.
options.why: The chapter describes engulfment and retention rather than an external partnership, and the compartment ends up inside the cell.

options.text: The nucleus divided in two, and one of the resulting compartments went on to specialize in respiration while the other retained the cell's genetic material.
options.why: Nothing of the kind is described, and the nucleus and the mitochondria have quite separate origins in this account.

items.stem: What does multicellularity buy an organism, on the chapter's account?

options.text: Division of labor: cells can specialize, and a specialist is far better at its one job than a generalist is at any job.
options.why: Correct. The alternative is a body of cells that all do everything and are all mediocre at it.

options.text: Redundancy: if one cell fails, another with the same capabilities can take over the work it was doing before it failed.
options.why: Backup is not the advantage the chapter names, and it would not require specialization at all.

options.text: Size: a larger body is harder for a predator to consume, which is the pressure that made staying together worth the cost.
options.why: Predation drives §3.1.6's speed argument rather than the origin of multicellularity, and body size is not given as the payoff.

options.text: Longevity: a body of many cells outlives any single one of them, so information can be preserved across a much longer span.
options.why: No claim about lifespan is made here, and preserving information is credited to DNA rather than to multicellularity.

items.stem: What is the coordination problem?

options.text: Information gathered by one kind of cell has to reach a different kind entirely, in time to be useful, because the cells that must act cannot sense.
options.why: Correct. Specialization creates the problem: a colony of identical cells has nothing much to coordinate.

options.text: Cells in a body compete for a limited energy supply, and something has to decide which of them is allowed to spend it.
options.why: Competition for energy is not the problem named here, though energy as a constraint returns as a major theme in §3.3.

options.text: Cells at the surface of a body are exposed to the environment while cells inside it are not, so the two age at different rates.
options.why: Nothing about differential exposure or aging is part of this chapter's argument.

options.text: A body of specialized cells needs some way of making new cells of every type, so each of the specialists has to retain a full copy of the instructions.
options.why: Every cell carrying the full genome is true of biology, but it is not the problem §3.1.5 defines here.

items.stem: Which term names what specialization creates, in which what one kind of cell detects has to reach a different kind of cell in time to be acted on?

options.text: the coordination problem
options.why: Correct. Every complex multicellular organism has some version of it, and how urgent that version is depends on how the organism lives.

options.text: the sense to decide to act loop
options.why: That is the sequence an animal has to complete quickly, which is one urgent form the coordination problem takes rather than the problem itself.

options.text: division of labor
options.why: That is what specialization buys rather than the problem it creates, and it is the reason the difficulty exists at all.

options.text: multiple realizability
options.why: That is Module 1's claim that one function can run in different physical materials, and it has nothing to do with coordination.

items.stem: Two multicellular organisms are equally specialized, and one of them faces a far more urgent version of the coordination problem than the other. On the chapter's account, what settles which one?

options.text: How the organism makes its living, since a way of life that can go badly wrong in a second demands much faster coordination.
options.why: Correct. §3.1.6 turns this clause into its whole argument, and speed is the variable that separates animals from plants and fungi.

options.text: How many cells the organism has, since a larger body means a longer distance for any message to cross before it can be acted on.
options.why: Distance matters to §3.1.7's argument about diffusion, but the chapter makes urgency a question of the way of life rather than of body size.

options.text: How much energy the organism has available, since coordination is expensive and only a rich organism can afford to do it quickly.
options.why: Energy sets what is affordable rather than what is urgent, and the chapter treats the two as separate questions here.

options.text: How closely related the organism is to animals, since the machinery for fast coordination appears only in that one lineage.
options.why: Ancestry is what the three-way comparison holds constant rather than what explains the difference between the three strategies.

items.stem: What makes the chapter's comparison of plants, fungi and animals informative?

options.text: All three are complex, multicellular and descended from the same eukaryotic beginning, and only one of them evolved neurons.
options.why: Correct. Holding that much constant is what isolates the variable the section is looking for.

options.text: All three face identical pressures from predators, so any difference between them has to come from something internal.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: what separates animals is precisely that they eat and are eaten, which plants and fungi are not.

options.text: All three evolved neurons independently, which makes the comparison a case of convergence rather than of shared ancestry.
options.why: Only animals evolved neurons. The absence in the other two is the whole point of setting the three side by side.

options.text: All three are studied by the same methods, so any apparent difference between them cannot be an artifact of how they were measured.
options.why: Method is not what the section holds constant, and no measurement artifact is at issue in the comparison.

items.stem: How does setting plants, fungi and animals side by side mirror Module 2's more common use of the comparative method?

options.text: Module 2 more often asks why two things are alike; this section asks why three alike things differ.
options.why: Correct. Same method, run in the opposite direction, which is why the shared eukaryotic ancestry is what makes the question sharp.

options.text: Module 2 compares species; this section compares individuals within a single species across different environments.
options.why: No within-species comparison is made here. The three units compared are whole ways of making a living.

options.text: Module 2 compares living things; this section compares a living thing with an engineered one to see where the analogy fails.
options.why: The natural-artificial comparison is a separate thread, taken up at the end of §3.2 and again in §3.3.9.

options.text: Module 2 compares structures; this section compares the same structure at two different points in evolutionary time.
options.why: Nothing here is compared across time. All three strategies are contemporaries in the comparison as drawn.

items.stem: Comparing plants, fungi and animals, what separating variable does the chapter identify, and what makes it matter for animals in particular?

options.text: Speed, and it matters because animals eat other organisms and are eaten by them, so a response can be needed in a fraction of a second.
options.why: Correct. A plant threatened by drought has hours or days and answers with growth and chemistry, which is enough for a plant.

options.text: Size, and it matters because an animal's body is larger, so a signal has further to travel before it reaches the cells that must act.
options.why: Body size is not the variable the section isolates, and some plants are far larger than most animals.

options.text: Energy, and it matters because animals capture more of it than plants or fungi and can therefore afford more expensive machinery.
options.why: Animals do not out-earn plants in the chapter's account; the surplus that paid for neurons was available to all three lineages.

options.text: Reproduction, and it matters because animals produce fewer offspring, so each individual's survival counts for more in the next generation.
options.why: Reproductive strategy plays no part in the argument, and nothing about offspring number is claimed.

items.stem: What is the sense → decide → act loop?

options.text: Taking in information about the world, doing something with it, and producing an action fast enough for the action to still be the right one.
options.why: Correct. The final clause carries the weight: an action that arrives late is not merely slow, it is the wrong action.

options.text: The sequence by which a cell reads its DNA, copies it into RNA, and uses the result to build the proteins it needs.
options.why: That is the genetic sense of information processing §3.1.3 describes, which is a different operation entirely.

options.text: The cycle in which a neuron is depolarized by its arriving inputs, fires a single spike, and then waits out its refractory period before it can fire again.
options.why: That is the physical sequence of §3.3.3, and it happens within a single cell rather than between an animal and its world.

options.text: The process by which a population accumulates variation, some of it heritable, until selection has changed which variants are common.
options.why: That is natural selection as Module 2 gave it, running over generations rather than within a single animal's lifetime.

items.stem: Which term names taking in information about the world, doing something with it, and producing an action quickly enough for that action to still be the right one?

options.text: the sense to decide to act loop
options.why: Correct. It returns at the algorithmic level as what the neuron computes, and at the implementational level as what that computing costs.

options.text: the coordination problem
options.why: That is the difficulty specialization creates in a body, and this loop is one urgent form it takes rather than a name for it.

options.text: chemotaxis
options.why: That is a bacterium comparing nutrient concentrations over time, which is one instance of the loop rather than the general name for it.

options.text: saltatory conduction
options.why: That is a spike jumping between the bare gaps in a myelin sheath, a mechanism of transmission rather than a description of behavior.

items.stem: The chapter says the sense → decide → act loop is not a problem unique to living things. What follows from that, in the chapter's own terms?

options.text: Any system that has to operate on its own in a changing world faces some version of it, so a robot or a self-driving car needs its own answer.
options.why: Correct. The neuron is presented as evolution's answer rather than as the only possible one, which is what keeps the comparison open.

options.text: Machines built to face the loop will converge on designs that resemble neurons, since the problem admits of a single good solution.
options.why: The chapter treats the neuron as one answer among possible ones, and §3.3.9 argues that the two substrates force different architectures.

options.text: The loop must therefore have been present in the earliest replicating molecules, since even bare chemistry has to respond to an environment that changes.
options.why: The loop is credited to cells that sense and act rather than to bare replicators, and §3.1.3 is where it first appears.

options.text: Only living systems face the loop, since its urgency comes entirely from the threat of being eaten by something else.
options.why: Predation is what makes it urgent for animals, but the chapter states the problem in a form that covers systems facing no predators at all.

items.stem: In a predator-prey arms race, why does a small advantage in speed of response get amplified across generations?

options.text: The animal that senses, decides and acts slightly faster is the one that eats or the one that escapes, and both outcomes are written into the next generation.
options.why: Correct. Selection acts on the same margin from both directions at once, which is what makes the premium on speed relentless.

options.text: Faster animals grow larger, and larger animals produce more offspring, so speed spreads through the population indirectly.
options.why: No link between speed and size or fecundity is drawn. The advantage in the chapter's account is immediate and direct.

options.text: Predators evolve faster than prey do, so any speed advantage in a predator lineage is retained while the same advantage in prey is lost.
options.why: The chapter treats both sides symmetrically, and gives no lineage a higher rate of change than the other.

options.text: Speed is inherited more reliably than other traits, so a fast individual is more likely to have fast offspring than a strong one is.
options.why: Nothing about differential heritability is claimed, and the argument does not need it.

items.stem: Comparing plants, fungi and animals, the chapter asks what can go wrong in a second for each of the three lineages. What does the answer establish?

options.text: For a plant or a fungus very little can, while for an animal it is being eaten, losing prey, or a bad step — which is why only animals need fast coordination.
options.why: Correct. That comparison carries the reasoning that makes the difference in coordination follow rather than merely be listed alongside the other differences.

options.text: All three lineages face the same immediate hazards, and the difference between them lies in how quickly each can repair the damage afterward.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: what can go wrong in a second differs enormously across the three, which is the whole point of asking.

options.text: Plants face the most severe hazards of the three, since unlike animals they cannot move away from whatever threatens them.
options.why: Being rooted is part of the comparison, but the chapter concludes that very little goes wrong for a plant on the timescale of a second.

options.text: The hazards each lineage faces are unrelated to the kind of coordination it evolved, since coordination is set by body size instead.
options.why: The comparison exists precisely to connect the hazards to the coordination, and body size is not a factor it considers.

items.stem: What is the relationship between the oxygen windfall and everything expensive that life built afterward?

options.text: The windfall is what paid for it: after aerobic respiration, arrangements that had not been affordable became worth their price.
options.why: Correct. That relation is the chapter's energy thread, and it is what §3.3's accounting eventually returns to and closes.

options.text: The windfall made expensive arrangements unnecessary, since a cell with more energy has less need for elaborate machinery.
options.why: The chapter argues the reverse: a surplus is what makes elaborate machinery possible rather than what makes it redundant.

options.text: The windfall was a consequence of those arrangements, since more complex cells were able to extract more energy from the same food.
options.why: The order is reversed. Using oxygen came first and is what the later complexity was paid for out of.

options.text: The windfall was unrelated to them, since the arrangements in question are built from proteins rather than paid for in energy.
options.why: Everything a cell does costs energy, and the chapter opens §3.1.4 by saying so before naming the currency.

items.stem: Why does a colony of identical cells not face much of a coordination problem?

options.text: Nothing has been divided up, so no cell needs information that a different kind of cell is the only one able to gather.
options.why: Correct. The problem is created by specialization, which is why bones, muscles and skin are what it looks like once it has run for a while.

options.text: The colony is small enough that a chemical signal reaches every one of its cells in well under a second in any case.
options.why: Size is not what the chapter appeals to here, and colonies of identical cells are not claimed to be uniformly small.

options.text: The cells in a colony are genetically identical, so each of them independently reaches the same decision about what to do next.
options.why: Shared genetics does not produce shared information about the environment, and the chapter does not argue in this way.

options.text: Colonies coordinate through growth rather than through signaling, which is slower but requires nothing to be transmitted at all.
options.why: Growth as a response belongs to the plant strategy in §3.1.6, and it is not offered as how colonies avoid the problem.

items.stem: The chapter says that after oxygen, "the arithmetic changed underneath them." In a short paragraph, explain what did change and what did not, and why the distinction matters.
items.answer: What did not change was the variation. Mutations pushing toward greater complexity — a larger cell, an extra compartment, more machinery — arose before oxygen just as they always do, and they died out because they cost more energy than they returned. What changed was the energy available to pay for them, so that the very same variants were now worth keeping and their carriers left more descendants rather than fewer. The distinction matters because it blocks the reading in which life was waiting with plans it could not yet afford. Selection never looked ahead; it only ever compared the variants that already existed.
rubric: States that the complexity-increasing variation was present before oxygen and was being lost.
States that what changed was the available energy rather than the mutations themselves.
Explains the consequence: the same variant went from unaffordable to worth keeping.
Draws the anti-teleology point — selection compares existing variants and does not anticipate.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how comparing plants, fungi and animals isolates speed as the variable that explains neurons, and say what the comparison has to hold constant for that to work.
items.answer: The comparison holds constant almost everything that might otherwise explain the difference: all three lineages are complex, all three are multicellular, and all three descend from the same eukaryotic beginning. Against that shared background, only one of the three evolved neurons, so whatever separates that one is a candidate explanation. What separates animals is that they eat other organisms and are eaten by them, which means a response can be needed within a fraction of a second, where a plant facing drought has hours or days. Speed is therefore the variable left standing.
rubric: Names what the comparison holds constant: complexity, multicellularity and shared eukaryotic ancestry.
Notes that only one of the three lineages evolved neurons.
Identifies speed as the separating variable.
Grounds the speed premium in the animal way of making a living — eating and being eaten.

items.stem: Specialization is described as both an advantage and the source of a new problem. In a short paragraph, explain both halves.
items.answer: The advantage is division of labor. If every cell must do every job, every cell will probably be mediocre at all of them; if cells can specialize, each can be far better at its one job than any generalist could be at any job. The problem is that a body of specialists has to act as one thing, and the cells that must act on what a sensor detects cannot detect it themselves. So information gathered by one kind of cell has to reach a different kind entirely, and in time for it to be useful. That is the coordination problem, and how urgently it needs solving depends on how the organism makes its living.
rubric: Names division of labor as the advantage, with the generalist-versus-specialist contrast.
States that the sensing cells and the acting cells are different cells.
Names the coordination problem and includes the timing requirement.
Notes that the urgency of the problem varies with the organism's way of life.

items.stem: What does photosynthesis do, and what does it release as waste?

options.text: It uses light to build sugar out of carbon dioxide and water, and its waste product is oxygen.
options.why: Correct. It turns a renewable and enormous energy source into a storable chemical one, which is what makes the rest of §3.1 possible.

options.text: It uses light to break sugar down into carbon dioxide and water, and its waste product is a proton gradient across the membrane.
options.why: The direction is reversed: sugar is built here and broken down later, and a proton gradient is machinery rather than waste.

options.text: It uses oxygen to extract energy from sugar, and its waste product is the carbon dioxide the cell then releases into its surroundings.
options.why: That is aerobic respiration, which is the process oxygen later made possible rather than the one that produced the oxygen.

options.text: It uses chemical gradients to drive protons across a membrane, and its waste product is the heat released as they flow back down.
options.why: That is the older chemiosmotic scheme, which works everywhere but produces very little and releases no oxygen at all.

items.stem: Giving the yield of aerobic respiration, the lecture stops to tell the room that the ratio is the content. What point is it making?

options.text: Aerobic respiration yields something like fifteen times as much ATP from a molecule of sugar — not fifteen percent more.
options.why: Correct. The size of the multiple is what makes everything expensive that life built afterward affordable at all.

options.text: Aerobic respiration yields about fifteen percent more ATP, which compounds over evolutionary time into a very large advantage.
options.why: The lecture names this reading explicitly in order to rule it out; the gain is a multiple rather than a percentage.

options.text: Aerobic respiration is about fifteen times faster than the older methods, though it extracts the same total energy from the food.
options.why: The claim is about how much energy comes out of the same meal rather than about how quickly it comes out.

options.text: Aerobic respiration was adopted about fifteen times independently, which is why it is found in so many separate lineages today.
options.why: No count of independent origins is given, and the figure quoted is a yield rather than a tally.

items.stem: How does the lecture describe what happened to most life on Earth when oxygen accumulated?

options.text: A very large number of lineages were killed by pollution produced by other organisms.
