options.why: Correct. Framing the Great Oxygenation Event as pollution keeps the windfall from reading as progress: it was a catastrophe first.

options.text: A very large number of lineages adapted to oxygen quickly, which is why aerobic respiration is now nearly universal.
options.why: Adaptation came afterward and to some lineages; the immediate effect the lecture stresses is an extinction.

options.text: A very large number of lineages moved deeper into the oceans, where oxygen concentrations remained low enough to survive.
options.why: No migration of that kind is described anywhere in the lecture or the chapter.

options.text: A very large number of lineages began producing oxygen themselves, which accelerated the accumulation still further.
options.why: Photosynthesis arose in some lineages and is the source of the oxygen rather than a response to it.

items.stem: The lecture makes the misreading of affordable concrete before rejecting it. How does it put the misreading, and what is wrong with it?

options.text: Plans in a drawer and blueprints for a bigger cell, with life saving up — wrong because nothing was waiting and no plans existed.
options.why: Correct. The mutations arose all along and died out; what changed was the energy available to pay for them, not the variation.

options.text: A ladder with rungs to be climbed once each was affordable — wrong because the rungs turn out to have been climbed in a different order.
options.why: The ladder is the previous slide's target, and reordering its rungs would not fix what is wrong with it.

options.text: A bank account that life drew down — wrong because the surplus was spent immediately rather than accumulated over time.
options.why: No claim about the timing of the spending is made; the error being corrected is about anticipation, not about saving.

options.text: An engineer choosing between designs — wrong because selection compares designs that have already been built rather than proposed ones.
options.why: This is close to the right correction, but it is not the image the lecture uses, and it still credits selection with comparing designs.

items.stem: The lecture repeats one sentence and says it is the sentence the whole module turns on. Which sentence?

options.text: The cells that must act on what a sensor detects cannot detect it themselves.
options.why: Correct. Everything after it — the three strategies, the speed premium, the trade — is about how that gap gets closed and how fast.

options.text: A colony of identical cells has nothing much to coordinate, so coordination is a cost of specialization.
options.why: That is the setup for the problem rather than the sentence the lecture stops and repeats.

options.text: Every complex multicellular organism has some version of the coordination problem.
options.why: The lecture does say this, but as the generalization that follows rather than as the sentence it asks the room to hold.

options.text: If every cell must do every job, every cell will probably be mediocre at all of them.
options.why: That is the argument for specialization, which creates the problem rather than stating it.

items.stem: The lecture gives a one-line condition for when neurons are worth building. What is it?

options.text: Neurons only become worth paying for if what can go wrong in a second is something that can go wrong in a second.
options.why: Correct. It makes the table's third row into the criterion, which is what stops plants and fungi from reading as lineages that fell short.

options.text: Neurons only become worth paying for once a body has grown large enough that diffusion cannot cross it in useful time.
options.why: Body size matters to §3.1.7's argument, but the condition the lecture states is about the tempo of the hazards a lineage faces.

options.text: Neurons only become worth paying for once a lineage has enough energy surplus to run them without reducing its reproduction.
options.why: The surplus is necessary and is not what the lecture offers as the condition on this slide.

options.text: Neurons only become worth paying for in lineages that move, since a stationary organism has nothing to aim a fast signal at.
options.why: Movement is one row of the table rather than the criterion, and the lecture puts the weight on what a second can cost.

items.stem: The lecture makes three points about the sense → decide → act loop before leaving it, one of which the chapter never states anywhere. What is that point?

options.text: The loop closes through the world rather than inside the animal: the action changes the situation, and the changed situation is what gets sensed next.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes it a loop rather than a sequence, and it is why an action that arrives late is the wrong action rather than a slow one.

options.text: The loop runs faster in predators than in prey, since a predator initiates the encounter and the prey can only respond.
options.why: The lecture treats both sides of the arms race symmetrically, and gives neither a structural advantage in speed.

options.text: The loop must complete within a single second, which is the interval the comparison of the three strategies is built around.
options.why: The table's row is about what can go wrong in a second rather than a deadline the loop has to meet.

options.text: The loop is unique to animals, since a system that stays put has little need to sense and act on what it senses.
options.why: The lecture's third point is the opposite: any system operating on its own in a changing world faces some version of it.

items.stem: The lecture pauses on how early cells made ATP and tells the room to hold on to the shape of the arrangement. Describe the arrangement, and say where the lecture promises the same shape will return.
items.answer: Energy from chemical reactions is used to pump protons across a membrane so that they pile up on one side. They then flow back through a protein that spins as they pass, and that spinning is the mechanical force that pushes phosphate groups together against their electrical repulsion, which is what making ATP requires. Water behind a dam is the comparison, because the arrangement stores energy as a difference held across a barrier and collects it on the way down. The lecture promises the same shape will return in the third lecture of the module, where a membrane again holds a difference across itself — this time to keep a neuron ready to fire rather than to manufacture ATP.
rubric: Describes protons pumped to one side and flowing back through a spinning protein.
Notes that the spinning supplies the force that pushes repelling phosphates together.
Names the shape as energy stored as a difference held across a barrier.
Says the same shape returns in the third lecture, at the resting membrane potential.

pools.title: Why Chemistry Was Not Fast Enough

items.stem: What is a neuron, on the computational-level definition the chapter gives?

options.text: The cell specialized to turn an event into a signal that travels fast, travels far without weakening, and arrives at one specific destination.
options.why: Correct. All three properties are what the trade buys, and each is something diffusion cannot deliver.

options.text: The cell specialized to release chemical messengers into the bloodstream so that many tissues can be reached at once.
options.why: That is what a hormone-releasing cell does, and it is the cheap broadcast method neurons gave up rather than the one they adopted.

options.text: The cell specialized to store an animal's past experience, so that a later response can take account of what happened before.
options.why: Storage over time is not part of this definition, and how a connection changes with experience is deferred to Module 5.

options.text: The cell specialized to convert food into usable energy, which is what allows the rest of an animal's body to remain active.
options.why: That is metabolic work. Neurons are among the largest spenders of the energy in an animal rather than producers of it.

items.stem: Which term names the cell specialized to convert an event into a signal that is fast, does not weaken with distance, and arrives at one place rather than everywhere?

options.text: neuron
options.why: Correct. The definition is given at the computational level, so it says what the cell is for rather than what it is built from.

options.text: protocell
options.why: That is an early membrane-bound package of replicating molecules, from long before either animals or signaling cells existed.

options.text: eukaryote
options.why: That is a cell with a nucleus and internal compartments, which is a category that includes plant and fungal cells too.

options.text: ribozyme
options.why: That is a catalytic RNA molecule, named in the origin-of-life section and unrelated to signaling between cells.

items.stem: A small molecule crosses a micrometer by diffusion in about a millisecond. Roughly how long does the chapter say it takes to cross a meter?

options.text: On the order of a decade.
options.why: Correct. The figure is startling on purpose: it is what makes chemical signaling hopeless as a way of crossing a large animal.

options.text: On the order of a few minutes.
options.why: Several minutes is the figure the chapter gives for a millimeter, which is a thousand times shorter than a meter.

options.text: On the order of a second.
options.why: A second is far faster than diffusion manages over that distance, and the chapter's whole argument depends on the gap.

options.text: On the order of an hour.
options.why: An hour still enormously understates the wait, and hormones travel in the bloodstream rather than by diffusion alone.

items.stem: Diffusion time grows with the square of distance rather than in proportion to it. What does that mean for a signal that has to cross twice as far?

options.text: It waits about four times as long.
options.why: Correct. Every doubling of distance quadruples the wait, which is why the penalty becomes catastrophic over the length of an animal.

options.text: It waits about twice as long.
options.why: That is the proportional relationship the chapter explicitly rules out, and it would make diffusion far more usable than it is.

options.text: It waits about the same time.
options.why: Diffusion has no run-up. Molecules move randomly rather than accelerating along a path.

options.text: It waits about eight times as long.
options.why: The chapter states a square relation rather than a cube, and the quantity that scales is time rather than volume.

items.stem: Beyond being slow, what two further limitations does the chapter attribute to chemical signaling?

options.text: It spreads in every direction at once, so it cannot be aimed; and it lingers, so it cannot easily be switched off.
options.why: Correct. Both limitations are about control rather than about speed, and both are things neural signaling buys back.

options.text: It weakens with distance and it picks up noise, so what arrives cannot be told apart from what was already there.
options.why: Degradation of that kind is what §3.2.4 attributes to a graded signal, and it is a different argument from this one.

options.text: It requires special apparatus to produce and cannot be made by an ordinary cell, so only some tissues can send a message at all.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: chemical signaling needs no special apparatus beyond making the molecule and responding to it.

options.text: It can only carry one message at a time, so a body using it cannot coordinate two different processes simultaneously.
options.why: No such restriction is claimed, and animal bodies run many hormonal signals at once.

items.stem: The chapter calls the arrival of neurons a trade rather than an improvement. What is given up, and what does that imply about chemical signaling today?

options.text: Cheap broadcast reach is given up in exchange for speed, distance and aim — and chemical signaling was joined rather than replaced.
options.why: Correct. Both systems still run in every animal body, each doing the jobs it suits, which is why hormones remain everywhere.

options.text: Reliability is given up rather than gained, and chemical signaling survives only in tissues where accuracy matters more than time does.
options.why: Reliability is something neural signaling gains rather than loses, since what arrives at the far end is exactly what left.

options.text: Energy efficiency is given up in exchange for reach, and chemical signaling has been retained only in the very smallest animals.
options.why: Reach is what neural signaling gives up rather than gains, and chemical signaling is described as running in every animal body.

options.text: Specificity is given up in exchange for cost, and chemical signaling now handles everything that has to arrive at a single destination.
options.why: This inverts the trade in both directions: aim is what neurons buy, and arriving everywhere is what chemistry does.

items.stem: Which kind of message can afford to travel by diffusion, and which cannot?

options.text: Grow, get hungry or begin reproducing can; the left side of the body should contract, now cannot.
options.why: Correct. The dividing line is whether a delay of minutes or longer changes whether the message is still the right one.

options.text: Messages between neighboring cells can; messages that stay inside a single cell cannot.
options.why: Diffusion works well over short distances, so the short-range case is the one it handles best rather than worst.

options.text: Messages that have to reach many tissues can; messages that have to reach a single tissue quickly can as well.
options.why: The second half fails: a message needing one destination quickly is exactly the case diffusion cannot serve.

options.text: Messages an animal produces while at rest can; messages produced while it is moving cannot.
options.why: The animal's activity is not what settles it. What matters is the deadline the message has to meet.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say neurons took hold in animals and not in plants or fungi?

options.text: Because the lineages whose sense → decide → act loop ran faster were the lineages that ate rather than were eaten.
options.why: Correct. The selective advantage is specific to a way of living, which is what keeps this from being a claim about superiority.

options.text: Because plants and fungi never evolved the membrane machinery a signaling cell needs, so the option was closed to them.
options.why: No such limitation is claimed. The chapter's argument is about what was worth paying for rather than what was possible.

options.text: Because plants and fungi capture less energy than animals do, so the expense of neurons was beyond what either could pay.
options.why: Energy availability is not what separates the three, and photosynthesis is a very substantial energy source.

options.text: Because plants and fungi reproduce too slowly for selection to have acted on signaling speed within the time available.
options.why: Generation time plays no part in the argument, and both lineages are ancient enough for the point to be moot.

items.stem: The chapter attaches a cost to the trade neurons made. How does that cost connect to its earlier argument about oxygen?

options.text: The surplus that made animals possible in the first place is the same surplus neurons spend in order to signal.
options.why: Correct. The energy thread closes on itself here, which is why §3.3's accounting reads as the same story rather than a new topic.

options.text: The cost is paid out of a separate budget, since neural signaling uses a form of energy that respiration does not supply.
options.why: There is only one currency in the chapter's account, and every stage of neural signaling is priced in it.

options.text: The cost is small compared with the surplus, which is why the chapter treats the expense of neurons as a minor consideration.
options.why: The chapter treats the expense as anything but minor; it is the second of the two facts said to organize the whole module.

options.text: The cost fell over evolutionary time as neurons became more efficient, so the surplus was needed only at the beginning.
options.why: No such trend is described, and §3.3 argues that the running cost still shapes how brains are built today.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, set out the trade neurons made: what chemical signaling is good at, what it cannot do, and what neural signaling gives up to get around it.
items.answer: Chemical signaling is cheap, it reaches everywhere, and it needs no special apparatus beyond the ability to make the molecule and respond to it. What it cannot do is arrive quickly over any distance, since diffusion time grows with the square of the distance; it also cannot be aimed, because it spreads in every direction, and cannot easily be switched off, because it lingers. Neural signaling gives up exactly the cheap broadcast reach that chemistry has, and buys speed, distance and aim in return. The two coexist in every animal body, with hormones still carrying everything that can afford to be slow.
rubric: Names at least two of chemical signaling's advantages: cheap, broadcast reach, no special apparatus.
Names its limitations, including the slowness of diffusion and at least one of aim or persistence.
States what neural signaling gives up (broadcast reach) and what it buys (speed, distance, aim).
Notes that the two systems coexist rather than one replacing the other.

items.stem: The lecture names the single most common way to get the comparison between chemical and neural signaling wrong. What is it?

options.text: Reading it as neural signaling having replaced chemical signaling, when the two coexist in every animal body doing the jobs each suits.
options.why: Correct. Animals still run on hormones for everything that can afford to be slow, which is why both columns are still in use.

options.text: Reading it as chemical signaling being the cheaper option, when in fact the apparatus a hormone requires is considerably more elaborate.
options.why: Chemical signaling really is the cheap one, and the lecture says it needs no special apparatus beyond making the molecule.

options.text: Reading it as neural signaling being faster, when the two are comparable in speed and differ mainly in where the message arrives.
options.why: The speed difference is enormous and is the whole point of the trade rather than a misreading of it.

options.text: Reading it as a list of properties, when the rows are meant to be read downward as a sequence of historical developments.
options.why: The table is a comparison of two systems in use at once rather than a chronology.

items.stem: Comparing chemical with neural signaling point by point, the lecture picks out one thing as what neurons actually bought. What is it?

options.text: A message that is aimed, and arrives now.
options.why: Correct. Every other row is a cost or a property the two systems share; that cell is the capability that did not exist before.

options.text: A signal regenerated at full strength along a fiber.
options.why: That is the mechanism by which the capability is delivered rather than the thing bought.

options.text: The kinds of message that chemical signaling suits best.
options.why: Those messages stayed with chemical signaling, which is the half of the table the lecture insists is still in use.

options.text: The fact that neural signaling is expensive to run.
options.why: The expense is what the trade costs rather than what it buys, and it is the subject of the third lecture.

items.stem: The lecture introduces chemical signaling in a way the chapter does not: as something already in hand when the coordination problem arose. How does it put that?

options.text: The obvious solution was already available, and animals still use it — so the question is not what to try first but why trying it was not enough.
options.why: Correct. Framing chemistry as the incumbent is what makes the three limitations a diagnosis rather than a list of facts about diffusion.

options.text: The obvious solution had to be invented alongside multicellularity, since single cells had no occasion to signal to one another at all.
options.why: Cells had been signaling chemically for billions of years before animals existed, which is the lecture's opening claim on this slide.

options.text: The obvious solution was already tried and abandoned, which is why hormonal signaling survives in only a few tissues in a modern animal body.
options.why: Nothing was abandoned. Animal bodies use chemical signaling constantly, for everything that can afford to be slow.

options.text: The obvious solution was unavailable until neurons existed, because a hormone needs a nervous system to release it at the right moment.
options.why: Hormone release does not depend on neurons, and the lecture presents chemical signaling as by far the older of the two systems.

items.stem: The lecture closes by saying its answer is a trade rather than an upgrade. What is given up and what is bought?

options.text: Cheap broadcast reach is given up; speed, distance and aim are bought.
options.why: Correct. Calling it a trade rather than an upgrade is what keeps the older system in the picture as something still worth having.

options.text: Reliability is given up; speed and cheapness are bought, which is why hormones remain in use for anything that must not fail.
options.why: Reliability is gained rather than surrendered, since an all-or-nothing signal arrives exactly as it left.

options.text: Aim is given up; reach and durability are bought, which is what lets one signal reach many tissues at once.
options.why: This inverts the trade: reach is what is given up, and aim is one of the three things bought.

options.text: Nothing is given up; neural signaling improves on chemical signaling in every respect the table lists.
options.why: If nothing were given up the word trade would be doing no work, and chemical signaling would not still be in use.

pools.title: Roles, Integration, and Threshold
pools.covers: reading §3.2.1, §3.2.2, §3.2.3 · lecture 3.2 slides the_algorithmic_question, four_jobs_no_parts, circuit_not_puddle, sum_compare_act

items.stem: What distinguishes the algorithmic question about a neuron from the computational one?

options.text: The algorithmic question asks about procedure — how the job is done — where the computational question asks about purpose.
options.why: Correct. Both are questions about the same cell, and neither is answered by naming the material the cell is built from.

options.text: The algorithmic question asks about the material a cell is made of, where the computational question asks about its shape.
options.why: Material and mechanism belong to the implementational level, which is the third of the three rather than either of these two.

options.text: The algorithmic question applies to machines and the computational question applies only to living things that evolved.
options.why: Marr's levels apply to any system. The chapter uses that generality on purpose when it compares neurons with artificial units.

options.text: The algorithmic question asks what a whole animal does, where the computational question asks what one of its cells does.
options.why: Scale is not what separates the levels. Any one of the three can be asked about a cell, an organ or a whole animal.

items.stem: Turning to the algorithmic level, the chapter sets the biology aside deliberately and says so out loud. Why make the move visible rather than simply making it?

options.text: Because the same move recurs in every module from here on, and it is Module 1's tractability argument being paid for and cashed in a concrete case.
options.why: Correct. The chapter gives a functional description here and a physical one in §3.3, so the price and the payoff are both on display.

options.text: Because the biology being set aside turns out to be irrelevant to how a neuron works, which the reader should not have to guess at.
options.why: §3.3.1 says the opposite: every one of the physical details matters to how the computation is actually carried out.

options.text: Because readers without a biology background would otherwise be unable to follow the chapter's later sections at all.
options.why: Accessibility is not the reason given, and §3.3 goes on to assume no more background than §3.2 did.

options.text: Because the abstraction is controversial among researchers, and the chapter wants to signal that it is taking a side.
options.why: The controversy the chapter flags is about how much sum-and-threshold leaves out, not about whether abstraction is legitimate.

items.stem: Which three verbs does the chapter use to describe what a neuron does at the algorithmic level?

options.text: receive, integrate, transmit
options.why: Correct. Everything else in §3.2 is detail fleshing out those three, and none of them names a part of the cell.

options.text: sense, decide, act
options.why: That is the loop an animal has to complete quickly, stated at the computational level in §3.1.6 about behavior rather than about one cell.

options.text: depolarize, repolarize, recover
options.why: Those are the phases of a single action potential, described in §3.3.3 at the implementational level.

options.text: store, retrieve, compare
options.why: None of the three is a verb the chapter uses for a neuron, and storage in particular is deferred to a later module.

items.stem: The chapter says receiving, integrating and transmitting require four things. Which set does it name?

options.text: An input surface, an integrator, an output that carries the verdict away, and a junction where one cell's output becomes the next cell's input.
options.why: Correct. All four are named as jobs rather than as objects, which is what keeps the description at the algorithmic level.

options.text: Dendrites, a soma, an axon, and a synapse between one cell's ending and the next cell's input surface.
options.why: Those are the physical parts, and they belong to §3.3.1. Naming them here would collapse two of Marr's levels into one.

options.text: A sensory neuron, an interneuron, a motor neuron, and a muscle for the resulting verdict to act on.
options.why: That is the chain §3.2.10 traces through a worm, which is an arrangement of several cells rather than roles within one.

options.text: A threshold, a firing rate, a weight on each connection, and a baseline the cell returns to when nothing is arriving.
options.why: Those are quantities in the model of §3.2.8 rather than the four jobs a single cell has to fill.

items.stem: Why does the chapter single out one-way flow as mattering more than any of the four roles?

options.text: Because a cell with a distinct input end and a distinct output end can be wired in a definite direction, which is what makes a circuit possible.
options.why: Correct. Direction is what turns a collection of cells into something whose connections can be traced and reasoned about.

options.text: Because signals running backward would cancel the signals running forward, so a cell allowing both would produce no output at all.
options.why: Cancellation is not the argument. The problem with two-way flow is that activity spreads rather than travels anywhere in particular.

options.text: Because one-way flow is what keeps a neuron from being influenced by its own output once the signal has left the cell.
options.why: Self-influence is not what the section is concerned with, and the argument it makes is about wiring between cells.

options.text: Because the four roles could each be filled by more than one part of the cell, whereas the direction of flow is fixed.
options.why: Whether a role has one filler or several is not discussed, and the four roles map cleanly onto four parts in §3.3.1.

items.stem: Two neurons are pressed right up against each other, and a third sits at the far end of the animal's body. What does the chapter say about which pairs are connected?

options.text: Nothing follows from position: one cell's output line may reach the distant cell while the adjacent one receives nothing, because connection is a matter of wiring.
options.why: Correct. That independence from proximity is what makes it possible to ask what a given input leads to and get an answer.

options.text: The adjacent pair is certainly connected and the distant one certainly is not, since a signal weakens over the length of a body.
options.why: Neural signals are regenerated at full strength rather than weakening, which is exactly what §3.2.4 goes on to establish.

options.text: The adjacent pair is connected more strongly, and the distant pair more weakly, in proportion to the distance between them.
options.why: Connection strength in this chapter is a weight set by the wiring, and nothing ties it to physical separation.

options.text: All three are connected, since any cell in a nervous system can influence any other one given enough intervening cells.
options.why: Indirect influence through a chain is a different question from whether two cells are connected, which is what the section is defining.

items.stem: What would go wrong if signals could enter and leave a neuron anywhere on its surface?

options.text: Every cell would influence every neighbor it touched in every direction, so activity would spread outward instead of traveling anywhere in particular.
options.why: Correct. The chapter names that as the same defect chemical signaling had: a message that goes everywhere says nothing about where it was meant to arrive.

options.text: Every cell would fire continuously, since signals entering anywhere on its surface would keep pushing it past its threshold.
options.why: Constant firing is not the failure described, and the section is about where signals go rather than about how often cells fire.

options.text: Signals would weaken as they spread, so no message would reach a cell more than a short distance from where it started.
options.why: Weakening is a property of graded signals discussed in §3.2.4, and it is not what makes the puddle a puddle.

options.text: Cells would be unable to receive more than one input at a time, so integration across many sources would become impossible.
options.why: Nothing about surface-wide flow would limit the number of inputs; if anything it would increase them.

items.stem: What is integration, as a neuron performs it?

options.text: Combining the many arriving signals into one total, which the cell then compares against its threshold.
options.why: Correct. It is the middle of the three verbs, and it is what has to happen because many signals come in and only one goes out.

options.text: Passing each arriving signal along unchanged to the next cell in the chain, in the order the signals arrived.
options.why: That is the relay picture the section rejects. A neuron produces one output from many inputs rather than forwarding each.

options.text: Increasing the strength of an arriving signal so that it can travel further before it fades below the level of the noise.
options.why: Amplification of that kind is not what the term names, and a neuron's output is all-or-nothing rather than variable in size.

options.text: Selecting the strongest of the arriving signals and discarding the rest before producing an output based on that one.
options.why: Nothing is discarded. All of the arriving signals contribute to the total the cell evaluates.

items.stem: What is a neuron's threshold?

options.text: The level the summed input has to reach: below it the cell does nothing at all, and at or above it the cell acts.
options.why: Correct. Comparing against a level rather than reporting the total is what makes the cell an evaluator rather than a relay.

options.text: The maximum number of spikes a cell can produce in a second, which is set by how long that cell takes to recover after each one it fires.
options.why: That is the ceiling on firing rate, which §3.3.3 explains by way of the refractory period rather than the threshold.

options.text: The strength of an individual connection, which determines how much one input contributes to the cell's total.
options.why: That is a weight, defined in §3.2.8, and it is a property of a connection rather than of the receiving cell.

options.text: The background rate at which a neuron fires when it is receiving no input from any of the cells connected to it.
options.why: That is the baseline firing rate, which the model of §3.2.8 writes as a separate term from anything to do with a level.

items.stem: Which term names the level a neuron's summed input must reach before the cell produces any output at all?

options.text: threshold
options.why: Correct. Below it the neuron does nothing, and at or above it the neuron produces a full response rather than a proportional one.

options.text: weight
options.why: That is the strength and sign of one connection, which affects how much a given input contributes to the total being compared.

options.text: firing rate
options.why: That is the number of spikes produced in a stretch of time, which is the cell's output rather than the level its input must reach.

options.text: baseline
options.why: That is the low background rate at which most neurons fire when nothing is arriving, written as its own term in the model.

items.stem: Which term names the combining of many arriving signals into a single total, the middle of a neuron's three jobs?

options.text: integration
options.why: Correct. It is what has to happen in between, because a neuron receives from many cells at once and produces just one output.

options.text: transmission
options.why: That is the third of the three verbs, the carrying of the resulting verdict away from the cell.

options.text: modulation
options.why: That is a third category of signaling that changes how strongly a cell responds to everything else, rather than a way of combining inputs.

options.text: depolarization
options.why: That is the rising phase of an action potential in physical terms, which belongs to the implementational account in §3.3.3.

items.stem: Why does the chapter call a single neuron a small evaluator rather than a wire or a relay?

options.text: Because it pools evidence from many sources and answers one question with it — given everything arriving now, act or not.
options.why: Correct. A relay would forward what it received; an evaluator reaches a verdict that none of its inputs contains on its own.

options.text: Because it can choose which of its inputs to attend to and ignore all of the rest, depending on what the animal happens to be doing at that moment.
options.why: Selective attention of that kind is not attributed to a single cell here, and integration sums everything arriving.

options.text: Because it remembers the inputs it has received before and compares each new one against that record.
options.why: The description at this level has no history in it at all, which §3.2.9 lists among the model's deliberate omissions.

options.text: Because it converts a chemical signal into an electrical one, which is a transformation rather than a transfer.
options.why: The chemical-to-electrical conversion is real but belongs to §3.3, and it is not the reason the word evaluator is used.

items.stem: The chapter stresses how little a neuron needs to know in order to do its job. What does that amount to?

options.text: It needs no view of the animal's situation and no idea what its inputs mean; it sums them and compares the total against a level.
options.why: Correct. That poverty is the point: almost everything in the book is built from this operation repeated in enormous numbers.

options.text: It needs to know only which of its inputs are excitatory, since inhibitory inputs can be ignored without changing the verdict.
options.why: Inhibitory inputs are subtracted rather than ignored, and §3.2.7 makes that arithmetic the source of real computation.

options.text: It needs to know only how far away each of its inputs originated, since nearer inputs carry more weight than distant ones.
options.why: Distance plays no part in the description, and §3.2.2 has already said that connection is a matter of wiring rather than proximity.

options.text: It needs to know what the animal as a whole is trying to do, since the very same input can call for quite different responses in different situations.
options.why: Internal state does reach circuits, through modulation in §3.2.7, but the individual cell's operation requires nothing of the kind.

items.stem: Immediately after describing a neuron as summing and thresholding, the chapter adds a hedge. What does the hedge say?

options.text: That sum-and-threshold is a choice about how closely to look, and whether a real neuron does something considerably richer is an open question.
options.why: Correct. The description is adopted because it is simple enough to reason about and to build with, which is a different claim from its being complete.

options.text: That sum-and-threshold applies to an artificial neuron but not to a biological neuron, which works on a quite different principle.
options.why: The chapter argues the reverse: the description was arrived at by describing a cell, and the artificial unit was copied from it.

options.text: That sum-and-threshold has been shown to be incorrect, and is retained only because no better description is available yet.
options.why: Nothing has been shown incorrect. The chapter says the question is open and live rather than settled against the model.

options.text: That sum-and-threshold holds only for neurons in the cortex, and that cells elsewhere in the nervous system work differently.
options.why: No such regional restriction is made, and the researchers §3.2.9 cites raise their objection about cortical cells in particular.

items.stem: The chapter says each of the four jobs is a real piece of a real cell with a name and a shape, then declines to give the names until much later. Why?

options.text: Because naming the parts would import the implementational level into an account that is deliberately abstract, and the physical account is where they belong.
options.why: Correct. The abstraction is the method being demonstrated, and it would be given away by describing the cell in terms of its anatomy.

options.text: Because the names differ across species, so no single set of terms would apply to every animal with neurons.
options.why: No cross-species variation in the anatomy is claimed anywhere, and §3.3.1 names four parts without qualification.

options.text: Because the parts had not yet been identified when the functional description was first worked out historically.
options.why: The chapter's ordering is pedagogical rather than historical, and it does not tie the abstraction to any period of research.

options.text: Because a single part can fill more than one of the four roles, so a one-to-one naming would be misleading.
options.why: §3.3.1 pairs the four roles with four parts one to one, so no such complication is being avoided.

items.stem: What is the structural fact about a neuron that forces something to happen between its input and its output?

options.text: It receives from many cells at once and produces only one output.
options.why: Correct. Many in and one out is what makes a combining step unavoidable, and that step is integration.

options.text: It receives signals of many sizes and sends only one size.
options.why: All-or-nothing output is real and comes in §3.2.4, but the section grounds integration in the many-to-one arrangement instead.

options.text: It receives continuously but sends only in short bursts.
options.why: The refractory period is an implementational fact from §3.3.3 rather than what motivates integration here.

options.text: It receives one output for each input and must amplify each one.
options.why: Amplification is not part of the account, and neural signals are described as arriving without having weakened.

items.stem: A researcher wants to trace what a particular input to a nervous system eventually leads to. What makes that question answerable at all, on the chapter's account?

options.text: Connection is a matter of wiring rather than proximity, so there is a definite set of cells each signal reaches and a path to follow.
options.why: Correct. In a puddle the same question has no answer, because activity spreads outward instead of going anywhere in particular.

options.text: Signals weaken steadily as they travel, so the path can be reconstructed afterward by measuring how much of the original signal still remains at each point.
options.why: Neural signals do not weaken along the way; that is precisely what §3.2.4 and §3.3.5 establish about regeneration.

options.text: Each neuron connects to exactly one other neuron, so following a signal is a matter of tracing a single unbranched chain.
options.why: A cell's output line reaches multiple destinations, and the chapter is careful not to imply a single downstream target.

options.text: Every input eventually reaches every cell, so the question is answered the same way for any input one might pick.
options.why: That is the puddle case, and in it the question the researcher is asking would carry no information at all.

items.stem: The chapter says almost everything in the book is built out of the sum-and-threshold operation. Where does it locate the complexity that follows?

options.text: In how the neurons are wired together, rather than in what any one of them computes.
options.why: Correct. The same point returns in §3.2.10 about the worm and again in the Close about meaning.

options.text: In the variety of thresholds different cells have, which is what lets a nervous system respond to a wide range of inputs.
options.why: Variation in threshold is not offered as the source of complexity anywhere in the chapter.

options.text: In the size of the spike each cell produces, which encodes how strongly that particular cell was driven.
options.why: Spike size does not vary, which §3.2.4 names as the single most counterintuitive fact about neurons.

options.text: In the chemistry inside each cell, which is far richer than the functional description at this level suggests.
options.why: Single-cell richness is raised as an open question in §3.2.9, but it is not where this section puts the complexity.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe what a neuron does with the signals arriving at it, and explain why the chapter says this makes it an evaluator rather than a relay.
items.answer: The arriving signals are added up, which is integration. The neuron then does not report that total: it compares the total against a threshold, and below that level it does nothing at all while at or above it the cell acts. A relay would pass on what it received, so that the output was a copy of the input. This cell instead pools evidence from many sources and answers a single question with it — given everything arriving right now, act or not — and the answer is not contained in any one of the inputs.
rubric: States that arriving signals are summed (integration).
States that the total is compared against a threshold rather than reported.
Gives both outcomes: nothing below threshold, action at or above it.
Explains the evaluator contrast: a verdict reached from many inputs rather than a copy of one.

items.stem: Explain, in a short paragraph, the difference between a circuit and a puddle as the chapter draws it, and why the chapter says the puddle repeats a defect it has already discussed.
items.answer: In a circuit, signals run one way through each cell — in at the input surface, out along the output line — so cells can be wired to each other in a definite direction, and whether two cells are connected has nothing to do with whether they are near each other. In a puddle, signals can enter and leave anywhere, so every cell influences every neighbor it touches in every direction, and activity spreads outward from wherever it began rather than traveling anywhere in particular. That is the same defect chemical signaling had: a message that goes everywhere carries no information about where it was meant to arrive.
rubric: Identifies one-way flow as what makes a circuit possible.
States that in a circuit connection depends on wiring rather than on proximity.
Describes the puddle as activity spreading outward rather than traveling to a destination.
Connects the puddle to chemical signaling's inability to be aimed.

items.stem: The lecture gives a reason why describing a neuron functionally rather than materially buys anything. What is the reason?

options.text: A description in terms of what a thing is made of can only be compared with other things made of the same stuff; a description of what it does is comparable to anything that does the same.
options.why: Correct. That is the abstraction Module 1 argued makes comparison between brains and machines possible at all.

options.text: A description in terms of what a thing is made of will not support a prediction about anything the thing has not already been observed doing.
options.why: Testability is not the argument, and §3.3's implementational account is presented as extremely well tested.

options.text: A description in terms of what a thing is made of changes as the biology is revised, while a functional description stays fixed once written.
options.why: Neither description is claimed to be permanent, and the lecture treats the functional model's correctness as an open question.

options.text: A description in terms of what a thing is made of is only available for systems we have built, so it cannot be applied to living cells at all.
options.why: The material description of a neuron is exactly what the third lecture supplies, at length.

items.stem: The lecture explains what would be lost by attaching the four cell parts to "receive, integrate, transmit" straight away. What is it?

options.text: The functional and physical descriptions fuse in memory, and the question of whether something else made of something else could fill the four jobs stops being askable.
options.why: Correct. The separation is presented as the reason the chapter is organized this way rather than as tidiness.

options.text: The four parts would have to be taught twice, once at each level, which the module does not have the meeting time to do.
options.why: Time is not the argument, and the third lecture does introduce the parts once rather than twice.

options.text: The names of the parts would be learned before the functions, which is harder for students who have not taken biology before.
options.why: Ordering by difficulty is not the reason given; the reason is about what fusing the two descriptions costs.

options.text: The parts differ between species, so pairing them with the three verbs would produce a description true only of vertebrates.
options.why: No cross-species variation is claimed anywhere in the module.

items.stem: The lecture connects the puddle back to the first lecture of the module. What is the connection?

options.text: A puddle has exactly the defect diffusion had: a message that goes everywhere carries no information about where it was meant to arrive.
options.why: Correct. A neuron without directionality would have the same problem, which is why one-way flow is what makes a circuit possible.

options.text: A puddle spreads more slowly than a circuit, in the same way that diffusion is slower than a regenerated signal along a fiber.
options.why: Speed is not the defect being drawn out here; the shared failure is about aim rather than about time.

options.text: A puddle cannot be switched off, in the same way that a chemical signal lingers after the event that produced it.
options.why: Persistence is one of diffusion's limitations, but the defect the lecture points at in the puddle is the absence of a destination.

options.text: A puddle is cheaper to build than a circuit, in the same way that chemical signaling needs no special apparatus.
options.why: No cost comparison between the two arrangements is drawn.

items.stem: Comparing two moments in which a cell integrates different inputs, the lecture points out that the threshold is identical in both. Why does that matter?

options.text: Because the cell is not adjusting anything: all that differs between the two cases is what arrived.
options.why: Correct. The threshold is a fixed level the total is compared against rather than something the cell moves to suit its inputs.

options.text: Because the threshold is the same in every neuron, so both cases would look this way in any cell one cared to draw.
options.why: No claim that all cells share a threshold is made, and the point is about one cell across two moments.

options.text: Because the threshold rises as more input arrives, so keeping it fixed is a simplification the third lecture removes.
options.why: Nothing in the module has the threshold rising with input; that would undo the comparison the cell is performing.

options.text: Because the comparison is schematic, so no information about the actual voltages involved can be read off it.
options.why: The lecture's point is substantive rather than a caveat about the drawing's scale.

items.stem: The lecture says it will "perform the move out loud rather than just do it." What move, and why announce it?

options.text: Setting the biology aside and describing the neuron as though its material were unknown — announced because it is a method rather than an omission.
options.why: Correct. The lecture also names the price: some things said at this level are true only at this level, and the third lecture goes back for the biology.

options.text: Replacing the chapter's examples with new ones — announced so that students can tell which illustrations came from the reading.
options.why: Module 3's lectures deliberately reuse the chapter's own examples, on Jon's call, rather than swapping them.

options.text: Skipping the material a student can get from the reading — announced as a choice about coverage rather than a method.
options.why: The abstraction is a level of description rather than a decision about what to leave to the reading.

options.text: Introducing a model before the evidence for it — announced because the evidence only arrives in the third lecture of the module.
options.why: The move being flagged is about setting the biology aside, not about the order of model and evidence.

items.stem: The lecture names four jobs and refuses to name the parts that fill them until the next meeting. In a short paragraph, give the four jobs and explain the reason for the refusal.
items.answer: The four jobs are an input surface where signals from other cells arrive, an integrator where those signals are pooled and a verdict is reached, an output that carries the verdict away, and a junction where one cell's output becomes the next cell's input. Each is a real piece of a real cell with a name and a shape, and all four names belong to the third lecture. The reason for holding them apart is that learning "receive, integrate, transmit" with four cell parts attached fuses the functional description and the physical description into one thing in memory. Once they are fused, the question the course is built on — could something else, made of something else, fill these four jobs? — stops being askable.
rubric: Names all four jobs as jobs rather than as parts.
States that each is filled by a real part whose name comes in the third lecture.
Gives the reason: the functional and physical descriptions would fuse in memory.
States what that fusion costs — the multiple-realizability question becomes unaskable.

pools.title: The Spike, and Where the Message Is
pools.covers: reading §3.2.4, §3.2.5, §3.2.6 · lecture 3.2 slides all_or_nothing, three_discrete_codes, where_the_message_is, two_time_scales

items.stem: What is an action potential?

options.text: A brief, stereotyped electrical event a neuron produces once its inputs push it past threshold, which travels the length of the cell without weakening.
options.why: Correct. Its shape does not vary, which is what the word stereotyped is doing, and it is commonly called a spike.

options.text: A gradual shift in a neuron's membrane voltage whose size is proportional to how strongly the cell has been stimulated.
options.why: That is a graded signal, which is the design the chapter says neurons rejected because it degrades over distance.

options.text: The chemical released by a sending cell that crosses the gap and binds to receptors on the cell receiving from it.
options.why: That is a neurotransmitter, defined in §3.2.7, and it carries the signal between cells rather than along one.

options.text: The steady voltage a neuron holds across its membrane while it is at rest and receiving no input at all.
options.why: That is the resting membrane potential of §3.3.2, which is the state from which an action potential departs.

items.stem: Which term names the property of being produced at full size or not at all, with no small, large or partial versions?

options.text: all-or-nothing
options.why: Correct. Cross the threshold and a full spike follows; fall short and nothing does, with no intermediate outcome available.

options.text: graded
options.why: That describes a signal whose size means something, which is the design an all-or-nothing signal is contrasted with.

options.text: saltatory conduction
options.why: That describes a spike jumping between the bare gaps in a myelin sheath, which is about how it travels rather than its size.

options.text: sparse
options.why: That describes activity in which only a small share of cells are strongly active at once, which is a property of a population.

items.stem: A student writes that a stronger stimulus makes a neuron produce a larger action potential. What does the chapter say instead?

options.text: Every spike a given neuron fires is essentially identical to every other one; a stronger stimulus produces more spikes, faster.
options.why: Correct. The chapter calls this the single most counterintuitive fact about neurons, which is why it corrects it twice.

options.text: A stronger stimulus makes the neuron produce a spike that travels faster, though the size of that spike itself does not change.
options.why: Conduction speed is set by the axon rather than by the stimulus, and myelin rather than intensity is what §3.3.5 credits it to.

options.text: A stronger stimulus produces a spike that lasts longer, so the duration rather than the height carries the amount.
options.why: Duration does not vary either. The event is stereotyped in shape, which covers its length as well as its height.

options.text: A stronger stimulus produces a larger spike only in sensory neurons, which are the cells where the amount of a stimulus actually has to be reported.
options.why: Sensory neurons are exactly the case §3.2.5 works through, and they report amount by rate rather than by size.

items.stem: Asked why a signaling system would throw away the option of letting a signal's size carry the message, what answer does the chapter give?

options.text: A graded signal fades, blurs and picks up noise over distance, so after a meter nothing tells us how much of what arrived was the message.
options.why: Correct. An all-or-nothing signal is regenerated at full strength the whole way, which makes it as reliable at a meter as at a micrometer.

options.text: A graded signal would take considerably longer to produce, and that delay alone would be enough to lose an animal the fraction of a second it has to act in.
options.why: Speed of production is not the argument. What a graded signal loses is integrity over distance rather than time at the outset.

options.text: A graded signal would cost more energy to send, and a message that expensive is one an animal could not afford to repeat often.
options.why: Cost is a major theme in §3.3, but §3.2.4 grounds the design choice in reliability rather than in expense.

options.text: A graded signal could not be produced by a cell at all, since a membrane can only be either polarized or depolarized.
options.why: The chapter never claims graded signals are impossible; small graded voltage shifts are exactly what arriving inputs produce.

items.stem: The chapter gives two other systems that arrived at the same discrete-signal solution. What are they, and what do the three cases share?

options.text: Digital electronics and the four-base code of DNA: in each, a value that is fully one thing or another can be restored rather than merely approximated.
options.why: Correct. Making the convergence three-way rather than two-way is what turns it from an analogy into an argument about the design.

options.text: Hormonal signaling and photosynthesis: in each, a chemical process was replaced by one that carries information more reliably.
options.why: Neither is a discrete-signal system, and photosynthesis is about capturing energy rather than about carrying a message.

options.text: Chemotaxis and saltatory conduction: in each, a signal is renewed at intervals rather than being sent once and left to fade.
options.why: Chemotaxis is a behavior rather than a signaling code, and saltatory conduction is a way of moving a spike rather than a third instance.

options.text: Myelin and the sodium-potassium pump: in each, a biological system spends energy in order to make a signal more reliable.
options.why: Both are real mechanisms in §3.3, but neither is an independent arrival at a discrete rather than continuous code.

items.stem: What is a neuron's firing rate?

options.text: The number of spikes it produces in a stretch of time, which is what varies with the strength of a stimulus.
options.why: Correct. Because every spike is identical, the count rather than the size of any one of them is what can carry a quantity.

options.text: The speed at which a single spike travels from one end of the cell to the other along its output line.
options.why: That is conduction velocity, which §3.3.5 discusses in connection with myelin rather than with what the cell is reporting.

options.text: The size of the voltage change a single spike produces, measured from the resting level to its peak.
options.why: Spike size does not vary from one event to the next, which is exactly why the chapter has to look elsewhere for the message.

options.text: The level of input a neuron requires before it produces any output at all, expressed as spikes arriving per second.
options.why: That is a description of the threshold, which is a property of the input side rather than a measure of the output.

items.stem: Which term names how many spikes a neuron produces in a stretch of time, the quantity that changes when a stimulus gets stronger?

options.text: firing rate
options.why: Correct. The sequence of spikes itself is called a spike train, and the rate is the property of it that carries the amount.

options.text: action potential
options.why: That is the individual event, and its size and shape are the same every time rather than varying with the stimulus.

options.text: resting membrane potential
options.why: That is the voltage a neuron holds when it is not signaling, which is a state rather than a measure of output.

options.text: threshold
options.why: That is the level the summed input must reach for the cell to act, which is about the input rather than about the output.

items.stem: The chapter compares a neuron's message to the meaning of a sentence. What is the comparison making?

options.text: The meaning is not in any one word, and a neuron's message is not in any one spike: it is in how many, and when.
options.why: Correct. The analogy relocates the message from the individual event to the pattern the events make together.

options.text: The meaning depends on the order the words arrive in, and a neuron's message depends on which of its inputs fired first.
options.why: Which input fired is a property of the wiring rather than of the cell's own output, and the analogy is about the output.

options.text: The meaning is agreed between speaker and listener, and a neuron's message means whatever the receiving cell treats it as meaning.
options.why: That point is made in the Close about wiring and meaning, and it is not what this analogy is doing here.

options.text: The meaning can be conveyed in many different words, and a neuron's message can be conveyed by many different spikes.
options.why: Spikes are all identical, so there is no variety among them for this version of the analogy to draw on.

items.stem: A fingertip has to report not just that contact happened but how firmly, most of a meter away. What goes wrong if the report is sent chemically?

options.text: The amount is easy to encode, but left to diffusion the message takes years to cross the arm, and carried in the blood it arrives everywhere.
options.why: Correct. Both routes fail, and they fail differently: one on time and one on aim, which is why the section runs them separately.

options.text: The amount cannot be encoded chemically at all, since the quantity of a substance released does not vary with the pressure applied.
options.why: The chapter says the reverse: the quantity released can be made proportional to the pressure, which is what chemistry is good at.

options.text: The message arrives quickly enough but has faded so much over the distance that the amount it originally carried can no longer be recovered at the far end.
options.why: Fading over distance is the problem with a graded electrical signal in §3.2.4, and diffusion's failure here is one of timing.

options.text: The message would arrive at the spinal cord but not the brain, since a chemical signal cannot cross from one to the other.
options.why: No such barrier is described, and the failure the chapter identifies is about speed and about arriving everywhere.

items.stem: Why does a rate code get what neither pure chemistry nor a single all-or-nothing spike could get on its own?

options.text: Identical regenerated spikes survive the trip intact, and the number of them in a second is a quantity that can take any value in a range.
options.why: Correct. What travels up the arm is a stream of identical pulses, and what arrives is a number.

options.text: Spikes vary slightly in size, and the accumulated variation across many of them is enough to encode an amount.
options.why: Spikes do not vary in size at all, and the chapter's whole argument depends on their being identical.

options.text: The rate can be adjusted mid-journey by the cells the signal passes through, so the amount is corrected as it travels.
options.why: No correction en route is described, and a spike travels the length of one cell rather than through a chain of correctors.

options.text: The rate is carried chemically while the individual spikes are carried electrically, which combines the strengths of both.
options.why: The rate is a property of the electrical events themselves, and nothing about it is carried by a separate chemical channel.

items.stem: Besides its rate, what else does the chapter say a spike train can carry?

options.text: The precise timing of the spikes, which in some systems carries a great deal of information.
options.why: Correct. The general point holds either way: meaning rides on patterns in the series, never on the size of any one pulse.

options.text: The size of each individual spike, which varies enough across a train to encode a second quantity alongside the rate.
options.why: Spike size is constant, so there is no second quantity of that kind available anywhere in the train.

options.text: The direction the signal is traveling, which lets a receiving cell tell where in the body the message originated.
options.why: Where a signal came from is a fact about the wiring rather than something encoded in the train itself.

options.text: The duration of the whole train, which encodes how long the stimulus that produced it lasted at the receptor.
options.why: Duration is not named as a carrier here, and the section's two answers are rate and timing.

items.stem: The chapter says rate and timing are not the only answers to how identical spikes carry information. What are the others, and why are they held back?

options.text: Which chemical crosses the junction, how strong that connection is, and which cell fired — all properties of the wiring rather than of one cell's output.
options.why: Correct. Rate and timing come first because they are what a single cell can vary from moment to moment on its own.

options.text: The size of the spike, the shape of the spike, and the speed of conduction — all properties the chapter has not yet defined.
options.why: Size and shape do not vary at all, so none of the three could carry information in the way the question supposes.

options.text: The number of dendrites, the length of the axon, and the thickness of the myelin — all anatomical facts held over to the physical account.
options.why: Anatomy is indeed held over, but these are not offered as further answers to how a spike train carries information.

options.text: The animal's internal state, its recent experience, and its species — all facts about the organism rather than the signal.
options.why: Internal state does reach circuits through modulation, but the three answers the section names are all properties of connections.

items.stem: A neuron's output is all-or-nothing, and a neuron's output is a rate that can take many values. How does the chapter reconcile the two descriptions?

options.text: They are descriptions at two different time scales rather than competing theories: one millisecond holds an event, a hundred milliseconds holds a count.
options.why: Correct. Someone who takes them for rival claims will be lost, which is why the reconciliation gets a section to itself.

options.text: Two different descriptions apply to two different cells: all-or-nothing to sensory neurons, a rate to the interneurons receiving from them.
options.why: No such division by cell type is drawn, and both descriptions are said to be true of the same cell.

options.text: The all-or-nothing description is the older view, replaced by the rate description once recording from single cells became possible.
options.why: The chapter presents them as two live descriptions rather than as a historical succession.

options.text: One of the two descriptions is a simplification offered for teaching; the other is what happens inside a working nervous system.
options.why: Both are said to be true, and neither is offered as a stand-in for the other.

items.stem: A neuron's output is described both as all-or-nothing and as a rate that varies. Which statement captures the chapter's reconciliation of the two most exactly?

options.text: A rate is what a lot of all-or-nothing events look like when they stop being looked at one at a time.
options.why: Correct. A rate is not an alternative to all-or-nothing signaling; it is the same signaling seen at a coarser grain.

options.text: A rate is an average over spikes that individually vary, so the variation cancels out and only the average is meaningful.
options.why: There is no variation among spikes to average over, which is what makes the count rather than the sizes informative.

options.text: A rate is a separate signal that a neuron computes alongside its spikes, so nothing about the two descriptions actually conflicts.
options.why: Nothing separate is computed or sent. The rate is a property of the spikes themselves.

options.text: A rate is an approximation that becomes exact only when a neuron is firing near its maximum possible speed.
options.why: No such condition is attached, and the account works equally well for a cell firing occasionally.

items.stem: What settles which of the two descriptions of a neuron's output — all-or-nothing, or a rate — is the right one to use?

options.text: The question being asked: behavior over a stretch of time calls for the rate, and how one event is physically produced calls for the single spike.
options.why: Correct. This is Marr's point arriving in a new place, and it is why the chapter can use both descriptions without contradiction.

options.text: The kind of neuron under study, since sensory cells are best described by rates and motor cells by individual events.
options.why: Cell type is not what decides. Both descriptions are offered as applying to the same cell.

options.text: The recording technique available, since some methods resolve single spikes and others only average activity.
options.why: Method is not the criterion the chapter gives, and its argument is about what is being asked rather than what can be measured.

options.text: The species being studied, since larger animals require the rate description and smaller ones the single-spike description.
options.why: No species-dependence of this kind appears anywhere in the chapter.

items.stem: The chapter announces that its algorithmic account will describe neurons in rates and its implementational account will describe a single spike in ions crossing a membrane. What does it say about the two descriptions looking nothing alike?

options.text: That it is not a problem to be resolved but what having multiple levels of analysis is for.
options.why: Correct. This is the chapter's cleanest statement of what Marr's levels buy, and §3.3.4 makes it concrete with two models.

options.text: That one of the two will eventually be shown to reduce to the other once the biology is fully understood.
options.why: Reduction of that kind is not what the chapter expects, and §3.3.4 argues that neither model is a version of the other.

options.text: That the difference is a sign the field has not yet settled on a single correct description of the cell.
options.why: The difference is presented as a feature of good explanation rather than as unfinished business.

options.text: That the rate description is a summary of the ion description, and so contains strictly less information.
options.why: The rate model answers questions the ion model cannot, so it is not simply a lossy summary of it.

items.stem: A receptor is stimulated twice, gently and then hard. What differs between the two responses?

options.text: How many spikes there are, and how close together they come.
options.why: Correct. Nothing about any individual spike has changed; what changed is the number of them in a stretch of time.

options.text: How large each spike is, and how long each one takes.
options.why: Neither quantity varies with stimulus strength, which is the correction §3.2.4 and §3.2.5 both make.

options.text: How far each spike travels before it fades away.
options.why: Spikes are regenerated at full strength and do not fade, which is the property that makes the whole scheme reliable.

options.text: How many cells the signal is sent onward to.
options.why: Recruitment across cells is a population-level idea, and the section is about what one cell's output does.

items.stem: In what sense is the information in DNA an instance of the same design choice as an all-or-nothing spike?

options.text: It is carried by which of four bases occupies each position rather than by how much of anything is present.
options.why: Correct. That is why a sequence can be copied for billions of years and still be read correctly: a discrete signal can be restored.

options.text: It is carried in a molecule that is chemically stable, so the message does not degrade even over very long periods.
options.why: Stability helps, but the design point is about discreteness rather than durability, and the chapter's argument turns on the former.

options.text: It is copied by a process that checks each new strand against the old one and repairs any differences it finds.
options.why: Proofreading is not what the chapter appeals to here; the discrete code is what makes checking possible in the first place.

options.text: It is stored in two complementary strands, so a damaged sequence can be reconstructed from the surviving half.
options.why: Complementary strands are mentioned in §3.1.3 for a different purpose, and they are not the discreteness argument.

items.stem: Which term names the sequence of spikes a neuron produces, considered as a series rather than as separate events?

options.text: spike train
options.why: Correct. Its rate is the first property the chapter draws information from, and the timing within it is the second.

options.text: connectome
options.why: That is a complete wiring diagram of a nervous system, which is a map of connections rather than a record of activity.

options.text: refractory period
options.why: That is the brief interval after a spike during which no amount of input can make the cell fire again.

options.text: sparse coding
options.why: That is activity in which only a small share of cells are strongly active at once, which describes a population.

items.stem: Having established that every spike a neuron fires is identical, what objection does the chapter raise against itself before answering it?

options.text: If every spike is identical, a cell that can produce only one signal looks as though it can carry only one message.
options.why: Correct. The section exists to answer that objection, and the answer is that the message lies in how many spikes and when.

options.text: If every spike is identical, then two different neurons cannot be told apart by anything they do.
options.why: Distinguishing cells is not the worry raised, and which cell fired is named later as a separate carrier of information.

options.text: If every spike is identical, then a neuron cannot signal anything at all, since identical events carry no information.
options.why: The objection as stated is that only one message is available rather than none, and the difference matters to the answer.

options.text: If every spike is identical, then the threshold serves no purpose, since any input above zero produces the same result.
options.why: The threshold is not what the objection targets, and inputs below threshold produce nothing at all.

items.stem: Using the fingertip example, explain in a short paragraph why a rate code solves a problem that neither chemical signaling nor a single all-or-nothing spike solves on its own.
items.answer: A receptor in the fingertip has to report not merely that contact happened but how firmly, and to report it most of a meter away. A chemical signal can carry the amount easily, since the quantity released can be made proportional to the pressure, but left to diffusion it takes years to cross the arm, and carried in the blood it arrives everywhere in the body rather than at the one place that needs it. A single all-or-nothing spike arrives in milliseconds and arrives intact, but it can only report that something was touched. The firing rate gets both: the spikes are identical and regenerated, so the message survives the trip, and the number of them in a second is a quantity that can take any value in a range.
rubric: States what the fingertip must report: both that contact happened and how much, over most of a meter.
Gives chemistry's failure — the amount is easy, but diffusion is far too slow and the bloodstream arrives everywhere.
Gives the single-spike failure — fast and intact, but reports only that, not how much.
Explains that the rate carries a quantity on a substrate that survives the distance.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how a neuron's output can be both all-or-nothing and a rate that takes many values, and what the chapter says that dual description illustrates.
items.answer: The two are descriptions at different time scales rather than rival theories. Looked at across a single millisecond there is either a spike or there is not, and any spike there is the same size as all the others. Looked at across a hundred milliseconds there is a count instead, and a count is a number that can land anywhere in a range. So a rate is not an alternative to all-or-nothing signaling; it is what a lot of all-or-nothing events look like when they stop being examined one at a time. The chapter uses this to illustrate what having multiple levels of analysis is for: two descriptions of one cell can look nothing alike without either being wrong.
rubric: Identifies the two descriptions as operating at different time scales.
Describes what is seen at the short scale (one event, fixed size) and at the long scale (a count).
States that a rate is not an alternative to all-or-nothing signaling but the same events seen together.
Connects the reconciliation to what multiple levels of analysis are for.

items.stem: Asking Marr's question about the all-or-nothing design, the lecture presses the objection harder than the chapter does. How does it press it?

options.text: Size is free, and size is right there — so throwing away the option of letting the signal's size carry the message needs an explanation.
options.why: Correct. Making the discarded option look obviously attractive is what turns the design into something requiring a reason rather than a fact to memorize.

options.text: Size is expensive, so a system that could avoid encoding anything in it would have a reason to do so from the beginning.
options.why: The lecture's point is the reverse: size costs nothing, which is exactly why discarding it looks strange until the reason arrives.

options.text: Size is unreliable in every signaling system, so no biological or engineered design has ever tried to use it.
options.why: Graded signals that carry meaning in their size are perfectly real, and the small voltage shifts arriving at a cell are among them.

options.text: Size is what chemical signaling already used, so a new system had to differ from it in order to be worth building.
options.why: Differing for its own sake is not the argument, and the trade the module describes is about speed, distance and aim.

items.stem: Having given digital electronics and DNA alongside the spike, the lecture states one sentence it calls the general principle underneath all three. What is it?

options.text: A discrete signal can be checked and restored; a continuous one can only be approximated.
options.why: Correct. Stating it as a principle rather than as three facts is what makes the convergence an argument about the design.

options.text: A discrete signal is cheaper to produce than a continuous one, which is why all three systems converged on it.
options.why: Cost is not the shared reason given; the shared problem is getting a message somewhere intact.

options.text: A discrete signal carries less information per event, which is compensated for by sending events more frequently.
options.why: Information per event is not the principle stated, though rate coding does exploit frequency.

options.text: A discrete signal is easier to generate biologically, which is why evolution found it twice before engineers did.
options.why: Ease of biological generation would not explain the digital-electronics case, which is one of the three.

items.stem: The lecture calls the objection it raises "exactly right" before answering it. What does it concede?

options.text: That if every spike is identical, a cell producing only one signal looks as though it can carry only one message.
options.why: Correct. Conceding the objection rather than brushing it aside is what makes the rate answer worth having.

options.text: That the all-or-nothing description is a simplification which the third lecture will have to correct.
options.why: The third lecture explains all-or-nothing firing rather than correcting it; the description stands.
