options.text: That a single neuron cannot carry enough information to be worth studying on its own.
options.why: No such concession is made, and the lecture's whole closing slide is about how much three or four cells can do.

options.text: That the firing rate is a less precise code than a graded signal would have been.
options.why: The lecture argues the reverse: a graded signal loses its precision entirely over distance.

items.stem: The lecture says reconciling the two time scales shows Marr's point "arriving in a new place and doing real work." What work is the point doing there?

options.text: It settles which description to use by asking which question is being asked, and so divides the labor between this lecture and the next.
options.why: Correct. Rates for what a cell contributes to a circuit; a single spike for how the cell physically produces one event.

options.text: It shows that the algorithmic level is more useful than the implementational one for most questions about behavior.
options.why: The lecture is careful that neither level is more useful in general; each answers a question the other cannot.

options.text: It proves that the two descriptions must eventually be unified, which is the work the next lecture begins.
options.why: Unification is what the module explicitly does not expect, and the two descriptions are kept side by side.

options.text: It demonstrates that a model can be tested by checking whether its two descriptions agree with each other.
options.why: Agreement between the descriptions is not a test, and the two are said to look nothing alike.

items.stem: The lecture runs the fingertip example by taking the two already-rejected options one at a time before giving the answer. Reconstruct that sequence in a short paragraph.
items.answer: The receptors have to report not merely that contact happened but how much of it, most of a meter away. Chemical only: the amount is easy, since the quantity released can be made proportional to the pressure, but left to diffusion the message takes years to cross the arm, and carried in the blood it arrives faster and also arrives everywhere rather than at the one place that needs it. Purely all-or-none: one spike for contact and nothing otherwise arrives in milliseconds and arrives intact, but it can report only that something was touched, not how firmly. The firing rate gets both, because the spikes are identical and regenerated so the message survives the trip, while the number of them in a second is a quantity that can take any value in a range.
rubric: States what the fingertip has to report, including the distance.
Gives chemistry's two failures — years by diffusion, everywhere by blood — alongside what it does well.
Gives the single-spike failure: fast and intact, but reports only that contact happened.
Explains that a rate carries a quantity on a substrate that survives the journey.

pools.title: Signed Inputs, and the Model Neuron
pools.covers: reading §3.2.7, §3.2.8, §3.2.9, §3.2.10 · lecture 3.2 slides push_pull_and_dial, writing_a_neuron_down, what_the_model_is_worth, the_same_function_in_silicon, three_cells_in_a_row

items.stem: What is a neurotransmitter?

options.text: A chemical a sending cell releases at a junction, which crosses the gap and binds to the receiving cell.
options.why: Correct. Which transmitter arrives is what settles whether the effect on the receiving cell is excitatory or inhibitory.

options.text: A protein pore in the membrane that lets a particular kind of ion through when it is open and not when it is closed.
options.why: That is an ion channel, defined in §3.3.2. Transmitters are what open some of those channels rather than being the channels.

options.text: The brief electrical event that travels the length of a cell once its inputs have pushed it past its threshold.
options.why: That is the action potential, which arrives at the junction and causes release rather than being the thing released.

options.text: The strength and sign of a connection between two cells, which determines how much one input contributes to the total.
options.why: That is a weight, defined in §3.2.8 as part of writing the neuron down as an equation.

items.stem: Which term names the chemical released by a sending cell that drifts across the gap between cells and binds to the one receiving?

options.text: neurotransmitter
options.why: Correct. Signals usually cross the junction between cells chemically, and the identity of the chemical settles the effect.

options.text: ion channel
options.why: That is a protein pore through the membrane that admits a particular ion, which is what a transmitter's arrival can open.

options.text: action potential
options.why: That is the electrical event traveling along a cell, which triggers release at the end of the output line.

options.text: connectome
options.why: That is a complete map of every cell and every connection in a nervous system, rather than anything that crosses a gap.

items.stem: What does it mean for a neurotransmitter to be excitatory?

options.text: It pushes the receiving neuron toward its threshold, making a spike more likely.
options.why: Correct. The definition is given entirely in terms of the threshold, which is what keeps §3.2.7 at the algorithmic level.

options.text: It causes the receiving neuron to fire a spike immediately, regardless of what else is arriving at that cell.
options.why: No single input compels a spike. Excitatory inputs shift the total, and the threshold still decides the outcome.

options.text: It increases the size of the spike the receiving neuron produces, so a stronger message is passed further along.
options.why: Spike size does not vary at all, which is the all-or-nothing property established in §3.2.4.

options.text: It raises the receiving neuron's threshold, so that more input is needed before that cell will produce an output.
options.why: Raising the threshold would make firing less likely, which is closer to the opposite of what the word names.

items.stem: Which term names a neurotransmitter that pushes the receiving neuron away from its threshold, making a spike less likely?

options.text: inhibitory
options.why: Correct. Because the integrator sums both signs together, inhibition subtracts from the total rather than merely failing to add.

options.text: excitatory
options.why: That names the opposite effect: pushing the receiving neuron toward its threshold so that a spike becomes more likely.

options.text: modulatory
options.why: That names signals that change how strongly a cell responds to everything else rather than pushing it either way.

options.text: refractory
options.why: That describes the interval after a spike when no amount of input can make the cell fire, rather than a kind of transmitter.

items.stem: What is modulatory signaling?

options.text: Signals that change how strongly a neuron responds to everything else, turning its sensitivity up or down.
options.why: Correct. It is a third category alongside excitation and inhibition rather than a stronger version of either.

options.text: Signals that push a neuron toward its threshold so strongly that the cell fires whatever else is arriving at it.
options.why: That would be an unusually strong excitatory input rather than a different category of effect.

options.text: Signals that travel between cells electrically rather than chemically, and so arrive faster than a transmitter can.
options.why: Electrical transmission is not what the term names, and the chapter describes junction crossing as usually chemical.

options.text: Signals that change the strength of a connection permanently, so a later input has a different effect from an earlier one.
options.why: Lasting changes to a connection are Module 5's subject, and modulation as defined here is about present sensitivity.

items.stem: Which term names signals that turn a neuron's whole sensitivity up or down rather than pushing it toward or away from its threshold?

options.text: modulatory signaling
options.why: Correct. It is how an animal's internal state reaches into a circuit and changes what that circuit does with the same inputs.

options.text: inhibitory signaling
options.why: That pushes a neuron away from its threshold, which is one of the two directions modulation is defined against.

options.text: saltatory conduction
options.why: That is a spike jumping between the bare gaps in a myelin sheath, which concerns travel along one cell.

options.text: sparse coding
options.why: That describes only a small share of a population being strongly active at once, which is a fact about many cells.

items.stem: A circuit that recognizes food responds differently when an animal is hungry than when it is not, with the same input arriving either way. What does the chapter attribute that to?

options.text: Modulatory signaling, which is how an internal state reaches into a circuit and changes what it does with unchanged inputs.
options.why: Correct. The specific chemicals that do this work, and the account of value they make possible, are held over to Module 4.

options.text: A change in the wiring of the circuit, since hunger causes new connections to form between the cells involved.
options.why: Connections changing is Module 5's topic, and it operates far more slowly than a shift between hungry and not.

options.text: A change in the threshold of the sensory cells, so that a hungry animal detects food at a lower concentration than a fed one.
options.why: Sensory thresholds are not what the chapter adjusts here, and modulation is described as acting on the whole cell's responsiveness.

options.text: A change in which transmitter the sensory cells release, so the same input is reported to the circuit as a different signal.
options.why: Nothing about switching transmitters is described, and the input reaching the circuit is said to be the same.

items.stem: A neuron stays silent unless two of its inputs arrive close together in time. Which of the operations the chapter names does that describe?

options.text: A coincidence detector.
options.why: Correct. Summing signed inputs is what makes this possible, and it is one of three operations the section names.

options.text: A veto.
options.why: A veto turns on a single inhibitory input's power to silence the cell rather than on two inputs arriving together.

options.text: This and not that, on two inputs.
options.why: That operation turns on the combination of an active and a silent input rather than on timing between two active ones.

options.text: Modulation.
options.why: Modulation changes responsiveness generally rather than producing a requirement that two inputs coincide.

items.stem: What does the chapter say the balance between excitation and inhibition accomplishes?

options.text: It turns a chain of cells passing messages along into an assembly that computes something.
options.why: Correct. None of the operations it makes possible — this and not that, coincidence, veto — is a matter of relaying anything.

options.text: It keeps the overall level of activity in a nervous system steady, so that no region ever becomes overloaded.
options.why: Regulating total activity is not the function claimed here, though the energy budget in §3.3.8 does constrain how much firing is possible.

options.text: It ensures that every input a cell receives is eventually passed along, with inhibition merely delaying rather than blocking it.
options.why: Inhibition subtracts rather than delays, and a well-placed inhibitory connection can shut a cell down entirely.

options.text: It allows a cell to distinguish inputs that arrived from nearby cells from those that arrived from distant ones.
options.why: Distance is not encoded in the sign of an input, and §3.2.2 already separated connection from proximity.

items.stem: What is a connection's weight, in the chapter's model of a neuron?

options.text: Its strength together with its sign: positive for an excitatory input, negative for an inhibitory one.
options.why: Correct. Each input's rate is multiplied by its weight before everything is summed, which is how the sign does arithmetic.

options.text: The number of spikes arriving along that connection in a stretch of time, which the receiving cell then adds to its total.
options.why: That is the input's firing rate, which the model writes separately and then multiplies by the weight.

options.text: The level the receiving cell's total has to reach before that connection is able to produce any effect at all.
options.why: That is the threshold, which is a property of the receiving cell rather than of any one connection.

options.text: The physical distance the signal has to travel along that connection, which sets how long the input takes to arrive.
options.why: The model ignores timing entirely, which §3.2.9 lists first among its deliberate omissions.

items.stem: Which term names a connection's strength together with its sign, by which an input's rate is multiplied before the total is summed?

options.text: weight
options.why: Correct. In an artificial network the positive and negative weights play exactly the roles excitation and inhibition play in a cell.

options.text: baseline
options.why: That is the low background rate at which most neurons fire when nothing is arriving, written as its own term in the model.

options.text: threshold
options.why: That is the level the summed input must reach for the cell to act, rather than a property of an individual connection.

options.text: firing rate
options.why: That is the quantity a weight is applied to, namely how many spikes an input cell produces in a stretch of time.

items.stem: In the model y = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + b₃x₃, what does each part stand for?

options.text: Each input's rate multiplied by that connection's weight, all summed, with the cell's baseline firing rate added.
options.why: Correct. The equation is the rate description written down precisely enough to compute with and to wire to other units.

options.text: Each input's rate multiplied by the receiving cell's own threshold, all of them summed together, with the strongest of the inputs added on at the end.
options.why: The threshold is not a multiplier and does not appear in the equation at all; the multiplier is a weight per connection.

options.text: Each connection's weight added to the next, with the resulting total multiplied by the cell's own firing rate.
options.why: Weights multiply rates rather than being added to each other, and the cell's rate is the output rather than a multiplier.

options.text: Each input's spike size multiplied by the delay before it arrives, all summed across the inputs to the cell.
options.why: Spike size does not vary, and the model ignores timing entirely, so neither quantity is in the equation.

items.stem: A modeled neuron has baseline 5, an excitatory input of weight 2 firing at 10, and an inhibitory input of weight −3 that is silent. The inhibitory input then comes on at 5. What happens?

options.text: The output falls from 25 to 10 spikes per second, even though the excitatory drive did not change at all.
options.why: Correct. That is inhibition doing arithmetic, and it is the mechanism behind Module 4's claims about how circuits decide.

options.text: The output falls from 25 to 20 spikes per second, since the inhibitory input subtracts its own rate from the excitatory total.
options.why: The rate is multiplied by the weight before it is subtracted, so the reduction is 15 rather than 5.

options.text: The output stays at 25 spikes per second, since an inhibitory input can only prevent a cell from firing above its threshold.
options.why: Inhibition is summed into the total continuously rather than acting only as a block at the threshold.

options.text: The output falls to zero, since any inhibitory input arriving alongside excitation cancels the excitation entirely.
options.why: Nothing in the model cancels; inhibition contributes a negative term whose size depends on both its weight and its rate.

items.stem: Pushing the same worked example further gives a total of −20. What does the chapter conclude from that?

options.text: A neuron cannot fire a negative number of times per second, so the sum needs a further step holding the output at zero below zero.
options.why: Correct. A ceiling is needed too, since no neuron fires faster than a few hundred times a second, and Module 4 supplies both repairs.

options.text: The weights in the example were chosen badly, and a realistic set of weights would keep the total above zero.
options.why: The chapter uses the negative result deliberately, as a way of showing the model failing at its own edge.

options.text: The model is wrong and should be replaced by the Hodgkin-Huxley account, which never produces impossible values.
options.why: §3.3.4 argues that neither model is a version of the other, and the linear model is kept rather than replaced.

options.text: Inhibition must therefore be capped in real cells, so that pushing the example further can never drive a total below zero.
options.why: The repair the chapter proposes is applied to the output rather than to how much inhibition a cell can receive.

items.stem: Why does the chapter go to the trouble of writing the account down as an equation rather than leaving it in words?

options.text: A description precise enough to compute with makes predictions about untested cases, and can be wired to others like it, run and tested.
options.why: Correct. Module 2 called that the synthetic method: understanding by building rather than only by describing.

options.text: An equation is easier to remember than a paragraph of prose, which matters here because the account is drawn on repeatedly throughout the rest of the course.
options.why: Memorability is not the argument, and the chapter's case is about what precision buys rather than convenience.

options.text: Words are imprecise, so an equation is the only way to state what a neuron does without introducing errors of interpretation.
options.why: The chapter does not disparage the verbal account; it says a computable one does additional work the verbal one cannot.

options.text: An equation shows that a neuron's behavior is fully determined, which a description in words leaves open to doubt.
options.why: Determinism is not the point at issue, and §3.2.9 immediately lists what the equation leaves out.

items.stem: Which set of omissions does the chapter attribute to the linear rate model?

options.text: Timing, the complexity of what a real cell does with inputs arriving at different points, and any refractory period, history or noise.
options.why: Correct. Each omission is a way the model is wrong, and it is wrong in those ways on purpose.

options.text: The threshold, the baseline firing rate, and the difference in sign between excitatory and inhibitory connections.
options.why: All three of these are in the model. The threshold arrives as the function the sum has to pass through.

options.text: The number of inputs a cell receives, the direction in which its signals travel, and whether a connection exists between any two given cells at all.
options.why: None of these is omitted; the equation has one term per input and presupposes a definite set of connections.

options.text: The chemical identity of each transmitter, the shape of the cell, and the energy each spike costs to produce.
options.why: These are all outside the model, but they are not the omissions the section names when it evaluates it.

items.stem: The chapter says the way a model simplifies is itself a claim. A claim about what?

options.text: About which properties matter for which kinds of explanation, and which do not.
options.why: Correct. That is why the omissions are described as deliberate rather than as defects waiting to be repaired.

options.text: About which experiments would be worth running next, since a model's gaps show where the evidence is thinnest.
options.why: Directing research is not what the chapter says the simplification asserts, though good models often do that too.

options.text: About how the modeled system evolved, since the properties a model keeps are the ones selection acted on most strongly.
options.why: No connection between a model's simplifications and evolutionary history is drawn here.

options.text: About how much detail a reader can be expected to hold at once, which is why introductory models are simpler.
options.why: The claim is about the target system rather than about the audience, and the chapter is explicit that it is theoretical.

items.stem: Some researchers argue the linear model leaves out too much. What is their objection, and what is offered against it?

options.text: That a cortical neuron's branching input surface computes enough to make it a small network; against that, the model's precision and its wireability at scale.
options.why: Correct. The chapter presents this as an open empirical question rather than settling it, and cites both sides in Further Reading.

options.text: That neurons vary too much between species for one equation to describe them; against that, the equation's use in artificial networks.
options.why: Species variation is not the objection raised, and the dissent concerns single cortical cells rather than cross-species differences.

options.text: That the model omits energy costs; against that, the observation that the same costs apply to every model of a neuron equally.
options.why: Energy is §3.3's subject and is not among the omissions §3.2.9 lists, nor is it what the dissenters press.

options.text: That the model cannot be tested experimentally; against that, the claim that untestable models are still useful for teaching.
options.why: The chapter says the reverse: what precision buys is exactly the ability to predict untried cases.

items.stem: The model of a biological neuron turns out to be almost exactly the unit at the heart of an artificial neural network. Why, on the chapter's account?

options.text: Because the artificial unit was built as a stripped-down copy of real neurons, deliberately, and is a caricature rather than a discovery.
options.why: Correct. The resemblance is neither a coincidence nor a finding, which is why the chapter is careful about how much to make of it.

options.text: Because both were derived independently from the same mathematics, which is what makes the convergence significant.
options.why: Independent arrival is what makes the digital-signal convergence in §3.2.4 interesting; here the copying is direct.

options.text: Because artificial networks were reverse-engineered from recordings of real neurons made during the same period.
options.why: No such empirical derivation is described. The copy was made from the functional description rather than from data.

options.text: Because real neurons turn out to work in exactly the way the artificial unit does, which was discovered afterward.
options.why: §3.2.9 spends most of its length saying the model leaves a great deal out, so this overstates the match considerably.

items.stem: What is multiple realizability?

options.text: The idea that one and the same mental state can be realized in different physical systems and materials.
options.why: Correct. The chapter glosses Module 1's concept here so that Module 3's glossary stands on its own.

options.text: The idea that a single physical system can be described correctly at more than one of Marr's levels at a time.
options.why: That is the levels claim rather than this one. Multiple realizability concerns one function running in different materials.

options.text: The idea that the same behavior can be produced by more than one arrangement of the same set of components.
options.why: Rewiring the same parts is the vehicles lesson in the Close, and it is a different claim from this one.

options.text: The idea that a single neuron can take part in more than one circuit, contributing to several computations at once.
options.why: Nothing about shared membership in circuits is what the term names.

items.stem: Why does the chapter call the artificial neuron the most concrete case of multiple realizability the course has met?

options.text: Because the same receive-integrate-threshold function is running in wet tissue in one case and in silicon in the other.
options.why: Correct. Module 1 argued for the claim with thought experiments, and here both realizations are built and running.

options.text: Because artificial neurons can be built from many different materials, and every one of them behaves identically.
options.why: The chapter's contrast is between two substrates rather than among many, and §3.3.9 stresses how differently they behave.

options.text: Because the artificial neuron reproduces everything a biological neuron does, which shows the material makes no difference.
options.why: The model omits a great deal, and §3.3.9 argues that the material makes a very large difference at its own level.

options.text: Because a single artificial network can be trained to imitate any biological nervous system that has been mapped.
options.why: No such claim is made, and the one network-imitates-a-cell result cited is an argument against the model's sufficiency.

items.stem: What is a connectome?

options.text: A complete wiring diagram of a nervous system: every cell, and every connection between them.
options.why: Correct. C. elegans was the first animal for which one was worked out, with exactly 302 neurons in the adult hermaphrodite.

options.text: A record of every action potential a nervous system produces over a stretch of time, cell by cell.
options.why: That would be a record of activity rather than of structure, and no such map is what the term names.

options.text: A catalog of the neurotransmitters used at each junction in a nervous system, and of the receptors that respond to them.
options.why: Chemistry at the junctions is a different level of description from the wiring diagram the term picks out.

options.text: A map showing where in an animal's body each of its neurons is physically located relative to the others.
options.why: Position is not what a connectome records, and §3.2.2 has already said connection is a matter of wiring rather than proximity.

items.stem: Which term names a complete map of every cell in a nervous system and every connection between those cells?

options.text: connectome
options.why: Correct. The worm's was the first to be worked out, which is why the chapter uses that animal to close the algorithmic section.

options.text: spike train
options.why: That is the sequence of spikes one cell produces, which is a record of activity rather than a map of structure.

options.text: multiple realizability
options.why: That is Module 1's claim about one function running in different physical materials, unrelated to mapping connections.

options.text: coordination problem
options.why: That is the difficulty specialization creates in a multicellular body, from the computational section of the chapter.

items.stem: What is the architecture that produces C. elegans's behavior, as the chapter describes it?

options.text: Sensory neurons respond to chemicals, their output lines run to interneurons that sum and compare against a threshold, and those drive motor neurons.
options.why: Correct. Sense, integrate, act, in an animal, using three or four cells in a row — the loop of §3.1 made out of neurons.

options.text: A single layer of cells that both detect chemicals in the water and contract the muscles that bend the worm's body.
options.why: The chapter describes a chain of three kinds of cell, and the intervening step is where the integration happens.

options.text: A central cluster that receives from every sensory cell at once and issues commands to every muscle simultaneously.
options.why: No central cluster of that kind is described, and the arrangement given is a short chain rather than a hub.

options.text: A network in which each of the 302 neurons connects to all of the others, so any input can influence any output.
options.why: Full connectivity is not claimed, and it would make the connectome uninformative as a map.

items.stem: A student concludes that C. elegans behaves as richly as it does because each of its 302 neurons is individually sophisticated. What does the chapter say?

options.text: Most of what the worm can do depends on how its neurons are organized rather than on what any one of them computes.
options.why: Correct. The same point returns in the Close: meaning is a property of an arrangement rather than of a cell.

options.text: Each of the worm's neurons is indeed unusually complex, which is what compensates for there being so few of them.
options.why: No such compensation is claimed, and the cells are described as doing exactly what §3.2.3 said cells do.

options.text: The worm's behavior comes from chemical signaling rather than from its neurons at all, which is the reason so few nerve cells turn out to suffice.
options.why: The chapter attributes the behavior to the neurons and their arrangement rather than to a chemical route around them.

options.text: The worm's 302 neurons are too few to explain its behavior, which remains an unsolved problem in the field.
options.why: The section presents the worm as showing the gap is smaller than it looks rather than as an open puzzle.

items.stem: What does the chapter list among the things a 302-neuron worm actually does?

options.text: It steers toward the smell of food and away from damaging substances, reverses when its nose meets an obstacle, and changes what it does when it has not eaten.
options.why: Correct. That last one is a change with internal state, and the chapter hands the circuits behind it to Module 4.

options.text: It builds structures in the soil, navigates back to them, and returns along a remembered route after foraging.
options.why: None of these is attributed to the worm, and route memory in particular is not part of the example.

options.text: It communicates with other worms chemically, coordinating movement across a population toward the richest patch.
options.why: Signaling between worms is not described, and the behaviors given are those of an individual animal.

options.text: It learns to associate a new smell with food after a single pairing, and retains that association for the rest of its life.
options.why: Learning of that kind is Module 5's subject, and the chapter does not credit the worm with it here.

items.stem: Turning to excitation and inhibition, the chapter opens by naming a simplification it is about to correct and closes by deferring a question to the implementational level. Which pair is it?

options.text: The simplification was treating all inputs as pushing toward threshold; the deferred question is which particular chemicals do each job.
options.why: Correct. §3.2.7 teaches excitation and inhibition as functional categories and deliberately names no molecules at all.

options.text: The simplification was treating a neuron as summing its inputs; the deferred question is whether real cells sum at all.
options.why: The summing description is retained here, and the hedge about its sufficiency belongs to §3.2.3 and §3.2.9.

options.text: The simplification was treating every spike as identical; the deferred question is how a spike is physically produced.
options.why: Spikes really are identical in this chapter, so that is not a simplification being corrected in this section.

options.text: The simplification was treating connections as fixed; the deferred question is how they change with experience.
options.why: Changing connections is deferred to Module 5 rather than to §3.3, and it is not the simplification named here.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why summing inputs of two different signs lets a neuron do more than register how much is arriving, and give two of the operations the chapter names.
items.answer: If every input pushed the same way, the cell's total would only ever record how much input there was, and the cell's output would rise and fall with that quantity. Because the integrator sums excitatory and inhibitory inputs together, the total depends on which inputs are active rather than only on how many. That makes several operations available: firing only when one input is active while another is silent, which is the beginning of this and not that; staying quiet unless several inputs arrive close together, which is a coincidence detector; and being shut down entirely by a single well-placed inhibitory connection, which is a veto. None of these is relaying anything, which is why the chapter says the balance turns a chain into an assembly that computes.
rubric: Explains that inputs of one sign only would let the cell register quantity alone.
States that summing signed inputs makes the total depend on which inputs are active.
Names at least two of the three operations: this and not that, coincidence detection, veto.
Draws the conclusion that this is computing rather than relaying.

items.stem: The chapter says the linear model is "wrong on purpose." In a few sentences, explain what that means and what it implies about how the model should be judged.
items.answer: A model is a deliberate simplification, and the particular things it leaves out are not oversights: the way a model simplifies is a theoretical claim about which properties matter for which kinds of explanation and which do not. So the linear model's omissions — timing, the complexity of the input surface, any refractory period, history or noise — are assertions that those properties can be set aside for the questions the model is meant to answer. That makes the model's correctness an open, empirical question rather than a matter of listing what it omits: the omissions are the claim being tested, not a catalog of failures.
rubric: States that the simplification is deliberate rather than an oversight.
Explains that the way a model simplifies is a claim about which properties matter.
Names at least two of the model's actual omissions.
Concludes that whether the model is right is an open empirical question.

items.stem: A modeled neuron has a baseline of 5 spikes per second, an excitatory input of weight 2, and an inhibitory input of weight −3. Work out its output when the excitatory input fires at 10 and the inhibitory input at 5, and say what the calculation demonstrates.
items.answer: The output is 5 + 2(10) + (−3)(5), which is 5 + 20 − 15, or 10 spikes per second. Compared with the case where the inhibitory input is silent, which gives 25 spikes per second, the cell's output has fallen by more than half while the excitatory drive has not changed at all. What the calculation demonstrates is inhibition doing arithmetic: a negative weight subtracts a quantity proportional to its input's rate, so what the cell reports depends on the balance of its inputs rather than on how much excitation is arriving.
rubric: Sets up the calculation with each rate multiplied by its weight and the baseline added.
Arrives at 10 spikes per second.
Notes that the excitatory drive is unchanged while the output falls by more than half.
Draws the conclusion that inhibition subtracts arithmetically rather than merely blocking.

items.stem: In the chapter's model of a neuron, what is the baseline firing rate written as b₀?

options.text: The low background rate at which most neurons fire when nothing is arriving at them.
options.why: Correct. Most neurons are not silent when left alone, so the model adds this term to the weighted sum of the inputs.

options.text: The lowest rate at which a neuron can fire once its summed input has crossed the threshold and it has begun to respond.
options.why: The model has no separate minimum for a responding cell; what it adds is the rate the cell holds when nothing is arriving.

options.text: The rate at which the slowest of a cell's inputs is firing, which sets a floor on how much total input can arrive.
options.why: The inputs' rates appear in the equation as the terms being weighted, and none of them is picked out as a floor.

options.text: The maximum rate a neuron can reach, which the model imposes as a ceiling of a few hundred spikes per second.
options.why: A ceiling is a real constraint on a cell, but §3.2.8 raises it as something the linear model does not include.

items.stem: Introducing excitation and inhibition, the lecture says that at this level of description only two things are needed. What are they, and what is deferred?

options.text: A plus and a minus; which particular chemicals do which job is deferred to the third lecture of the module.
options.why: Correct. The slide keeps §3.2 free of molecule names on purpose, which is the same separation the four-jobs slide makes for the anatomy.

options.text: A threshold and a baseline; which inputs are excitatory and which inhibitory is deferred to the third lecture.
options.why: The signs are exactly what this slide supplies, and the threshold arrived two slides earlier.

options.text: A rate and a weight; the arithmetic that combines them is deferred until the account is written down as an equation.
options.why: Weights arrive later in this lecture, but they are not what the plus and minus stand for here.

options.text: A sender and a receiver; the chemistry of the junction between them is deferred to Module 4.
options.why: The junction's chemistry belongs to the third lecture of this module rather than to Module 4.

items.stem: The lecture calls one of the operations a plus and a minus make possible "a logical operation, performed by one cell." Which one?

options.text: Firing only when one input is active and another is silent — this and not that.
options.why: Correct. The lecture points at it specifically because it shows a single cell doing something no relay could do.

options.text: Staying quiet unless several inputs arrive close together in time, which is a coincidence detector.
options.why: That is one of the three operations named, but it is described as detecting coincidence rather than as a logical operation.

options.text: Being shut down entirely by a single well-placed inhibitory connection, which is a veto.
options.why: A veto is also named, and the lecture reserves the logical-operation description for the this and not that case.

options.text: Turning the cell's whole sensitivity up or down in response to the animal's internal state.
options.why: That is modulatory signaling, which the slide introduces as a separate third category rather than as an operation.

items.stem: Having driven the model to an impossible output of −20 spikes per second, the lecture declines to fix it. Why?

options.text: Because noticing that the model breaks is more useful than being handed the patch, so the repair is left as a problem for Module 4.
options.why: Correct. The floor and the ceiling are both stated as constraints the sum has to be made to respect rather than as difficulties to be smoothed over.

options.text: Because the repair requires mathematics the course has not covered, so it is deferred until students have the background.
options.why: No background requirement is given as the reason, and the repair is described as one of several simple modifications.

options.text: Because the negative result is an artifact of the numbers chosen, so a more realistic example would not produce it.
options.why: The lecture uses the negative result deliberately rather than treating it as a badly chosen illustration.

options.text: Because the linear model is abandoned at this point in favor of the Hodgkin-Huxley account given in the next lecture.
options.why: Both models are kept, and the next lecture argues at length that neither replaces the other.

items.stem: The lecture compresses its claim about simplification into one line it says generalizes far beyond neurons. What is the line?

options.text: A simplification is not a shrug. It is an assertion.
options.why: Correct. Which means it can be wrong, and whether a model is right about its simplifying claims is an open empirical question.

options.text: A simplification is not a model. It is a summary of one.
options.why: The lecture treats the simplification as constitutive of the model rather than as something separate from it.

options.text: A simplification is not a choice. It is forced by what can be measured.
options.why: The lecture presents the choice of what to leave out as deliberate rather than as imposed by the available data.

options.text: A simplification is not permanent. It is a placeholder for detail that later work supplies.
options.why: The omissions are presented as claims worth defending rather than as gaps awaiting filling.

items.stem: Having given the dissenting view that a cortical neuron is better understood as a small network, the lecture states what the argument for the model actually is. What is it?

options.text: That the trade is worth making — precision about untried input combinations, and simplicity enough to wire thousands together — not that the model is true.
options.why: Correct. The lecture is explicit that it is not resolving the live disagreement, and that the case for the model is a trade rather than a claim of truth.

options.text: That the dissenting researchers are describing a special case, since most neurons are not cortical and do not have branching input surfaces.
options.why: No such restriction is offered, and the lecture treats the disagreement as unresolved rather than as answered.

options.text: That the model is true of artificial neurons even if it is not true of biological ones, which is enough to make it worth teaching.
options.why: The model was arrived at by describing a biological cell, and the artificial unit was copied from it afterward.

options.text: That the dissent concerns details the model could absorb, so the disagreement is about emphasis rather than about substance.
options.why: The lecture calls it a live disagreement from people who work on this, and declines to resolve it.

items.stem: The lecture stresses one thing about C. elegans's neuron count that the chapter does not state. What is it?

options.text: There are exactly three hundred and two, not approximately, and the same three hundred and two in every individual.
options.why: Correct. That invariance is what makes a complete wiring diagram of the species a meaningful object rather than a portrait of one worm.

options.text: There are exactly three hundred and two in the adult, and a different number at every earlier stage of development.
options.why: Developmental change in the count is not discussed, and it is not what the lecture emphasizes.

options.text: There are exactly three hundred and two in the hermaphrodite, and no other nematode has been counted.
options.why: Other counts are not mentioned either way, and the emphasis falls on the invariance rather than on uniqueness.

options.text: There are approximately three hundred and two, and the figure is an average across the individuals mapped so far.
options.why: This is precisely what the lecture rules out by saying "not approximately, exactly."

items.stem: The lecture states multiple realizability rather than recalling it, and puts it as a conditional. What is the conditional?

options.text: If what makes something a neuron functionally is what it does rather than what it is made of, the same function could run in more than one kind of stuff.
options.why: Correct. The lecture then says this is not a thought experiment: here is one function running in wet tissue and in silicon, both built and both working.

options.text: If two systems compute the same function, then they must share some physical property rather than merely a functional description.
options.why: A shared physical property is close to the opposite of the claim, which is that the substrates could hardly be more different.

options.text: If a function can be written down as an equation, then any system that satisfies the equation counts as a mind in the relevant sense of the word.
options.why: The lecture makes no claim that satisfying the equation confers mindedness, and calls the artificial unit a caricature.

options.text: If a model of a cell resembles an engineered unit, then the engineered unit was probably derived from the biology.
options.why: The derivation is stated as a historical fact rather than inferred from the resemblance.

pools.title: The Membrane, the Spike, and Two Models
pools.covers: reading §3.3.1, §3.3.2, §3.3.3, §3.3.4 · lecture 3.3 slides the_implementational_question, how_a_spike_happens, why_all_or_nothing, two_models_of_one_neuron

items.stem: What are the dendrites of a neuron?

options.text: The input surface: a branching collection of tendrils reaching out from the cell body, each carrying signals from a different source.
options.why: Correct. There are often thousands of them, and §3.2.9's objection about single-cell complexity is about this surface in particular.

options.text: The output line: a single long fiber carrying the cell's verdict away, sometimes for a meter or more in a large animal.
options.why: That is the axon. A cell has many dendrites and one axon, which is part of what makes the flow through it one-way.

options.text: The junction where one cell's output becomes the next cell's input, across a narrow gap between them.
options.why: That is the synapse, which is a space between two cells rather than a part of either one.

options.text: The cell body, where the arriving signals are pooled together and the cell's verdict is finally reached.
options.why: That is the soma, which is the integrator among the four parts rather than the input surface.

items.stem: What is the soma of a neuron?

options.text: The cell body, where arriving signals are pooled and a verdict is reached.
options.why: Correct. It is the integrator of §3.2.2's four roles, given the part of a real cell that fills it.

options.text: The branching input surface, made of many fine processes each carrying signals from a different source.
options.why: Those are the dendrites, which reach out from the cell body rather than being it.

options.text: The narrow gap between one cell's axon ending and the next cell's input surface.
options.why: That is the synapse, and it is the junction between two cells rather than a structure inside one.

options.text: The fatty sheath wrapped around the output line in segments, with small bare gaps left between them.
options.why: That is myelin, which §3.3.5 introduces as a way of making conduction faster and cheaper.

items.stem: What is a neuron's axon?

options.text: The output line: a single long fiber that may run a millimeter or, in a large animal, a meter or more.
options.why: Correct. Its length is why the reliability of an all-or-nothing signal matters as much as §3.2.4 said it did.

options.text: The input surface, made of a branching collection of processes each carrying signals from a different source.
options.why: Those are the dendrites. A neuron has many of them and only one output line, which sets the direction of flow.

options.text: The protein pore through the membrane that lets a particular ion cross when it is open and not when it is closed.
options.why: That is an ion channel, which is a structure in the membrane rather than a part of the cell's overall shape.

options.text: The cell body itself, which pools the arriving signals and reaches the cell's verdict about whether to act.
options.why: That is the soma, and the output line is what carries the verdict away from it.

items.stem: What is a synapse?

options.text: The junction where one cell's output becomes the next cell's input: the narrow gap between an axon's ending and the next cell's dendrites.
options.why: Correct. It fills the fourth of §3.2.2's roles, and it is a space between two cells rather than part of either.

options.text: The point along an axon where the signal is regenerated, so that it does not weaken as it travels the length of the cell.
options.why: Regeneration happens along the axon itself, and at the bare gaps in myelin, rather than at the junction between cells.

options.text: The branching structure on which a cell receives signals from many different sources at once.
options.why: Those are the dendrites, which are one side of a synapse rather than the junction itself.

options.text: The interval during which a cell cannot fire again, however much input arrives at it during that time.
options.why: That is the refractory period, which is a stretch of time rather than a place.

items.stem: The chapter fills the four algorithmic roles with four parts of a real cell. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Input surface to dendrites, integrator to soma, output line to axon, junction to synapse.
options.why: Correct. The correspondence is one to one, which is what makes it possible to state the roles first without naming any part.

options.text: Input surface to soma, integrator to dendrites, output line to synapse, junction to axon.
options.why: Each of the four is misassigned. The cell body integrates rather than receives, and the axon carries rather than joins.

options.text: Input surface to axon, integrator to synapse, output line to dendrites, junction to soma.
options.why: This reverses the direction of flow through the cell, which §3.2.2 established runs one way and cannot run backward.

options.text: Input surface to synapse, integrator to axon, output line to soma, junction to dendrites.
options.why: The synapse is a junction rather than a surface, and the cell body is not what carries the verdict away.

items.stem: The chapter says the four parts are "not necessary" for its algorithmic description of how a neuron computes, and yet that every one of them matters. How can both be true?

options.text: The functional description does not depend on any particular physical arrangement, but some physical arrangement has to carry it out, and these are the ones that do.
options.why: Correct. It is the levels relationship stated about one concrete case, and §3.3.9 pushes the same point much further.

options.text: The parts matter for how fast the computation runs but not for what the computation is, so only timing depends on them.
options.why: Timing is one consequence among several, and the chapter's claim is broader than a statement about speed.

options.text: The algorithmic description was a simplification that the physical account corrects, so the parts matter and the earlier account does not.
options.why: §3.3 does not correct §3.2. The two are descriptions at different levels, and both are retained.

options.text: The parts are necessary in biological neurons but not in artificial ones, so the description holds only for the artificial case.
options.why: The functional description is offered for biological cells first, and the artificial unit was copied from it afterward.

items.stem: What is the resting membrane potential?

options.text: The voltage across a neuron's membrane when it is not signaling, with the inside negative relative to the outside.
options.why: Correct. Roughly seventy thousandths of a volt, and the number matters less than what it means: a cell held under tension.

options.text: The level a neuron's summed input has to reach before the cell will produce an action potential.
options.why: That is the threshold, which is about the input that arrives rather than the standing state of the membrane.

options.text: The voltage a neuron reaches at the very peak of an action potential, once sodium has rushed into the cell through its opened channels.
options.why: That is the top of the spike, which is where the membrane goes rather than where it rests.

options.text: The energy a neuron spends per second while it is receiving no input, expressed in molecules of ATP.
options.why: That is a cost rather than a voltage, though §3.3.6 shows the two are closely related.

items.stem: Which term names the voltage a neuron holds while it is not signaling, which the chapter compares to a charged battery or a drawn bow?

options.text: resting membrane potential
options.why: Correct. A neuron at rest is not switched off but held under tension, with everything in place for something to happen fast.

options.text: action potential
options.why: That is the brief event the cell produces once it has been pushed past threshold, rather than the state it departs from.

options.text: threshold
options.why: That is the level the summed input must reach, which is a criterion rather than a standing voltage.

options.text: depolarization
options.why: That is the rising phase of a spike, in which the voltage climbs from negative to positive.

items.stem: Sodium is concentrated outside a neuron and potassium inside, and both ions are positively charged. Why is the inside negative anyway?

options.text: The cell holds large negatively charged molecules that cannot cross at all, and potassium escapes more easily than sodium gets in.
options.why: Correct. Both reasons are needed; the chapter gives them as a pair and neither on its own settles the sign.

options.text: Potassium is negatively charged inside the cell even though it is positively charged outside it.
options.why: An ion's charge does not change with location, and both ions are described as positively charged throughout.

options.text: Chloride ions are concentrated inside the cell in far greater numbers than either sodium or potassium.
options.why: Chloride appears in §3.3.5 in connection with GABA rather than as the source of the resting negativity.

options.text: The membrane is impermeable to sodium and freely permeable to potassium, so no positive charge is inside at all.
options.why: Potassium is inside in quantity, and the membrane is leaky to both ions rather than sealed against one.

items.stem: What are ion channels?

options.text: Protein pores through the membrane that let particular ions across; a few kinds stand permanently open and most are gated.
options.why: Correct. Gated channels open in response to a chemical binding or to the membrane voltage itself, which §3.3.3 makes use of.

options.text: Proteins that drive sodium out of a cell and potassium in, spending a molecule of ATP for each cycle.
options.why: That is the sodium-potassium pump, which works against the gradients where a channel lets ions run down them.

options.text: Small membrane packets holding neurotransmitters, which fuse with the cell's outer surface and spill their contents into the gap between two cells.
options.why: Those are vesicles, described in §3.3.5 at the far end of the axon.

options.text: Regions of the membrane where the fatty layers are thinnest, so that charged particles can cross more easily.
options.why: Charged particles cannot cross the oily sheet on their own anywhere, which is the fact everything else in §3.3.2 rests on.

items.stem: Which term names the protein pores studded through a neuron's membrane that let particular ions cross it?

options.text: ion channels
options.why: Correct. A few kinds stand permanently open, and through those the gradients would run down within minutes if nothing pushed back.

options.text: vesicles
options.why: Those are the small membrane packets that hold neurotransmitters and release them into the gap between cells.

options.text: ribozymes
options.why: Those are catalytic RNA molecules from the origin-of-life section, and they have nothing to do with membranes.

options.text: mitochondria
options.why: Those are internal compartments dedicated to aerobic respiration, which arrived with eukaryotes in §3.1.5.

items.stem: What does the sodium-potassium pump do?

options.text: It drives sodium out of the cell and potassium in, against their gradients, spending a molecule of ATP for each cycle.
options.why: Correct. Formally the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, and it is what keeps the gradients from running down to nothing within minutes.

options.text: It lets sodium into the cell and potassium out, in the direction each ion would move on its own anyway.
options.why: That is what the permanently open leak channels do, and it is exactly what the pump exists to undo.

options.text: It generates the electrical signal that travels along the axon once the cell has passed its threshold.
options.why: The spike is produced by voltage-gated channels rather than by the pump, though the pump pays for it afterward.

options.text: It releases neurotransmitter into the gap between two cells whenever an action potential arrives at the far end of the output line.
options.why: That is done by vesicles fusing with the cell surface after calcium enters, described in §3.3.5.

items.stem: Which structure spends a molecule of ATP per cycle to push ions back against the gradients they have drifted down?

options.text: the sodium-potassium pump
options.why: Correct. It is why a resting neuron is holding a steady state rather than sitting still, and §3.3.6 prices what that costs.

options.text: a leak channel
options.why: Those let ions trickle downhill for free, which is the drift the pump is continually undoing.

options.text: a vesicle
options.why: That is a membrane packet holding neurotransmitter, which fuses with the cell surface to release its contents.

options.text: a voltage-gated sodium channel
options.why: That opens in response to the membrane voltage and produces the spike, letting ions run down gradients rather than restoring them.

items.stem: Having described the membrane, the gradients and the pump, the chapter asks the reader to register one thing before going on. What is it?

options.text: A neuron receiving no input and sending no signal is still spending energy continuously, and what that spending buys is readiness.
options.why: Correct. It is the sentence the whole metabolism half of §3.3 depends on, and §3.3.6 returns to put a figure on it.

options.text: A neuron at rest spends no energy at all, which is the reason the brain's total cost depends only on how often its cells happen to fire.
options.why: The chapter says the reverse, and §3.3.6 finds that holding the resting potential is a substantial slice of the budget.

options.text: A neuron's resting voltage is set by its size, so larger cells are held under greater tension than smaller ones.
options.why: Cell size plays no part in setting the resting potential in this account.

options.text: A neuron at rest is effectively switched off, and it is switched on again only when a transmitter arrives at it.
options.why: A neuron at rest is explicitly not switched off; it is held under tension like a charged battery or a drawn bow.

items.stem: Gated ion channels are divided into two kinds by what opens them. Which two?

options.text: Ligand-gated channels, opened when a particular chemical binds; and voltage-gated channels, opened by the membrane voltage itself.
options.why: Correct. The first are §3.2's inputs made physical, and the second are what turn a summed input into a spike.

options.text: Sodium channels, gated so as to admit positive charge; and potassium channels, gated so as to admit negative charge.
options.why: Potassium is positively charged too, and the division the chapter draws here is by what opens a channel rather than by which ion.

options.text: Fast channels, which open within a fraction of a millisecond; and slow channels, which take several milliseconds.
options.why: Speed does differ between the sodium and potassium channels, but it is not the division the section uses to classify them.

options.text: Channels on the dendrites, which receive; and channels on the axon, which transmit the resulting signal onward.
options.why: Location follows from the kind of gating rather than defining it, and the chapter classifies by mechanism.

items.stem: What is summation, described physically rather than algorithmically?

options.text: Small voltage shifts produced by opening ligand-gated channels arrive at the cell body and combine into one net change of potential.
options.why: Correct. An excitatory input lets in positive charge and nudges the voltage up; an inhibitory input pushes it back down.

options.text: Neurotransmitter molecules accumulate in the gap between cells until enough have gathered to trigger the next cell.
options.why: Accumulation in the gap is not the mechanism; transmitters bind to receptors and are then cleared away.

options.text: Spikes arriving from several cells merge into a single larger spike, whose size records how many arrived.
options.why: Spikes do not vary in size and do not merge; what combine are the small graded shifts they produce at the receiving cell.

options.text: The pump increases its rate whenever inputs arrive, and the resulting change in ion traffic is what the cell measures.
options.why: The pump restores gradients rather than performing the summation, and it is not a signaling mechanism.

items.stem: What is depolarization, in an action potential?

options.text: The rising phase, in which sodium rushes into the cell and the membrane voltage climbs from negative to positive.
options.why: Correct. It is a runaway: sodium entry opens more sodium channels, so once the loop starts it cannot be stopped partway.

options.text: The falling phase, in which potassium flows out of the cell and the voltage returns toward its resting value.
options.why: That is repolarization, which follows depolarization and is driven by a slower set of channels.

options.text: The interval after the event when the sodium channels have not reset and no input can make the cell fire.
options.why: That is the refractory period, which comes after both phases of the spike are complete.

options.text: The steady state in which the pump exactly balances the leak, so that the voltage measured across the membrane does not change at all.
options.why: That is the resting condition, which is the state depolarization departs from.

items.stem: Which term names the falling phase of an action potential, in which potassium flows out and the voltage returns toward rest?

options.text: repolarization
options.why: Correct. It is driven by slower potassium channels opening after the sodium channels have shut themselves off.

options.text: depolarization
options.why: That is the rising phase, in which sodium rushes in and the voltage climbs from negative to positive.

options.text: integration
options.why: That is the combining of arriving inputs into one total, which happens before the spike rather than during it.

options.text: saltatory conduction
options.why: That is the jumping of a spike between the bare gaps in a myelin sheath, which concerns how it travels rather than its shape.

items.stem: What is the refractory period?

options.text: The brief interval after a spike during which the sodium channels have not reset and no amount of input can make the cell fire.
options.why: Correct. It settles two of §3.2's assertions at once: one-way propagation, and the ceiling on how fast a cell can fire.

options.text: The interval before a spike during which the cell's summed input is climbing steadily toward its threshold.
options.why: The approach to threshold is not the refractory period, and inputs during it are perfectly capable of producing a spike.

options.text: The period during which a neuron produces spikes at its maximum possible rate, having been driven very hard.
options.why: Maximum-rate firing is a consequence of the refractory period rather than the period itself.

options.text: The delay between a transmitter binding to a receptor and the resulting voltage change reaching the cell body.
options.why: Conduction delays of that kind are not what the term names, and the model of §3.2.8 ignores timing entirely.

items.stem: Which term names the brief interval after an action potential when no amount of input will make a neuron fire again?

options.text: refractory period
options.why: Correct. It exists because the sodium channels have not yet reset, and it is what limits a cell to a few hundred spikes per second.

options.text: resting membrane potential
options.why: That is the voltage a neuron holds when it is not signaling, and a cell in that state can be made to fire.

options.text: threshold
options.why: That is the level the summed input has to reach, and during the interval in question no level of input is sufficient.

options.text: baseline firing rate
options.why: That is the low background rate at which most cells fire when nothing is arriving.

items.stem: The chapter asserts at the algorithmic level that a spike is all-or-nothing. What physical reason does it give once it reaches the implementational level?

options.text: The rising phase is a positive feedback loop, and such a loop has no intermediate settings: either it runs to completion or nothing happens.
options.why: Correct. This is the chapter's clearest case of an implementational account explaining an algorithmic fact rather than merely realizing it.

options.text: The membrane is able to hold only two voltages, so any intermediate value collapses to one or the other of them within a small fraction of a millisecond.
options.why: The membrane takes a continuous range of voltages, and the small graded shifts of summation are exactly that.

options.text: The threshold is set high enough that only a full-strength input can ever cross it, so a partial input produces nothing.
options.why: Inputs of many sizes cross the threshold; what does not vary is the response once the threshold has been crossed.

options.text: The pump restores the gradients so quickly that a partial spike would be erased before it could travel anywhere.
options.why: The pump works far too slowly for that, and the chapter attributes the all-or-nothing property to the feedback loop.

items.stem: Besides all-or-nothing firing, the refractory period settles two more of the chapter's earlier assertions about spikes. Which two?

options.text: That a spike travels in one direction down the axon, and that a neuron has a maximum firing rate of a few hundred per second.
options.why: Correct. The stretch a spike has just left cannot fire again for a moment, and the cell must wait the interval out between events.

options.text: That every spike is the same size, and that a stronger stimulus raises the firing rate rather than the size of any single event.
options.why: Both are true, but the chapter explains them by the positive feedback loop rather than by the refractory period.

options.text: That connection is a matter of wiring rather than proximity, and that a circuit differs from a puddle.
options.why: Those are §3.2.2's claims about how cells are joined, and they are not settled by anything in the spike's mechanism.

options.text: That a rate can take any value in a range, and that timing within a spike train carries information too.
options.why: Those are §3.2.5's claims about the code, and the refractory period constrains the rate rather than explaining the code.

items.stem: The same depolarization that opens the sodium channels also closes them. How, on the chapter's account?

options.text: Through a second and slower mechanism in the same protein: the channels open, then a fraction of a millisecond later shut themselves off.
options.why: Correct. It is one protein with two mechanisms on different time courses, which should not be compressed into "the channels close."

options.text: Because the potassium channels opening alongside them physically block the sodium channels from the inside.
options.why: The potassium channels drive the voltage back down but are not described as obstructing anything.

options.text: Because the sodium concentration outside the cell falls far enough during the spike that no more sodium can enter.
options.why: The gradient is not exhausted by a single spike, and the chapter attributes the shutdown to the channel protein itself.

options.text: Because the pump reverses direction during the spike and pulls the sodium channels closed as it does so.
options.why: The pump does not reverse, and it plays no part in ending the rising phase of the spike.

items.stem: What made the squid giant axon the right preparation for Hodgkin and Huxley's work?

options.text: It is a nerve fiber up to a millimeter thick, large enough to thread a wire down the inside of it, which no ordinary axon permits.
options.why: Correct. That access is what let them hold the membrane voltage at fixed values and measure the currents flowing at each.

options.text: It fires far more slowly than a mammalian axon does, so each stage of the event could be observed directly without any specialized equipment.
options.why: Nothing about a slower time course is claimed; the advantage the chapter names is size.

options.text: It survives outside the animal for weeks, which allowed the same fiber to be measured repeatedly over a long period.
options.why: Longevity of the preparation is not mentioned, and the argument turns entirely on the fiber's thickness.

options.text: It has no myelin, so the spike is regenerated continuously along it and can be watched at any point on its length.
options.why: Myelin is not discussed in this section, and the reason given for the choice is that a wire could be threaded inside.

items.stem: What was the striking result when Hodgkin and Huxley used their equations to calculate an action potential?

options.text: Out came a curve with the right shape, height and duration, and a conduction speed matching the real axon — none of which had been built in.
options.why: Correct. They had built something that behaved like a neuron in ways they had not put in by hand, which is the synthetic method working.

options.text: The calculated curve matched their measurements exactly, which confirmed that the constants had been fitted correctly.
options.why: Matching what was fitted would show only internal consistency; what impressed was the values that had not been put in.

options.text: The calculated curve was wrong in shape but right in duration, which was enough to establish the mechanism's timing.
options.why: No such partial result is described; the agreement the chapter reports is across all four properties.

options.text: The calculation could not be completed without a computer, so the equations were not tested for another two decades.
options.why: The two-decade delay in the chapter concerns observing individual channels rather than running the calculation.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the part worth dwelling on is what Hodgkin and Huxley did not have?

options.text: Nobody had seen an ion channel, and there was no direct evidence of discrete pores at all, yet the equations described the behavior of whatever was letting ions through.
options.why: Correct. When the channels were finally observed two decades later, they were largely as the equations required them to be.

options.text: They had no way to measure voltage accurately, so the constants in their equations were estimates rather than measurements.
options.why: Their measurements are exactly what the constants were fitted to, and the chapter treats those measurements as sound.

options.text: They had no access to living tissue, so the whole account was derived from theory without any experiment behind it.
options.why: They worked on a dissected living axon, and the experimental access is what made the work possible.

options.text: They had no knowledge of the sodium-potassium pump, so their model omitted the cell's resting energy expenditure.
options.why: The pump is not what the section says was missing, and the point being made is about the channels.

items.stem: How do the chapter's two models of a neuron differ in what they answer?

options.text: The rate model says what a cell contributes to a circuit; the Hodgkin-Huxley model says how a cell physically produces one event.
options.why: Correct. Neither is a simplified version of the other, and neither is more true; they answer different questions at different levels.

options.text: The rate model applies to artificial neurons and the Hodgkin-Huxley model applies to biological ones.
options.why: The rate model was arrived at by describing a biological cell, and the artificial unit was copied from it afterward.

options.text: The rate model describes cells at rest and the Hodgkin-Huxley model describes them while they are actively firing.
options.why: Both models describe active cells; what separates them is the time scale and the level rather than the state.

options.text: The rate model is an approximation of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, valid whenever the exact currents do not matter.
options.why: The chapter denies exactly this: neither model is a simplified version of the other.

items.stem: What does the chapter say would happen if ten thousand Hodgkin-Huxley models were wired together?

options.text: The result would teach very little more than the simpler model does, at enormous cost.
options.why: Correct. It is the counterintuitive half of the argument: a more detailed model can be worse for a particular question.

options.text: The result would reproduce the behavior of a real nervous system, which the simpler model cannot manage.
options.why: The chapter does not credit the detailed model with this, and it says the simpler model is where assembly behavior is worked out.

options.text: The result would be impossible to compute, since the equations have no solution when many are coupled together.
options.why: Cost rather than impossibility is what the chapter cites, and the objection is about value for that cost.

options.text: The result would settle the dispute about whether a single neuron is better modeled as a small network.
options.why: That dispute concerns the input surface's own computation, and this comparison does not bear on it.

items.stem: Having set its two models of a neuron side by side, what verdict does the chapter reach about them?

options.text: Both are wrong in the way all models are wrong, deliberately and in stated respects, and both are indispensable.
options.why: Correct. The two-models passage is the chapter's clearest demonstration that levels of explanation do not compete.

options.text: The Hodgkin-Huxley model is more accurate, so the rate model should be used only where computation is too expensive.
options.why: The chapter refuses this ranking explicitly, and says neither model is more true than the other.

options.text: The rate model is more useful, so the Hodgkin-Huxley model is of historical interest rather than current value.
options.why: The detailed model answers a question the simple one cannot touch, which is why the chapter keeps both.

options.text: Both models will eventually be replaced by a single one combining the strengths of each, once the biology is settled.
options.why: No such unification is anticipated, and the section's point is that different questions need different models.

items.stem: What starts the runaway that produces an action potential?

options.text: Combined inputs push the membrane voltage past a critical level, about fifteen thousandths of a volt above rest, and voltage-gated sodium channels begin to open.
options.why: Correct. Sodium entering pushes the voltage further up, which opens more channels, and the loop cannot then be stopped partway.

options.text: A transmitter binds directly to the voltage-gated channels along the axon, opening them all at once.
options.why: Ligand-gated channels are what transmitters open, and they sit at the receiving surface rather than being the runaway's trigger.

options.text: The pump briefly reverses, letting sodium flood inward until the voltage has climbed high enough to sustain itself.
options.why: The pump does not reverse, and it works far too slowly to have any part in an event lasting about a millisecond.

options.text: Potassium channels close, so the potassium that had been leaking out is retained and the interior becomes positive.
options.why: Potassium channels open later rather than closing first, and their opening drives the voltage back down.

items.stem: If a neuron's leak channels were left to themselves, what would happen, and what prevents it?

options.text: The gradients would run down to nothing within minutes; the pump prevents it by continuously pushing ions back against them.
options.why: Correct. That is why a resting neuron is holding a steady state rather than sitting still, and why rest costs energy at all.

options.text: The gradients would grow steadily larger, and the pump prevents that by releasing ions back across the membrane once the imbalance gets too great.
options.why: Leak channels erase the imbalance rather than deepening it, and the pump builds the gradient rather than relieving it.

options.text: The cell would fire continuously, and the pump prevents it by holding the membrane voltage below the threshold.
options.why: Leak alone does not produce spikes, and the pump maintains the gradients rather than acting as a brake on firing.

options.text: Nothing would change, since the leak channels are open only briefly and close again once the voltage has settled.
options.why: The leak channels stand permanently open, which is what makes the continuous restoration necessary.

items.stem: Turning to the implementational level, the chapter restates an earlier warning about time scales as it becomes operative. What is the warning?

options.text: The algorithmic account worked at the scale of firing rates over stretches long enough for behavior; the physical account works at the scale of one event lasting about a thousandth of a second.
options.why: Correct. Two different questions about the same cell, producing two descriptions that look quite different, which is what three levels are for.

options.text: The algorithmic account described artificial neurons and the physical account describes biological ones, so claims about the one say nothing about the other.
options.why: Both sections describe biological cells, and the artificial comparison is a separate thread running through both.

options.text: The algorithmic account was a simplification and the physical account is the accurate one, so where the two differ the later should be preferred.
options.why: The chapter refuses this ranking repeatedly; neither description corrects the other.

options.text: The algorithmic account concerned cells in isolation and the physical account concerns cells embedded in circuits, which behave differently.
options.why: Circuits are Module 4's subject, and both sections here describe a single cell.

items.stem: Stated in numbers, what does the membrane voltage do during a single action potential?

options.text: It sits near −70 millivolts, rises to a threshold near −55, climbs steeply to a positive peak, then falls past the resting level before returning slowly.
options.why: Correct. The whole event lasts about a millisecond, and its shape is the same every time.

options.text: It sits near +70 millivolts, falls to a threshold near +55, drops to a negative trough, and then climbs back slowly.
options.why: Every sign is reversed. The interior of a resting neuron is negative relative to the outside rather than positive.

options.text: It sits near −70 millivolts, rises smoothly in proportion to the input, and returns at the same rate once the input stops.
options.why: A proportional rise and fall is a graded response, which is precisely what an action potential is not.

options.text: It sits near 0 millivolts until an input arrives, then swings to −70 and back, which is what makes the event detectable.
options.why: A resting neuron is not at zero, and the swing described runs in the wrong direction.
