items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why a neuron that is doing nothing at all is nevertheless spending energy, and what that spending buys.
items.answer: The membrane is not perfectly sealed: a few kinds of ion channel stand permanently open, and through them potassium drifts out and sodium drifts in, each moving in the direction that erases the imbalance. Left alone, the gradients would run down to nothing within minutes. They do not, because the sodium-potassium pump continuously drives sodium out and potassium in against their gradients, spending a molecule of ATP for each cycle. So a resting neuron is holding a steady state rather than sitting still. What the spending buys is readiness: the gradients are the stored tension a spike is produced out of, and a cell that let them run down could not act fast when it needed to.
rubric: States that leak channels let ions drift down their gradients continuously.
States that the gradients would run down without something restoring them.
Names the sodium-potassium pump and its ATP cost per cycle.
Identifies readiness as what the continuous spending purchases.

items.stem: The chapter's algorithmic account asserts three things about spikes that it cannot itself explain. In a short paragraph, name them and give the physical explanation the implementational account supplies for each.
items.answer: First, spikes are all-or-nothing. The reason is that the rising phase is a positive feedback loop — sodium entering opens more sodium channels — and a positive feedback loop has no intermediate settings, so either the threshold is crossed and the loop runs to completion or nothing happens. Second, a spike travels in one direction along the axon. The reason is that the stretch it has just left is briefly in its refractory period and cannot fire again. Third, a neuron has a maximum firing rate of a few hundred spikes per second. The reason is the same interval: the cell has to wait the refractory period out between events.
rubric: Names all-or-nothing firing and explains it by positive feedback having no intermediate settings.
Names one-way propagation and explains it by the refractory state of the stretch just left.
Names the ceiling on firing rate and explains it by the need to wait out the refractory period.
Presents these as the implementational level explaining algorithmic facts rather than replacing them.

items.stem: The chapter builds two models of one neuron. In a short paragraph, say what each one represents, which question each answers, and why the chapter keeps both.
items.answer: The rate model represents firing rates and a weight on each connection, and it answers the question of what a cell contributes to a circuit over a stretch of time long enough for behavior. The Hodgkin-Huxley model represents currents crossing a membrane and a voltage, over the course of about a millisecond, and it answers the question of how a cell physically produces one event. Neither is a simplified version of the other and neither is more true. The chapter keeps both because a model is built for a question: the linear model has nothing whatever to say about how a spike is made, and wiring ten thousand Hodgkin-Huxley models together would teach very little more at enormous cost.
rubric: Says what the rate model represents and which question it answers.
Says what the Hodgkin-Huxley model represents and which question it answers.
States that neither is a simplified version of the other and neither is more true.
Gives a reason each is indispensable — what the other cannot do or cannot afford.

items.stem: What does the implementational question ask, and which discipline does the chapter attach to it?

options.text: What physical stuff actually does this, and by what means; the discipline is neuroscience.
options.why: Correct. The answer in this chapter is a cell made of fat, salt water and protein doing something quite specific with electricity.

options.text: What problem is being solved and why solving it matters; the discipline is evolutionary biology together with ecology.
options.why: That is the computational question, which §3.1 asked, and it is about the pressure that favored the structure.

options.text: What is represented and by what procedure; the disciplines are cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence.
options.why: That is the algorithmic question, which §3.2 asked and answered with receive, integrate and transmit.

options.text: How a structure develops in an individual over its lifetime; the discipline is developmental biology and embryology.
options.why: Development is not one of Marr's three levels, and the chapter touches it only in a single sentence about gastrulation.

items.stem: What is a neuron's membrane made of, and why does its construction matter for everything else in the implementational account?

options.text: Two layers of fatty molecules with their water-repelling ends facing each other, and charged particles cannot cross the oily sheet on their own.
options.why: Correct. Whatever is inside stays inside unless something lets it through, which is what makes gradients and gated channels possible at all.

options.text: A single layer of protein pores packed tightly together, which admits charged particles freely but keeps larger molecules out.
options.why: Protein pores are studded through the membrane rather than composing it, and the membrane is a barrier to charged particles.

options.text: A rigid wall of sugars laid down outside the cell, which gives the neuron its shape and keeps its contents from leaking away.
options.why: Nothing of the kind is described, and a rigid outer wall would not support the traffic of ions the section goes on to describe.

options.text: A sheet of myelin wrapped around the cell in segments, which insulates it and keeps ions from crossing except at the bare gaps.
options.why: Myelin wraps some axons from outside and belongs to §3.3.5; every neuron has a membrane whether or not it has any myelin.

items.stem: The lecture sets its tidy four-part account of a neuron against what real neurons look like in stained tissue, and tells the room to hold the gap in mind. What is the gap for?

options.text: It is the picture the researchers are looking at who say a cortical neuron is better described as a small network, since the dendrites overlap too thoroughly to follow one cell end to end.
options.why: Correct. The lecture uses the micrograph to make §3.2's dissenting view concrete rather than to illustrate the anatomy twice.

options.text: It shows that the tidy account is inaccurate, so the four parts should be treated as an approximation rather than as real structures.
options.why: The parts are real; the lecture's point is about how much the diagram leaves out, not that it misnames anything.

options.text: It shows that one neuron varies a great deal from the next, so no single diagram can represent them all.
options.why: Regional variation is not the argument, and the field shown is used to make a point about one cell's branching.

options.text: It shows that staining distorts tissue, which is why conclusions drawn from micrographs need to be checked against living cells.
options.why: No methodological caution about staining is raised anywhere in the lecture.

items.stem: Having given the neuron's four parts, the lecture names the one sentence that keeps the account "a Marr lecture rather than an anatomy lesson." What does that sentence say?

options.text: Those specific biological implementations are not necessary for the description of how a neuron computes, and something else could have filled the four roles.
options.why: Correct. Every one of them nonetheless matters to how the computation is physically carried out, which is what the rest of the lecture is about.

options.text: Those specific biological implementations are what the functional description was derived from, so the two accounts cannot come apart.
options.why: The lecture insists they can come apart, which is what makes the multiple-realizability comparison available at all.

options.text: Those specific biological implementations are shared by every neuron in every animal, so the anatomy is universal.
options.why: Universality across animals is not claimed, and it would not make the slide a Marr lecture in any case.

options.text: Those specific biological implementations explain the four roles, so the functional description can now be set aside.
options.why: Neither description is set aside; the module keeps both and spends its last lecture saying why.

items.stem: Explaining why a cell cannot produce half an action potential, the lecture adds a clarification about the kind of impossibility involved. What is it?

options.text: Not that the cell is forbidden to, but that there is no mechanism by which it could.
options.why: Correct. A positive feedback loop has no intermediate settings, so the outcome is either the full event or nothing at all.

options.text: Not that the cell never does, but that a half spike would fade before it travelled far enough to be detected.
options.why: Fading over distance is a property of graded signals; the lecture's claim is that the event cannot be produced partially at all.

options.text: Not that it is impossible, but that it is so rare that the all-or-nothing description holds for practical purposes.
options.why: The lecture treats the impossibility as structural rather than as a statistical approximation.

options.text: Not that the mechanism forbids it, but that the refractory period erases any partial event before it can propagate.
options.why: The refractory period settles one-way travel and the firing ceiling rather than the all-or-nothing property.

items.stem: The lecture says the all-or-nothing explanation shows what an implementational account buys. What does it say that is?

options.text: It does not merely say what the machinery is; it explains something the level above could only assert.
options.why: Correct. Three claims from the previous lecture are explained by one mechanism, and none of them has to be assumed any more.

options.text: It replaces the algorithmic description, which was only ever a placeholder until the biology could be described properly.
options.why: The algorithmic description is kept and used alongside the implementational one for the rest of the module.

options.text: It supplies the numbers the algorithmic description lacked, which is what makes the account quantitative rather than qualitative.
options.why: The linear model of the previous lecture was already quantitative, and the gain here is explanatory rather than numerical.

options.text: It shows which of the algorithmic claims were wrong, so that the earlier account can be corrected where it overreached.
options.why: None of the earlier claims is corrected; all three are confirmed and given a mechanism.

items.stem: Explaining one-way propagation, the lecture gives a compressed reason. What is it?

options.text: The wave cannot go backward because backward is exhausted.
options.why: Correct. The stretch of membrane a spike has just left is briefly in its refractory period and cannot fire again.

options.text: The wave cannot go backward because the channels ahead open first.
options.why: The ordering of channel states is not the reason given, and the relevant fact is about the stretch already passed.

options.text: The wave cannot go backward because the axon narrows as it runs.
options.why: No claim about axon geometry is made anywhere in the module.

options.text: The wave cannot go backward because the synapse admits one direction.
options.why: Synaptic directionality is a separate fact and does not explain why the spike does not reverse mid-axon.

items.stem: Comparing its two models of a neuron, the lecture singles out one comparison as the counterintuitive one, and says it is the one it would put on an exam. What does that comparison establish?

options.text: That a more detailed model can be worse for a question — not as a compromise or a limit of our computers, but as a fact about what models are for.
options.why: Correct. Wiring ten thousand Hodgkin-Huxley models together would teach very little more than the simpler model, at enormous cost.

options.text: That a more detailed model is always preferable when the computation can be afforded, so the choice is a practical one.
options.why: The lecture rejects the practical reading explicitly by saying it is not a limitation of our computers.

options.text: That the two models produce the same predictions when scaled up, which is why either may be used at the level of an assembly.
options.why: Sameness of prediction is not claimed; what is claimed is that the extra detail buys very little for that question.

options.text: That a simpler model becomes unreliable at scale, which is why assemblies are studied with the detailed model instead.
options.why: This inverts the row: the simpler model is the one that yields the behavior of the whole.

items.stem: The lecture says three claims from the previous meeting are explained by one mechanism, "none of them assumed." Name the three and give the mechanism behind each.
items.answer: First, a spike is all-or-nothing, because the rising phase is a positive feedback loop and such a loop has no intermediate settings — either the threshold is crossed and the loop runs to completion, or nothing happens. The cell cannot make half a spike, not because it is forbidden to but because there is no mechanism by which it could. Second, a spike travels one way down the axon, because the stretch it has just left is briefly in its refractory period: backward is exhausted. Third, a neuron has a maximum firing rate of a few hundred per second, because it must wait out that same refractory period between events. The point the lecture draws is that an implementational account explains what the level above could only assert.
rubric: Names all-or-nothing firing and explains it by positive feedback having no intermediate settings.
Names one-way propagation and explains it by the refractory state of the stretch just left.
Names the firing ceiling and explains it by the wait between events.
States the general point: implementation explains rather than merely realizing what the algorithmic level asserted.

pools.title: Down the Axon, and Across the Gap

items.stem: How does a spike get from one end of a long axon to the other?

options.text: Not as a single event traveling, but as a chain of events regenerating: each patch of membrane pushes the patch ahead of it past threshold.
options.why: Correct. Nothing is transmitted the way a wire transmits, which is the physical basis of the claim that what arrives is exactly what left.

options.text: As a wave of charge pushed along the inside of the fiber, weakening slightly with distance in the way that any ordinary electrical signal would.
options.why: Weakening is precisely what does not happen, and that reliability is what §3.2.4 said the animal way of life demanded.

options.text: As a chemical released at one end that diffuses along the inside of the axon until it reaches the far end.
options.why: Diffusion over that distance is what §3.1.7 ruled out; it would take years across the length of a large animal.

options.text: As a signal carried by the sodium-potassium pump, which hands each ion along the membrane to the next pump in line.
options.why: The pump restores gradients after the event rather than carrying anything, and it works on a far slower time scale.

items.stem: What is myelin?

options.text: A fatty sheath laid down around an axon in segments, with small bare gaps left between the segments.
options.why: Correct. Ion channels cluster at those gaps, so the spike is regenerated only there and the stretches between are crossed passively.

options.text: A protein pore in the membrane that admits sodium when it opens and shuts itself off a fraction of a millisecond later.
options.why: That is a voltage-gated sodium channel, which is what produces the spike rather than what insulates the fiber carrying it.

options.text: The narrow gap between an axon's ending and the next cell's input surface, across which a transmitter crosses.
options.why: That is the synapse, which is the junction between two cells rather than a covering on one of them.

options.text: A chemical released at the axon's ending that binds to receptors on the receiving cell and changes its voltage.
options.why: That is a neurotransmitter, and it acts between cells rather than along the length of one.

items.stem: Which structure makes conduction along an axon both far faster and considerably cheaper, by letting the signal jump between bare gaps?

options.text: myelin
options.why: Correct. Far fewer ions cross the membrane and far fewer have to be pumped back, which is where the saving comes from.

options.text: the synapse
options.why: That is the junction between two cells, and crossing it is a separate step from traveling along the fiber.

options.text: the soma
options.why: That is the cell body, where arriving signals are pooled, rather than anything on the output line.

options.text: the refractory period
options.why: That is an interval of time during which a cell cannot fire, and it limits rate rather than speeding conduction.

items.stem: Why is saltatory conduction cheaper as well as faster?

options.text: The spike is regenerated only at the bare gaps, so far fewer ions cross the membrane and far fewer have to be pumped back.
options.why: Correct. The saving is in the cleanup, which is where §3.3.6 finds most of the cost of signaling to be.

options.text: The insulated stretches conduct with no loss whatever, so no energy at all is spent at any point along the whole length of the axon.
options.why: The stretches are crossed passively rather than for free, and regeneration at the gaps still costs.

options.text: Myelin stores energy as the signal passes and releases it to power the next regeneration further along.
options.why: Nothing of the kind is described; myelin insulates rather than storing or supplying energy.

options.text: The signal travels so fast that the pump has less time to operate, so less ATP is consumed during the journey.
options.why: The pump's total work depends on how many ions crossed rather than on how long the journey took.

items.stem: What happens at the axon's ending when a spike arrives there?

options.text: Channels open and let calcium into the cell; calcium entry causes vesicles to fuse with the surface and spill transmitter into the gap.
options.why: Correct. The transmitter then crosses, binds to the ligand-gated receptors on the next cell, and the cycle begins again there.

options.text: The spike jumps directly across the gap into the next cell, since the two membranes are close enough together for charge to bridge the distance.
options.why: The chapter describes a chemical crossing rather than an electrical jump, and the signal changes form at this point.

options.text: The sodium-potassium pump reverses at the ending, expelling transmitter that had accumulated inside during the journey.
options.why: The pump moves ions rather than transmitters, and it never reverses in this account.

options.text: The myelin sheath ends and the bare membrane releases potassium into the gap, which the next cell detects.
options.why: Potassium leaving the cell is part of repolarization rather than a signal between cells, and myelin is not the release mechanism.

items.stem: What is glutamate?

options.text: The dominant excitatory transmitter in the brain, binding to receptors that open channels permeable to sodium.
options.why: Correct. Positive charge flows into the receiving cell and its voltage climbs toward threshold, which is what excitatory means.

options.text: The dominant inhibitory transmitter in the brain, binding to receptors that open channels permeable to chloride.
options.why: That is GABA, whose receptors admit a negatively charged ion and push the voltage away from threshold.

options.text: A category of transmitter that turns a cell's sensitivity to everything else up or down rather than pushing it either way.
options.why: That describes modulatory signaling, which §3.2.7 names as a third category rather than a particular molecule.

options.text: The molecule the sodium-potassium pump spends in order to drive ions back across the membrane against their gradients.
options.why: That is ATP, which is an energy currency rather than a signal between cells.

items.stem: What is GABA?

options.text: The dominant inhibitory transmitter in the brain, binding to receptors that open channels permeable to chloride.
options.why: Correct. Chloride is negatively charged, so negative charge flows in and the voltage is pushed away from threshold.

options.text: The dominant excitatory transmitter in the brain, binding to receptors that open channels permeable to sodium.
options.why: That is glutamate, whose receptors admit positive charge and drive the receiving cell's voltage toward threshold.

options.text: The fatty sheath wrapped around an axon in segments, which makes conduction both faster and considerably cheaper.
options.why: That is myelin, which is a structural covering rather than a chemical crossing between cells.

options.text: The protein that drives sodium out of a cell and potassium in, spending a molecule of ATP for each cycle it completes.
options.why: That is the sodium-potassium pump, which maintains gradients rather than carrying signals across a gap.

items.stem: Read as a causal chain, what actually makes glutamate excitatory and GABA inhibitory?

options.text: Their receptors open channels for different ions — sodium in one case, chloride in the other — and the charge that ion carries decides which way the voltage moves.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is explicit that the difference is a fact about a channel rather than about the molecule.

options.text: Glutamate is released in much larger quantities than GABA, so its effect on the receiving cell is correspondingly stronger.
options.why: Quantity is not what the chapter appeals to, and a larger excitatory effect would not explain an inhibitory one.

options.text: Glutamate binds to receptors on dendrites and GABA binds to receptors on the cell body, so the two act at different places.
options.why: Location is not the mechanism given, and both are described as binding to ligand-gated receptors on the receiving cell.

options.text: Glutamate opens channels and GABA closes them, so one increases the traffic across the membrane and the other stops it.
options.why: Both transmitters open channels; what differs is which ion the channels they open will admit.

items.stem: Why can the same neurotransmitter excite one cell and inhibit another?

options.text: Because the two cells carry different receptors, which open channels for different ions when the same transmitter binds.
options.why: Correct. This is what defeats learning transmitter identities as flashcards: the effect belongs to the receiving cell's machinery.

options.text: Because the transmitter arrives in different quantities at the two cells, and a small amount excites while a large amount inhibits.
options.why: Quantity is not what settles the effect, and no such reversal with dose is described.

options.text: Because the two cells are at different points in their refractory periods when the transmitter reaches them.
options.why: The refractory period determines whether a cell can fire at all rather than whether an input pushes it up or down.

options.text: Because one of the two cells is myelinated and the other is not, which changes how the arriving signal is interpreted.
options.why: Myelin affects travel along an axon and plays no part in what happens at the receiving surface.

items.stem: The chapter closes its account of synaptic transmission by pointing out that every stage of it costs energy. Which costs does it name?

options.text: The ions that crossed must be pumped back, transmitters must be manufactured and loaded into vesicles, and the vesicle membrane must be recovered and reused.
options.why: Correct. That closing sentence primes §3.3.6, which prices the whole sequence and finds cleanup dominating the bill.

options.text: The transmitter must be broken down in the gap, the receptor must be rebuilt after each binding, and the axon must be re-insulated.
options.why: None of these three is described. Clearing is largely by reuptake, and receptors and myelin are not consumed by a single event.

options.text: The membrane must be repaired after each spike, the gap must be refilled with fluid, and the cell body must synthesize new channels.
options.why: No damage or refilling of this kind occurs, and channels are reused rather than remade after every event.

options.text: The pump must run faster during transmission, the myelin must be thickened, and the dendrites must grow new branches.
options.why: Structural growth of this kind belongs to changes over much longer timescales and is not among the per-event costs.

items.stem: A student has memorized "glutamate is excitatory, GABA is inhibitory." In a short paragraph, explain what that pairing leaves out, and describe a case the student would get wrong.
items.answer: The pairing is true of the brain's dominant transmitters, but it treats excitatory as a property of a molecule, which it is not. What settles the effect is the channel a transmitter's receptor opens: glutamate binds to receptors opening channels permeable to sodium, so positive charge flows in and the voltage climbs toward threshold, while GABA binds to receptors opening channels permeable to chloride, a negative ion, so the voltage is pushed away from threshold. The case the student would get wrong is a transmitter that excites one cell and inhibits another: if two cells carry different receptors, opening channels for different ions, the same molecule arriving at both produces opposite effects.
rubric: States that the effect is a fact about the channel rather than about the molecule.
Names the ion each transmitter's receptors admit, and the charge it carries.
Connects the direction of charge flow to movement toward or away from threshold.
Gives the case the pairing cannot handle: one transmitter with opposite effects on two cells.

items.stem: Following glutamate and GABA each through the same causal chain, the lecture asks what actually differs between the two transmitters. What is the answer?

options.text: Only the ion the channel lets through — not the direction of flow, and not anything about the molecule's own nature.
options.why: Correct. Both transmitters open channels and both let charge flow into the receiving cell; the sign of that charge is what decides the effect.

options.text: Only the direction the charge moves, since the channel lets chloride out where it lets sodium through.
options.why: Both ions move into the receiving cell, which is the row the lecture points at to show the direction is shared.

options.text: Only the speed of the response, since chloride channels open more slowly than sodium channels do.
options.why: No difference in timing between the two is described.

options.text: Only which part of the receiving cell the transmitter binds to, since the two act at different points on the input surface.
options.why: Location of binding is not what the table varies, and it is not offered as the source of the difference.

items.stem: Describing myelin, the lecture tells the room to hold on to one of its two benefits. Which one, and why?

options.text: Cheaper, because it comes back near the end of the lecture as a design decision rather than a detail.
options.why: Correct. In §3.3.8 myelin returns as the same energy logic in a different place, alongside sparse firing and the wiring balance.

options.text: Faster, because conduction speed is what the first lecture's argument about the animal way of life turned on.
options.why: Speed matters, but the lecture flags the cheapness as the property that returns later in its own argument.

options.text: Cheaper, because a myelinated axon can be made thinner and so more of them fit in the same volume.
options.why: Packing density is not discussed, and the saving named is in ions crossing and being pumped back.

options.text: Faster, because the gaps let the signal skip stretches of membrane that would otherwise slow it down.
options.why: This describes the mechanism of the speed gain rather than the property the lecture asks the room to carry forward.

pools.title: What Signaling Costs, and What the Cost Forces
pools.covers: reading §3.3.6, §3.3.7, §3.3.8 · lecture 3.3 slides what_signaling_costs, the_most_expensive_organ, sparse_by_necessity

items.stem: What is bio-energetics?

options.text: The study of how an organism gets, stores, and spends energy.
options.why: Correct. Neural communication is one of its most interesting subjects, because signaling is unusually expensive.

options.text: The study of how a nervous system turns its input into behavior.
options.why: That is closer to what the whole module studies, and it is not what this term names.

options.text: The study of how energy flows through an ecosystem.
options.why: Energy flow across an ecosystem is ecology's subject, and the term here concerns the individual organism.

options.text: The study of how a cell's membrane holds a voltage.
options.why: That is membrane biophysics, which the chapter's Further Reading points to under a different heading.

items.stem: Which field studies how an organism gets, stores, and spends energy?

options.text: bio-energetics
options.why: Correct. The chapter names it as the frame for the whole metabolism half of §3.3, beginning with the cost of one spike.

options.text: ecology
options.why: That studies the relations between organisms and their environments, and the chapter pairs it with evolution at the computational level.

options.text: neuroscience
options.why: That is the discipline the chapter attaches to the implementational level generally rather than to energy in particular.

options.text: cognitive psychology
options.why: That is paired with artificial intelligence at the algorithmic level, where the question is what procedure a system follows.

items.stem: Why is neural signaling expensive, on the account the chapter gives?

options.text: A spike happens by letting ions run down gradients built at a cost, and every ion that crossed has to be hauled back afterward.
options.why: Correct. The cost of computing with neurons is dominated not by the computing but by the cleanup that restores the gradients.

options.text: Producing a spike requires the cell to synthesize fresh membrane, which is among the most expensive materials any cell has to manufacture.
options.why: Membrane synthesis is not what the chapter prices, and the spike consumes no membrane.

options.text: The signal has to be amplified at every point along the axon, and each amplification costs more than the last.
options.why: Regeneration keeps the signal at full strength rather than amplifying it progressively, and the cost per regeneration does not escalate.

options.text: Neurons must maintain a much higher temperature than surrounding tissue in order for their channels to open quickly.
options.why: No thermal claim of any kind is made in the chapter.

items.stem: Attwell and Laughlin's budget for the brain's gray matter reached two conclusions the chapter insists on keeping separate. What are they?

options.text: About three-quarters of the energy goes to signaling rather than housekeeping; and almost all of that signaling cost goes on the sodium-potassium pump.
options.why: Correct. The two have different denominators, and combining them into a single figure about the brain's total ATP is a misstatement.

options.text: About three-quarters of the energy goes to the sodium-potassium pump; and almost all of the rest goes to housekeeping.
options.why: This is the collapse the chapter guards against: the pump's share is of the signaling portion rather than of the whole budget.

options.text: About one-quarter of the energy goes to signaling; and almost all of that goes to manufacturing neurotransmitters.
options.why: The signaling share is the larger of the two, and transmitter recycling is one of the smallest items within it.

options.text: About half the energy goes to action potentials; and the other half goes to holding the resting potential steady.
options.why: Those are two items within the signaling share, and neither takes half of the whole budget.

items.stem: Within the signaling share of the brain's gray-matter budget, which number does the chapter single out as the one to notice?

options.text: That simply holding the resting potential accounts for about an eighth, meaning a substantial slice is spent by cells doing nothing but staying ready.
options.why: Correct. It follows directly from §3.3.2, where a neuron receiving nothing and sending nothing is already spending continuously.

options.text: That action potentials account for roughly half, which shows that the cost of a brain is driven mainly by how often it fires.
options.why: That figure is given, but the chapter picks out the resting share as the surprising one rather than the largest one.

options.text: That effects at the receiving side of synapses account for about a third, which is larger than most readers would expect.
options.why: The postsynaptic figure is reported without special emphasis; the resting figure is the one flagged.

options.text: That transmitter recycling accounts for almost nothing, which shows that chemistry is a minor part of the cost.
options.why: Recycling is indeed small, but it is not the item the chapter says is worth noticing.

items.stem: What does the chapter give as the cost of a single spike?

options.text: On the order of two and a half billion molecules of ATP, on Peter Lennie's estimate.
options.why: Correct. That unit price is what §3.3.8 then runs in reverse to work out how much firing a brain can afford.

options.text: On the order of two and a half million molecules of ATP, which is roughly what a resting cell spends in a second.
options.why: The figure is a thousand times larger than this, and it is a cost per event rather than a resting rate.

options.text: On the order of a single molecule of ATP, since one pump cycle restores the ions that one spike moved across.
options.why: One ATP is the cost of a single pump cycle, and an enormous number of cycles are needed after one spike.

options.text: The chapter declines to give a figure, since the cost of a spike varies too much between cell types to be estimated.
options.why: An estimate is given and attributed, with the appropriate hedge that it is on the order of that value.

items.stem: What is the relationship between the brain being about 2% of body weight and using about 20% of the body's oxygen at rest, and the twenty-watt figure from Module 0?

options.text: The percentages and the wattage are one measurement stated two ways, as a share and as power.
options.why: Correct. Nothing new is being added by the second figure, which is why the chapter says so explicitly rather than listing three facts.

options.text: The percentages describe the resting brain and the wattage describes the brain during demanding mental work.
options.why: The chapter attaches all of these figures to the resting condition rather than splitting them by activity.

options.text: The percentages describe an adult and the wattage describes a child, whose brain takes a much larger share.
options.why: The childhood figure is stated separately, as reaching as much as half of the body's oxygen use.

options.text: The percentages come from oxygen measurements and the wattage from a separate estimate that does not agree with them.
options.why: The chapter presents them as agreeing, which is what makes them one fact stated two ways.

items.stem: What does the chapter give for how much of the daily energy budget different mammals devote to the brain?

options.text: Humans something like 20–25%, other primates 8–10%, and non-primate mammals 3–5%.
options.why: Correct. Three ranges are given rather than a superlative, which is what the comparative data actually support.

options.text: Humans about 20%, and every other mammal a figure too small to have been measured reliably.
options.why: Figures for other primates and for non-primate mammals are both given, and neither is treated as unmeasurable.

options.text: Humans about 50%, other primates about 20%, and non-primate mammals about 10%.
options.why: The human figure of about half belongs to childhood rather than adulthood, and the other two are overstated here.

options.text: All mammals devote roughly the same share, and what differs between them is only the absolute quantity involved.
options.why: The whole point of the comparison is that the share differs substantially across the three groups.

items.stem: What kind of metabolic outlier is the human brain, on the chapter's account?

options.text: One that is expensive because it holds a great many neurons, since running a single human neuron costs about what running a primate neuron costs.
options.why: Correct. The cost is large because the brain is large, on an ordinary primate body plan, rather than because human neurons are special.

options.text: One whose individual neurons are unusually expensive to run, which is what distinguishes human tissue from that of other primates.
options.why: The chapter says the per-neuron cost is not remarkable, and that the difference lies in how many neurons there are.

options.text: One whose cost is unremarkable in absolute terms but unusual as a share, because the human body is comparatively small.
options.why: Body size is not offered as the explanation, and the argument turns on neuron number instead.

options.text: One whose cost cannot be compared with other species at all, since the measurements were made by incompatible methods.
options.why: The comparison is made and the figures are given; the chapter's caution is about how to read them.

items.stem: The chapter says a number like twenty percent invites a misreading. What is the misreading, and what does the chapter offer instead?

options.text: It invites reading as an achievement; better read as a constraint, since a brain that expensive has to be fed every day.
options.why: Correct. That constraint limits what else an animal can be and what it must eat, which is a very different claim from superiority.

options.text: It invites reading as a measurement error; better read as a rough estimate, since a working brain cannot easily be metered.
options.why: The measurement caution is real and belongs to §3.3.6, but it is not the misreading this section is guarding against.

options.text: It invites reading as a fixed quantity; better read as varying, since the share changes with how demanding the task is.
options.why: Task-dependent variation is not what the section discusses, and the figures are given for the resting condition.

options.text: It invites reading as a human peculiarity; better read as universal, since every mammal spends the same share on its brain.
options.why: The chapter gives three different ranges across mammal groups, so the shares are not universal.

items.stem: What is sparse coding?

options.text: Activity in which only a small proportion of neurons are strongly active at any one moment.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is emphatic that it is a consequence of the energy budget rather than an accident or an inefficiency.

options.text: Activity in which each neuron fires at a low but steady rate, so that the total across the population stays constant.
options.why: A constant low rate for every cell is not sparseness; what matters is that only a few cells are strongly active at once.

options.text: A method of storing information in as few connections as possible, so that a nervous system can be built more cheaply.
options.why: The term describes a pattern of activity rather than a way of economizing on connections.

options.text: The practice of recording from only a small sample of neurons, since recording from all of them is not feasible.
options.why: That would be a fact about experimental method rather than about how a brain operates.

items.stem: Which term names the pattern in which only a small share of cortical neurons — on the order of one in a few hundred — are strongly active at any given moment?

options.text: sparse coding
options.why: Correct. The share follows from running the energy accounting in reverse, given what the brain costs and what a spike costs.

options.text: rate coding
options.why: That is carrying information in how many spikes a single cell produces in a stretch of time, which is a different idea entirely.

options.text: the refractory period
options.why: That is the interval after a spike during which one cell cannot fire again, rather than a property of a population.

options.text: saltatory conduction
options.why: That is a spike jumping between the bare gaps in a myelin sheath, which concerns travel along a single axon.

items.stem: How does the chapter arrive at the number of roughly one neuron in a few hundred being strongly active at once?

options.text: By running the energy accounting in reverse: given what the brain costs to run and what a spike costs, the sustainable average is a fraction of a spike per neuron per second.
options.why: Correct. It is the chapter's clearest instance of a quantitative argument a reader can reconstruct rather than simply accept.

options.text: By counting active cells directly in imaging studies, which consistently find about that proportion lit up at any moment.
options.why: Imaging is cited for a different purpose — showing activity throughout the brain — rather than as the source of this figure.

options.text: By assuming that the ten-percent claim is roughly right and correcting it downward for the cells that are only weakly active.
options.why: The ten-percent claim is rejected outright rather than adjusted, and it asserts something quite different.

options.text: By measuring the maximum firing rate a neuron can sustain and dividing it by the number of neurons in the cortex.
options.why: The maximum rate is set by the refractory period and is not what this derivation uses; the budget is.

items.stem: What exactly does the claim that we use only ten percent of our brains assert, and why is it false?

options.text: It asserts that most of the brain sits idle as unused capacity; nothing supports that, since every region does something and damage almost anywhere produces a deficit.
options.why: Correct. Imaging finds activity throughout as well, so the claim fails on every reading that would make it interesting.

options.text: It asserts that we could think ten times faster with training; that is false because a neuron's maximum firing rate is fixed.
options.why: The claim is about idle capacity rather than speed, and the refutation the chapter gives is about the whole brain being used.

options.text: It asserts that only ten percent of neurons are firing at any instant; that is false because the true figure is closer to half.
options.why: The instantaneous share really is small, which is the fact the myth mangles; what is false is calling the rest a reserve.

options.text: It asserts that ninety percent of the brain has no known function; that is false because functions have now been assigned to all of it.
options.why: The claim is about idleness rather than about our state of knowledge, and the chapter's refutation is about activity and damage.

items.stem: The chapter says what is true in the neighborhood of the ten-percent myth is "narrower and considerably stranger." What is it?

options.text: At any instant only a small share of neurons fire hard, and which small share changes moment to moment, so the whole brain is used but never all at once.
options.why: Correct. Both halves are needed: a single sparse snapshot on its own would simply be the myth drawn as a picture.

options.text: Only a small share of the brain has been mapped, and which parts are understood changes as new methods arrive.
options.why: That would be a claim about the state of research rather than about the brain, and it is not what the section says.

options.text: Only a small share of neurons survive into adulthood, and which ones survive depends on what the animal has experienced.
options.why: Developmental loss of cells is not discussed anywhere in this chapter.

options.text: Only a small share of the brain is active during rest, though nearly all of it becomes active during demanding tasks.
options.why: Sparseness is presented as a standing constraint set by the budget rather than as a feature of the resting state alone.

items.stem: The chapter gives two reasons a brain with most neurons firing most of the time would be worse. What are they?

options.text: It would code for information less effectively, since there is information in which cells are silent; and it could not be fed.
options.why: Correct. The information reason is handed forward to Module 4, and the energy reason follows from the budget just derived.

options.text: It would overheat, and it would wear out its cells faster than they could be repaired or replaced.
options.why: Neither heat nor wear is raised about brains here; heat appears only in the comparison with packed transistors.

options.text: It would respond more slowly, and it would be unable to distinguish one input from another at all.
options.why: Speed is not the argument, and the information point is about which cells are silent rather than about total confusion.

options.text: It would need far more connections, and the wiring alone would take up more space than a skull could hold.
options.why: Wiring cost is raised in a different place, as one side of a balance, rather than as a reason against dense activity.

items.stem: Besides sparse firing, where else does the chapter find the energy budget shaping how a brain is built?

options.text: In myelin, which cuts both the delay and the ion traffic, and in the balance between the cells that compute and the fibers that connect them.
options.why: Correct. Wiring costs energy too, and a brain has to buy both computing and connecting out of one budget.

options.text: In the thickness of the skull and the volume of blood supplied to the brain, both of which scale with the brain's demand.
options.why: Neither is discussed in this chapter, and the examples given are about the nervous tissue itself.

options.text: In the number of neurons a species can grow, which is set directly by how much food that species can find.
options.why: Neuron number features in §3.3.7's discussion of scale, but it is not offered here as a design response to the budget.

options.text: In the length of the refractory period, which evolved to keep firing rates within what the budget can pay for.
options.why: The refractory period is explained mechanically in §3.3.3 rather than as an adaptation to the energy budget.

items.stem: Which phrase does the chapter use for energy considered as one of the forces determining what a nervous system can look like?

options.text: a metabolic constraint
options.why: Correct. The move from "brains are expensive" to "the expense explains features of how brains are built" is the section's payoff.

options.text: the coordination problem
options.why: That is the difficulty specialization creates in a multicellular body, from the computational section of the chapter.

options.text: multiple realizability
options.why: That is the claim that one function can run in different physical materials, which the chapter treats separately.

options.text: the sense to decide to act loop
options.why: That is the sequence an animal has to complete quickly, which is a problem rather than a limit on solutions.

items.stem: Opening its account of what the brain's energy cost explains, the chapter draws a distinction about that cost. What is it?

options.text: If the cost were merely large it would be a fact about brains; what makes it interesting is that it is also a design pressure.
options.why: Correct. Everything after that sentence is an instance of the pressure showing up in how brains are built and used.

options.text: If the cost were merely large it would be a problem for the animal; what makes it manageable is that the brain can reduce it at will.
options.why: No mechanism for reducing the cost on demand is described, and the section is about standing constraints rather than adjustments.

options.text: If the cost were merely large it would still be about affordable; what makes it a problem is that it rises steeply with brain size.
options.why: A steep scaling law of that kind is not what the section argues, and §3.3.7 says the per-neuron cost is ordinary.

options.text: If the cost were merely large it would be worth measuring; what makes it worth explaining is that nobody has measured it directly.
options.why: The measurement difficulty is noted in §3.3.6, but it is not the distinction this section opens with.

items.stem: How does the brain's share of the body's oxygen use change across a human life?

options.text: In the middle of the first decade of childhood, while the brain is still being built, the share reaches as much as half.
options.why: Correct. A growing child is, metabolically speaking, mostly a brain with a body attached.

options.text: It rises steadily from birth to old age, since an aging brain has to work harder to do the same tasks.
options.why: No trend of this kind is described, and the peak the chapter names is in early childhood.

options.text: Its share stays at about twenty percent throughout, since the brain grows in proportion to the rest of the body.
options.why: The chapter is explicit that the share is not evenly distributed across a life.

options.text: It is highest in adolescence, when the brain's connections are being pruned most rapidly.
options.why: The peak is given as the middle of the first decade, and pruning is not discussed in this chapter.

items.stem: Where does the ATP spent on an action potential actually go?

options.text: Into hauling back across the membrane, one molecule at a time, every ion that crossed it during the event.
options.why: Correct. Signaling runs gradients down for free and the restoration is what costs, which is why cleanup dominates the bill.

options.text: Into forcing the sodium channels open at the start of the event, which is the step that requires the most energy.
options.why: The channels open in response to voltage, and sodium enters down its gradient rather than being pushed.

options.text: Into propagating the spike along the axon, since each regeneration requires a fresh supply delivered to that point.
options.why: Regeneration also works by letting ions run downhill; the cost arrives afterward, when they are pumped back.

options.text: Into manufacturing the myelin that insulates the axon, which is renewed after each spike passes along it.
options.why: Myelin is not consumed by a passing spike, and its role is to reduce ion traffic rather than to be replaced.

items.stem: Why does the chapter hedge the brain's energy figures the way it does?

options.text: Because a working brain cannot easily be metered, so the standard figures come from an accounting that priced each step of signaling and added it up.
options.why: Correct. The figures are modeled at an assumed average firing rate rather than measured directly, which is worth knowing before quoting them.

options.text: Because the figures vary so much between individuals that no single number could apply to more than one person.
options.why: Individual variation is not what the hedge is about, and the chapter quotes single figures freely once it has explained their basis.

options.text: Because the measurements were made decades ago with equipment that would not meet current standards.
options.why: Nothing about the age of the measurements is raised, and the accounting is presented as careful rather than outdated.

options.text: Because researchers disagree about whether the brain's energy use should be measured in oxygen or in ATP.
options.why: Both units appear in the chapter without any dispute between them being reported.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what is wrong with the claim that we use only ten percent of our brains, and state the narrower fact that the myth has mangled.
items.answer: The claim asserts that most of the brain sits idle, a reserve of unused capacity waiting to be unlocked, and nothing supports that: every region does something, damage almost anywhere produces some deficit, and imaging finds activity throughout. What is true is narrower and considerably stranger. At any given instant only a small share of neurons are firing hard — on the order of one in a few hundred, which is what the energy budget affords — and which small share it is changes from moment to moment. So over any stretch of time the whole brain is in use; it is simply never all in use at once.
rubric: States what the claim actually asserts: idle capacity held in reserve.
Gives at least two grounds for rejecting it — regional function, deficits from damage, or imaging.
States the true fact: only a small share is strongly active at any instant.
Adds that the active share changes moment to moment, so the whole brain is used over time.

items.stem: The human brain uses a much larger share of the body's energy than other mammals' brains do. In a short paragraph, explain what kind of outlier that makes us, and how Module 2's warning applies.
items.answer: The cost of running a single human neuron is not remarkable — about the same as a primate neuron. What is unusual is how many of them there are, so the cost is large because the brain is large, on an ordinary primate body plan, rather than because human neurons are special. Module 2's warning applies because a figure like twenty percent invites reading as an achievement, as evidence that we are the animal that invested most in thinking. It is better read as a constraint: a brain that expensive has to be fed every day, which limits what else an animal can be and what it must eat. Every lineage that did not build a big brain was not failing to; it was solving its own problems at a price it could afford.
rubric: States that the per-neuron cost is ordinary and that the number of neurons is what differs.
Explains that the brain is expensive because it is large rather than because its cells are special.
Names the misreading — a share read as an achievement.
Gives the constraint reading, including that other lineages were not failing at anything.

items.stem: The chapter says the cost of computing with neurons is dominated by cleanup rather than by computing. In a few sentences, explain what that means and give the finding about resting cells that follows from it.
items.answer: A spike is produced by letting ions run down gradients that were built at a cost, so the signal itself is the spending of stored energy. Every ion that crossed then has to be hauled back across the membrane afterward, one ATP at a time, by the sodium-potassium pump and related systems. That restoration, rather than any act of computing, is where most of the money goes. The finding that follows is that a substantial slice of the brain's budget is spent by neurons doing nothing at all except staying ready: within the signaling share, simply holding the resting potential accounts for about an eighth.
rubric: States that a spike spends gradients that were built at a cost.
Identifies restoring those gradients, at one ATP per pump cycle, as the dominant expense.
States that cells doing nothing still account for a substantial share of the budget.
Cites the roughly one-eighth figure for holding the resting potential within the signaling share.

items.stem: The lecture names two collapsed versions of the Attwell and Laughlin findings and rules both out. Which two?

options.text: "Three-quarters of the brain's energy goes to the pump" and "seventy percent of brain ATP goes to the pump" — both merge two figures with different denominators.
options.why: Correct. Three-quarters of gray-matter energy goes to signaling rather than housekeeping, and almost all of that signaling cost goes on the pump.

options.text: "Three-quarters of the brain's energy goes to signaling" and "half of the signaling cost goes to action potentials" — both overstate their shares.
options.why: The second is a figure the lecture gives approvingly. The first is not: its denominator is gray-matter energy rather than the brain's energy.

options.text: "The brain uses twenty percent of the body's oxygen" and "the brain is twenty watts" — both state a share as though it were a quantity.
options.why: Those two are described as one measurement stated two ways rather than as an error.

options.text: "Neurons are expensive" and "the brain is cheap" — both leave out what the cost is being measured against.
options.why: That tension is resolved in the final lecture rather than being listed as a false collapse.

items.stem: The lecture gives three ranges for the brain's share of the daily energy budget and says it is doing so deliberately. What is the alternative it is refusing?

options.text: A superlative — "more than any other mammal" — which the comparative data do not support.
options.why: Correct. Humans 20–25%, other primates 8–10%, non-primate mammals 3–5%; the ranges are what the evidence carries.

options.text: A single average across mammals, which would obscure how much the figure varies from one group to another.
options.why: An average is not what the lecture rejects; it rejects a ranking claim about humans.

options.text: A figure for the developing brain, which would be higher and so would overstate the adult case.
options.why: The childhood figure is given separately and openly rather than avoided.

options.text: A comparison with artificial systems, which the lecture holds back until the very end.
options.why: That comparison is deferred but is not the alternative being refused here.

items.stem: The lecture calls the derivation of sparse firing "the nice move." What makes it nice?

options.text: The same accounting that gave the cost of a single spike is run in reverse, so what the budget permits falls out of what a spike costs.
options.why: Correct. Given what the brain costs to run and what a spike costs, the sustainable average is a fraction of a spike per neuron per second.

options.text: The figure was arrived at by imaging rather than by calculation, so it confirms the budget from an independent direction.
options.why: Imaging is cited to show activity throughout the brain rather than to establish the sparse figure.

options.text: The derivation applies equally to artificial networks, which is why sparse activity is used in machine learning too.
options.why: No claim about artificial networks' activity levels is made in this module.

options.text: The derivation needs no numbers at all, since sparseness follows from the structure of the argument alone.
options.why: The derivation is explicitly quantitative and turns on the per-spike cost and the whole-brain budget.

items.stem: The lecture gives two independent reasons a brain with most neurons firing most of the time would not be better. Why does it stress that they are independent?

options.text: Because each would stand without the other: such a brain would code information less effectively, and it also could not be fed.
options.why: Correct. The information reason is handed forward to Module 4, and the energy reason follows from the budget just derived.

options.text: Because one is established and the other is speculative, so a student should weight them differently.
options.why: Both are given as reasons rather than one being flagged as speculative.

options.text: Because the two reasons apply to different species, so which one bites depends on whose brain is in question.
options.why: No species-dependence is attached to either reason.

options.text: Because the two reasons conflict, so establishing either one would undermine the case for the other.
options.why: They are complementary rather than in tension, which is why the lecture can offer both at once.

items.stem: The lecture says two of Attwell and Laughlin's findings "get collapsed constantly and the collapsed version is false." State both findings correctly, and explain what the collapse gets wrong.
items.answer: The first finding is that about three-quarters of the energy in gray matter goes to signaling rather than to housekeeping such as building proteins and maintaining the cell. The second is that almost all of that signaling cost goes on the sodium-potassium pump. The collapse merges them into a single claim about the brain's total energy — that three-quarters, or seventy percent, of the brain's ATP goes to the pump. What it gets wrong is the denominator: the pump's share is a share of the signaling portion, not of the whole budget, so combining the two figures produces a number that neither finding supports.
rubric: States the first finding with its denominator: signaling versus housekeeping in gray matter.
States the second finding as a share of the signaling cost specifically.
Identifies the collapse as a single claim about the brain's total energy going to the pump.
Explains that the error is one of denominator rather than of arithmetic.

pools.title: Silicon, and What a Neuron Cannot Do Alone
pools.covers: reading §3.3.9, §3.3.10, the unnumbered Close · lecture 3.3 slides the_same_function_in_silicon, expensive_and_cheap

items.stem: Set a neuron and a transistor side by side as physical implementations. What does the chapter say we find?

options.text: Protein pores moving salt against gradients in warm water and paying for every ion, against charge on a conductor and a switch thrown by a field, with no chemistry at all.
options.why: Correct. The equation described both about equally well, and at the level of what they are made of the resemblance vanishes completely.

options.text: Two arrangements that turn out to work by the same physical principle, differing only in the scale at which each operates.
options.why: The chapter's claim is the opposite: the two are not doing the same kind of physical thing at all.

options.text: Two arrangements that differ in speed but are otherwise built the same way, since both rely on moving charge through a medium.
options.why: A neuron moves ions bodily rather than moving charge along a conductor, which is exactly the difference the section presses.

options.text: Two arrangements whose physical differences turn out to make no difference to what either one can compute.
options.why: §3.3.9's whole argument is that implementation sets terms the levels above have to respect.

items.stem: Where does the chapter locate the place the comparison between minds and machines actually strains?

options.text: At the implementational level, since the two are extremely similar algorithmically and could hardly be more different in what they are made of.
options.why: Correct. The opening of the chapter promised this location in advance, and §3.3.9 is where it is finally worked out.

options.text: At the computational level, since a brain and a machine were built to solve entirely different problems in the first place.
options.why: The chapter draws no such divergence of problems, and the artificial unit was copied from the biological one precisely to solve the same one.

options.text: At the algorithmic level, since the linear model turns out to describe artificial units well and biological ones badly.
options.why: The chapter says the same short equation served both, which is what makes the algorithmic level the point of agreement.

options.text: Nowhere in particular, since the comparison is an analogy and analogies are not the kind of thing that can strain.
options.why: The chapter treats the comparison as substantive and says explicitly where it breaks down.

items.stem: An action potential takes about a millisecond and a transistor switches in a small fraction of a billionth of a second. Why does the chapter say no amount of engineering care would close that gap?

options.text: Because the two are not doing the same kind of physical thing: a neuron moves ions bodily across a membrane, which is chemistry and takes time.
options.why: Correct. A transistor moves charge through a conductor, which does not, so the difference is in the kind of process rather than its refinement.

options.text: Because a biological system cannot be optimized by design, so building a part that takes less time is not an option evolution has open to it.
options.why: The argument is about physics rather than about who is doing the optimizing, and it would apply to a designed neuron too.

options.text: Because the gap is a measurement artifact, and a spike measured the same way a transistor is measured would be much faster.
options.why: No measurement problem is raised, and the two figures are treated as comparable.

options.text: Because neurons are limited by their refractory period, which sets a floor no cell can go below however it is built.
options.why: The refractory period limits how often a cell can fire rather than how long one event takes, and the chapter's reason here is chemical.

items.stem: Module 1 noted that brains are built from slow components and drew a consequence. What was it, and what does this module add?

options.text: A system answering in a few hundred milliseconds with parts that take a millisecond each must do many things at once; this module adds the reason the parts are slow.
options.why: Correct. The consequence was already available in Module 1, and the implementational level is what supplies its explanation.

options.text: That brains must therefore be larger than machines doing similar work; this module adds the energy figures that show how much larger.
options.why: Size is not the consequence Module 1 drew, and the added material here is about why a chemical process takes time.

options.text: That brains cannot run long sequences at all; this module adds that the limit is absolute rather than a matter of degree.
options.why: The claim is about what a system has to do instead rather than an absolute prohibition, and no such absolute is asserted.

options.text: That machines will eventually outperform brains at every task; this module adds the speed comparison that makes the point concrete.
options.why: No such prediction is made anywhere, and the chapter is careful that the two are not doing the same job.

items.stem: What does the chapter claim about the standing of the implementational level relative to the levels above it?

options.text: Implementation is not merely where a function gets realized with everything settled above it; it sets terms the levels above have to respect.
options.why: Correct. Neurons being slow and expensive is why brains are massively parallel and mostly quiet, so sparse coding is a consequence rather than a preference.

options.text: Implementation determines the function completely, so any two systems built differently must compute different things.
options.why: That would deny multiple realizability, which the chapter has just used the neuron and the artificial unit to illustrate.

options.text: Implementation is irrelevant to the levels above it, which is why the same equation could describe a cell and a transistor.
options.why: The chapter argues against exactly this, and calls the point a reason not to treat implementation as a footnote.

options.text: Implementation can be chosen freely once the algorithm is fixed, since any substrate can realize any procedure equally well.
options.why: Equal suitability is what the section denies: each substrate forces a different architecture above it.

items.stem: What architecture does each substrate force on the levels above it?

options.text: Slow, expensive neurons force brains that are massively parallel and mostly quiet; fast, cheap transistors allow long sequences run very quickly.
options.why: Correct. Two implementations of a similar function, two sets of constraints, and two quite different architectures built on top of them.

options.text: Slow neurons force brains to run long sequences carefully; fast transistors allow machines to do many things at once.
options.why: The two consequences have been swapped: parallelism is the brain's answer to slow parts, and sequences are the machine's advantage.

options.text: Both substrates force the same architecture, since the function being implemented is what determines how a system is organized.
options.why: The section exists to deny this, and it is the reason it calls the levels separable but not independent.

options.text: Neither substrate forces any architecture, since organization is settled at the algorithmic level before implementation begins.
options.why: That is the picture of implementation as a footnote which §3.3.9 explicitly rejects.

items.stem: What does the chapter say limits how many transistors can usefully be packed together?

options.text: The heat produced has to be carried away, and the power has to come from somewhere outside the machine.
options.why: Correct. The constraints on the two substrates are different in kind rather than one being simply better than the other.

options.text: The signal weakens as it passes through more of them, so long chains become unreliable beyond a certain length.
options.why: Signal degradation over a chain is not raised, and digital signals are described as restorable rather than degrading.

options.text: The switching time rises as more are added, so the speed advantage over a neuron shrinks with scale.
options.why: No such scaling penalty on switching time is described in the chapter.

options.text: The cost of manufacturing rises steeply, which is the reason machines are not built with more of them.
options.why: Manufacturing cost is not among the constraints the chapter names.

items.stem: Which Module 1 claim does the chapter say the neuron-and-transistor comparison illustrates?

options.text: That the levels are separable but not independent.
options.why: Correct. The same function runs in two substrates, and the substrates nonetheless force different architectures above them.

options.text: That mental states are simply identical to brain states.
options.why: An identity claim of this kind would rule out multiple realizability, which the section is illustrating rather than denying.

options.text: That the mind can be studied without reference to the brain.
options.why: The section argues the reverse: implementation sets terms the algorithmic level has to respect.

options.text: That two systems computing one function are built alike.
options.why: The whole comparison depends on two very different builds computing similar functions.

items.stem: Eighty-six billion neurons run a human mind on about twenty watts, while artificial systems doing far narrower things consume orders of magnitude more. What caution does the chapter attach?

options.text: That the comparison should not be pushed too hard, since the two are not doing the same job and the accounting is not really commensurable.
options.why: Correct. The figures are used to reframe the brain's budget rather than to award a verdict on efficiency.

options.text: That the figure for artificial systems is not reliably known, so a system doing narrow work cannot be compared with one doing much broader work.
options.why: The chapter uses the comparison rather than dismissing it; what it declines is treating the numbers as a like-for-like score.

options.text: That the brain's twenty watts covers only signaling, so the true comparison would be considerably less favorable.
options.why: No such partial accounting is suggested, and the twenty watts is given as the whole organ's consumption.

options.text: That artificial systems will become more efficient over time, so the gap should be expected to close.
options.why: No prediction about future efficiency appears anywhere in the chapter.

items.stem: The chapter spends four subsections calling neurons expensive and then calls the brain cheap. How does it resolve that?

options.text: The two verdicts use different denominators: expensive against the animal's whole budget, and cheap against the work done.
options.why: Correct. A large share of a small budget, and a small price for what it delivers — which is a resolution rather than a hedge.

options.text: The earlier sections call individual neurons expensive and the later one calls the whole brain cheap, and the two scales do not compare.
options.why: Both verdicts are about the same organ, and the chapter's resolution is about what each is measured against.

options.text: The earlier sections describe the developing brain and the later one the adult brain, whose costs are much lower.
options.why: The developmental figure is higher rather than lower, and it is not what the reconciliation turns on.

options.text: The earlier verdict has been superseded, since the comparison with artificial systems shows the brain is not costly after all.
options.why: Neither verdict is withdrawn; the chapter says both are right at once.

items.stem: Answering the first of the chapter's two opening questions, where does the complexity of a cell come from?

options.text: It accumulated rather than being assembled in one step: molecules copied imperfectly, membranes enclosed them, and DNA, RNA and proteins each took on different work.
options.why: Correct. The accumulation reading is what keeps the narrative from being a story of steps upward toward something.

options.text: It arrived with the eukaryotic cell, which acquired in a single event most of the machinery a modern cell has.
options.why: Endosymbiosis is one event in a much longer sequence, and a great deal was already in place before it.

options.text: It appeared once oxygen made complexity affordable, and very little of consequence existed before that point.
options.why: Oxygen answers the second question rather than the first, and LUCA already had a complex metabolism.

options.text: It cannot be answered, since no evidence from that period survives in any form that could be examined today.
options.why: The chapter gives an answer and hedges particular claims within it rather than declining the question.

items.stem: The chapter says the question of why the complexity was worth the effort has two halves. What are they?

options.text: Oxygen answered one, by making expensive cells affordable; the other is an accounting, since what the outlay buys is acting before something else does.
options.why: Correct. The bill is enormous and it has been worth paying every time it has come due, which is the chapter's summary verdict.

options.text: One half concerns single cells and the other concerns multicellular bodies, and the two were answered before the chapter reached the neuron at all.
options.why: That is not how the chapter divides the question, and both halves of its answer are about cost and what cost buys.

options.text: One half is evolutionary and the other is developmental, since a brain has to be built anew in every individual.
options.why: Development is barely touched in this chapter and is not one of the two halves named at its close.

options.text: One half has been answered and the other remains open, since nobody knows what neurons are ultimately for.
options.why: Both halves are answered, and §3.1 gave the computational answer to what neurons are for.

items.stem: Which sentence states the chapter's thesis most completely?

options.text: Neurons exist because life became rich enough to run them, persist because what they do is worth what they cost, and are built as they are because life still cannot afford to run them carelessly.
options.why: Correct. All three clauses are energy claims, which is why the chapter says the whole thing is one continuous story.

options.text: Neurons evolved because animals move, persist because movement is useful, and are built as they are because movement demands speed.
options.why: Movement is part of the computational answer, but the chapter's thesis is stated in terms of cost throughout.

options.text: Neurons exist because chemistry was too slow, persist because nothing better has evolved, and are built as they are by historical accident.
options.why: "Nothing better has evolved" and "historical accident" are both weaker and different from the claims the chapter makes.

options.text: Neurons exist because multicellularity created a coordination problem, and everything else about them follows from that problem alone.
options.why: The coordination problem is one step in §3.1 rather than the whole thesis, and the energy arc is what ties the chapter together.

items.stem: The chapter says it has built a neuron three times over. Which three?

options.text: Once as a solution to a problem, once as a function, and once as a physical machine with a running cost.
options.why: Correct. It is the Marr structure stated as a result rather than as a plan, matching what the opening promised.

options.text: Once as a cell, once as a circuit, and once as a whole nervous system capable of producing behavior.
options.why: Circuits and nervous systems are Module 4's subject, and the chapter stays on the single cell throughout.

options.text: Once in words, once as an equation, and once as a drawing, which are three ways of stating the same account.
options.why: Two models are built, not three, and they sit at different levels rather than being three formats of one description.

options.text: Once in an animal, once in a bacterium, and once in an artificial network, which are three realizations of one design.
options.why: Bacteria have no neurons, and the three are levels of description rather than three systems.

items.stem: The Close says the chapter's three answers do not resemble one another in the slightest. Why is that not a problem?

options.text: Because they are answers to three different questions rather than competing answers to one.
options.why: Correct. It is a full turn of the wheel Module 1 promised, and the wheel now turns once per module for the rest of the course.

options.text: Because two of the three answers will eventually be shown to reduce to the third once the biology is fully understood.
options.why: No such reduction is anticipated, and §3.3.4 argues that neither of the chapter's two models is a version of the other.

options.text: Because only one of the three is a scientific claim, and the other two are ways of organizing the material for teaching.
options.why: All three are treated as genuine explanations, each with its own discipline attached to it.

options.text: Because the disagreement between them is a sign that the field has not yet settled on a single account of the neuron.
options.why: The chapter presents the difference as what having levels is for rather than as unfinished business.

items.stem: Give a neuron an excitatory input from one smell and an inhibitory input from another, and wire its output to something that steers. What does the Close say happens?

options.text: The arithmetic is well within a single cell: its rate climbs with the first smell and falls with the second, and the animal moves toward one and away from the other.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is careful here, because the obvious version of its closing limitation — that one cell cannot do this — is false.
