options.text: The cell cannot produce that behavior, since weighing one input against another requires a circuit rather than a single neuron.
options.why: This is exactly the claim the Close corrects. Summing signed inputs already is weighing, as §3.2.7 established.

options.text: The cell produces the behavior only if a modulatory signal has already set its sensitivity to the first smell appropriately.
options.why: Modulation changes what a circuit does with the same inputs, but nothing in this example depends on it.

options.text: The cell produces approach in one animal and avoidance in another, depending on which transmitter each species uses.
options.why: The chapter's variation is in what the cell is wired to rather than in which transmitter is involved.

items.stem: If a single neuron can do approach-versus-avoid arithmetic, what is the limitation the Close actually states?

options.text: None of the meaning is in the cell: a rate is only a rate, and it becomes approach because of what the cell happens to be wired to.
options.why: Correct. Value, goals and states that outlast their causes are properties an arrangement has rather than properties a neuron has.

options.text: The cell can perform the arithmetic only once, since its refractory period then prevents it from responding again for a short interval afterward.
options.why: The refractory period lasts a fraction of a second and has nothing to do with the limitation being drawn.

options.text: The cell's approach-and-avoid arithmetic is too imprecise to rely on, so a circuit is needed to average across many cells.
options.why: No claim about imprecision or averaging is made, and the arithmetic is described as well within a single cell.

options.text: The cell cannot hold a state that outlasts its inputs, which is the only thing missing from the single-cell account.
options.why: States that outlast their causes are indeed named, but they are named alongside value and goals as properties of an arrangement.

items.stem: How does the Close connect its point about meaning to Module 1's Braitenberg vehicles lab?

options.text: In the lab the behavior changed completely depending on how the wires crossed while the parts stayed the same, which is the same lesson about arrangement.
options.why: Correct. The very same cell wired to the opposite muscles would produce avoidance rather than approach.

options.text: In the lab the vehicles' behavior changed when their sensors were made more sensitive, which shows that components matter most.
options.why: Sensitivity is not what the Close recalls from the lab, and the point being made is about wiring rather than components.

options.text: In the lab each vehicle had only one possible behavior, which is a lesson about how a simple system's response is fixed by its parts.
options.why: The lab's lesson is the opposite: the same parts produced quite different behavior depending on the arrangement.

options.text: In the lab the vehicles were driven by chemical rather than neural signals, which shows the substrate does not matter.
options.why: The substrate point belongs to §3.3.9, and the vehicles are recalled here for the wiring lesson instead.

items.stem: What does the Close say about value, goals, and states that outlast their causes?

options.text: They are properties an arrangement has rather than properties a neuron has, and none of them comes from building a better neuron.
options.why: Correct. That is what sets up Module 4, which begins from exactly these limitations of a single cell.

options.text: They are properties of the most complex neurons, which is why simple animals show them and simple circuits do not.
options.why: The chapter locates them in arrangements rather than in any cell, however complex.

options.text: They emerge once a nervous system is large enough, and no smaller system has any of the three.
options.why: Size as such is not the criterion; the claim is about organization rather than about a threshold number of cells.

options.text: They are properties of behavior rather than of any physical structure at all, so no account given in terms of cells will ever manage to reach them.
options.why: The chapter locates them in arrangements of cells, which is a physical account rather than a refusal of one.

items.stem: How does the Close bookend the chapter's energy thread?

options.text: Neurons became affordable only after oxygen made life rich enough to pay for them, and the brain still spends a fifth of the resting budget staying ready and cleaning up.
options.why: Correct. The opening story and the closing story really are one story, which is what the chapter promised at the outset.

options.text: Neurons were expensive when they first evolved but have become far cheaper since, as myelin and sparse coding reduced the bill.
options.why: Myelin and sparse coding are responses to a cost that remains large rather than evidence that it has fallen.

options.text: Neurons were cheap when they first evolved and became expensive only in large-brained animals like ourselves.
options.why: The chapter treats neurons as expensive from the beginning, which is why the oxygen surplus was needed to afford them.

options.text: Neurons cost about what any other cell costs, and the brain's large share simply reflects how many cells it holds.
options.why: The per-neuron point in §3.3.7 is a comparison between primates rather than a claim that neurons cost what other cells cost.

items.stem: Restating the artificial parallel at the close, where does the chapter say the comparison genuinely strains?

options.text: Not at the algorithm but at the substrate.
options.why: Correct. Artificial networks are named after this cell and modeled on it, and the divergence is in what the two are made of.

options.text: Not at the substrate but at the algorithm.
options.why: The same short equation served both, which is what makes the algorithmic level the point of agreement rather than of strain.

options.text: At the whole system rather than the single unit.
options.why: Scale is not where the chapter locates the strain, and §3.3.9 is explicit that it is the implementational level.

options.text: Nowhere, since the artificial unit is an exact copy.
options.why: The chapter calls the artificial unit a caricature and devotes a whole subsection to where the resemblance ends.

items.stem: What does the chapter say it adds to Module 1's treatment of multiple realizability?

options.text: Module 1 argued for it with thought experiments; here it is in a single cell, with both realizations built and running.
options.why: Correct. Moving from an imagined case to two working ones is what lets the section then locate exactly where they diverge.

options.text: Module 1 argued for it from evidence; here the chapter shows that the evidence was misinterpreted.
options.why: Nothing is retracted, and the section extends Module 1's claim rather than correcting it.

options.text: Module 1 applied it to whole minds; here the chapter shows that it does not hold for anything smaller than a whole mind after all.
options.why: The section applies it to a single cell precisely to show that it does hold there.

options.text: Module 1 treated it as settled; here the chapter shows that it remains a live philosophical dispute.
options.why: The live dispute the chapter reports is about single-neuron complexity rather than about multiple realizability.

items.stem: The Close calls the chapter "a full turn of the wheel." What is the wheel, and what happens to it next?

options.text: Working one capacity at all three of Marr's levels, which Module 1 promised and which now turns once per module for the rest of the course.
options.why: Correct. The correspondence of section to level to lecture is what makes the rhythm something a reader can feel arriving.

options.text: The cycle by which a neuron fires and recovers, which recurs in every module because every module concerns neurons.
options.why: The firing cycle is a mechanism within one section rather than the structure of the course.

options.text: The alternation between biological and artificial systems, which the course takes up in turn from here on.
options.why: The natural-artificial comparison is a thread running through modules rather than the wheel the Close names.

options.text: The sequence from computational to algorithmic to implementational within a single lecture, repeated three times a week.
options.why: The wheel turns once per module rather than within a lecture, with one level per meeting.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what the chapter means by saying the implementational level "sets terms the levels above have to respect," using both substrates as evidence.
items.answer: The claim is that implementation is not merely where a function gets realized once everything important has been settled above it. Neurons are slow and expensive, so a system built from them cannot run a long sequence of steps and has to do many things at once instead, and it cannot have most of its cells active — which is why brains are massively parallel and mostly quiet, and why sparse coding is a consequence of a constraint rather than a design preference. Transistors are fast and individually cheap, so machines can run long sequences very quickly, but packing enough of them together produces heat that has to be carried away and power that has to come from outside. Two implementations of a similar function, two sets of constraints, and two quite different architectures: the levels are separable but not independent.
rubric: States the claim that implementation constrains rather than merely realizes.
Gives the neuron case: slow and expensive parts force parallelism and sparse activity.
Gives the transistor case: fast cheap parts allow long sequences but bring heat and external power.
Concludes with separable but not independent, or an equivalent statement that the architectures differ because the substrates do.

items.stem: The Close states carefully what a single neuron cannot do. In a short paragraph, say what a single cell can do, what it cannot, and why the distinction matters.
items.answer: A single cell can do the arithmetic. Give a neuron an excitatory input from one smell and an inhibitory input from another and its firing rate will climb with the first and fall with the second; wire that output to something that steers and the animal moves toward one and away from the other. What is not in the cell is any of the meaning. A rate is only a rate: it becomes approach because of what the cell happens to be wired to, and the very same cell wired to the opposite muscles would produce avoidance. The distinction matters because it locates the limitation correctly — value, goals and states that outlast their causes are properties an arrangement has, and none of them comes from building a better neuron.
rubric: States that the approach-versus-avoid arithmetic is within a single cell.
States that what the cell lacks is the meaning rather than the computation.
Explains that the same cell wired differently would produce the opposite behavior.
Concludes that value, goals and lasting states are properties of an arrangement.

items.stem: The chapter calls the brain both expensive and cheap. In a few sentences, explain how both can be right without contradiction.
items.answer: The two verdicts are measured against different things. Against the animal's whole budget, the brain is expensive: one organ taking about a fifth of everything the body spends at rest, which really does limit what else that animal can be and what it must eat. Against the work done, the brain is cheap: eighty-six billion neurons running an entire mind on about twenty watts, less than a dim light bulb, where artificial systems doing far narrower things consume orders of magnitude more. So the brain is a large share of a small budget and a small price for what it delivers, and the apparent conflict comes only from leaving the denominator unstated.
rubric: Identifies the two different denominators explicitly.
Gives the expensive verdict against the body's own budget, with the roughly one-fifth figure.
Gives the cheap verdict against the work done, with the twenty-watt figure.
States that the two do not conflict because they are measured against different things.

items.stem: The lecture says setting a neuron beside a transistor does something the earlier multiple-realizability claim did not. What does the comparison add?

options.text: It locates the divergence: extremely similar at the algorithmic level, and could hardly be more different at the implementational one.
options.why: Correct. That is where the comparison between minds and machines actually strains — not in what they compute, but in what they are made of.

options.text: It supplies the evidence for multiple realizability, which the previous lecture could only assert without support.
options.why: The previous lecture already had both realizations built and running; what the table adds is where they come apart.

options.text: It shows that multiple realizability fails at the implementational level, so the claim holds only for functional descriptions.
options.why: Multiple realizability is a claim about function across substrates, and the divergence in substrate is what it predicts.

options.text: It measures how similar the two systems are, so the strength of the analogy can be stated numerically.
options.why: No measure of similarity is offered, and the lecture keeps the energy comparison qualitative on both sides.

items.stem: The lecture calls one claim "the biggest idea in this lecture" and says it is no longer a slogan. Which claim?

options.text: That the implementational level sets terms the levels above have to respect, which is Module 1's separable-but-not-independent made concrete.
options.why: Correct. Neurons are slow and expensive, so brains are parallel and mostly quiet, and sparse coding is a consequence rather than a preference.

options.text: That the same function can run in two substrates, which Module 1 argued with thought experiments and this module has built twice.
options.why: Multiple realizability is the previous slide's material, and the lecture treats this claim as going beyond it.

options.text: That a more detailed model can be worse for a question, which is a fact about what models are for.
options.why: That claim belongs to the two-models slide earlier in this lecture.

options.text: That expensive and cheap are both right, because the two verdicts are measured against different things.
options.why: That reconciliation comes on the closing slide rather than here.

items.stem: The lecture names a tempting way to end the module and says it is false. What is the temptation, and why is it wrong?

options.text: Saying a single neuron is too simple to do anything interesting — wrong because the approach-versus-avoid arithmetic is well within a single cell.
options.why: Correct. Give it an excitatory input from one smell and an inhibitory input from another, and its rate climbs with one and falls with the other.

options.text: Saying a single neuron is the unit of thought — wrong because meaning is a property of an arrangement rather than of any cell.
options.why: The lecture does hold that meaning belongs to an arrangement, but the temptation it names is the opposite overstatement.

options.text: Saying the module has explained the mind — wrong because Modules 4 through 7 are still required to reach behavior.
options.why: Scope of the course is not the temptation being corrected on this slide.

options.text: Saying neurons are expensive — wrong because the closing comparison shows that the brain is cheap for the work it does.
options.why: Both verdicts are said to be right, so neither is offered as a temptation to resist.

items.stem: Reconciling expensive with cheap, the lecture gives the two things the brain is being measured against. What are they?

options.text: The animal's whole budget, where one organ takes a fifth of everything the body spends; and the work done, where twenty watts runs an entire mind.
options.why: Correct. A large share of a small budget, and a small price for what it delivers — two denominators rather than a hedge.

options.text: The brain's own resting cost, and its cost during demanding mental work, which differ by roughly the factor in question.
options.why: No split by mental effort is made anywhere in the module; the figures given are for the resting condition.

options.text: The developing brain and the adult brain, whose shares differ enough to make both descriptions true at different ages.
options.why: The childhood figure is given separately and is not what the reconciliation turns on.

options.text: Other primates and non-primate mammals, against which the human brain looks expensive and cheap respectively.
options.why: Both cross-species comparisons make the human brain look expensive, so neither supplies the cheap verdict.

items.stem: The lecture's handoff to Module 4 states a limitation of a single neuron very carefully. In a short paragraph, give the limitation as the lecture gives it, and say what it deliberately avoids claiming.
items.answer: What it avoids claiming is that a single neuron is too simple to do anything interesting. That is false: give a neuron an excitatory input from one smell and an inhibitory input from another, its rate climbs with the first and falls with the second, and wiring that output to something that steers moves the animal toward one and away from the other. The arithmetic is well within a single cell. The limitation is about meaning rather than about computation. A rate is only a rate; it becomes approach because of what the cell happens to be wired to, and the very same cell wired to the opposite muscles would produce avoidance. So value, goals and states that outlast their causes are properties an arrangement has rather than properties a neuron has, and none of them comes from building a better neuron.
rubric: States that the arithmetic, including approach versus avoid, is within a single cell.
Identifies the limitation as one about meaning rather than about computation.
Explains that the same cell wired differently would produce the opposite behavior.
Concludes that value, goals and lasting states belong to an arrangement.
